name: GHC Haskell lightweight threads (skynet 1M-spawn benchmark vs pthread/std::thread)
baseline: pthread_create and std::thread (C/C++ OS threads, 8 kB pthread stacks) running the skynet recursive spawn-and-sum benchmark
workload: skynet microbenchmark: a root unit spawns 10 children, each spawns 10 more, down to 1,000,000 leaves that return their ordinal; sums flow back up; time per spawned unit (GHC thread versus OS thread).
claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per unit (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us, std::thread 52-73 us and std::async 106-122 us per thread (average over 10,000, because 1,000,000 OS threads exhausted resources): about 870x-1,460x lower per-unit cost (derived from page data; sizes differ). The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++, 16C/32T, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, so C++ user-space fibers match the Haskell row.
compiler_and_flags: C++ side (page): gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (-O3), pthreads created with 8 kB stacks, std::thread with the system default 1-2 MB stacks, glibc malloc or tcmalloc (-ltcmalloc). Haskell side (page): stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1 only. The skynet repo's haskell/skynet.cabal sets ghc-options -O2 -threaded -rtsopts and its README runs 'stack exec skynet +RTS -N', but the Boost page does not say which Haskell variant or RTS options it used.
hardware: dual Intel Xeon E5-2620 v4 2.2 GHz, 16C/32T, 64 GB RAM, Linux x86_64
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (github.com/ghc/ghc is a read-only mirror of gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc, which was not opened)
tradeoffs: GHC threads are heap-allocated stack chunks scheduled by the GHC runtime (garbage-collected, optional -threaded and -N). Foreign calls and unsafe FFI interact with the scheduler differently from C.
caveats: Variant mismatch (main finding): atemerev/skynet haskell/src/Main.hs runs five implementations under criterion (Parallel, MVar, Chan, TBQueue, Unagi); its own comments give, on an i7-4930K with +RTS -N6, Parallel 0.017 s and MVar 1.7 s per 1,000,000-leaf run. The Boost row (0.05-0.06 us x 1,000,000 = 50-60 ms) matches the Parallel variant's order of magnitude, not the forkIO+MVar one (inference; the page does not name the variant). Parallel.hs computes a pure tree sum with parMap rpar: it creates sparks (work-stealing pool entries the parent may evaluate itself), no forkIO threads and no channel messages, whereas the C++ port (boostorg/fiber performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp) creates about 11,110 detached pthreads for its 10,000 leaves and passes every value through a mutex/condition-variable buffered_channel. So the comparison is sparks (or green threads) against kernel threads, not the same work, and the win is the runtime's, not Haskell codegen's. Scale differs (1,000,000 units for Haskell, 10,000 for pthread/std::thread). The skynet README's own Haskell (GHC 7.10.3) results range from 41-44 ms (i7-4771, Ubuntu) to 2820-6181 ms (Windows, OS X), consistent with different variants being run. Toolchains date from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). The baseline is OS threads, not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency; Boost.Fiber on the same page reaches 0.05-0.09 us. No Haskell benchmark code lives in boostorg/fiber (performance/ holds only fiber/ and thread/). The repo_url is the GHC mirror (gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc is upstream); the skynet sources are MIT, last commit 2023-11-10. GHC's licence file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).
found_via: WebSearch: 'lightweight threads comparison goroutines vs pthreads creation time Go faster than C pthreads paper evaluation' surfaced the Boost.Fiber performance page; the Haskell row is on the same page.
why_faster: Implied by the page rather than argued: GHC threads are runtime-scheduled green threads, pthreads are OS threads. No explicit mechanism is given.

verification.tier_reason: boostorg/fiber doc/performance.qbk (Boost.Fiber author, independent of GHC) shows Haskell 0.05-0.06 us per unit at 1,000,000 units against pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us at 10,000 threads on a stated Xeon E5-2620 v4 with gcc-6.3.1 release/speed, but the Haskell build flags, RTS options and which of the five skynet Haskell variants ran are unstated, the gain is ~870-1,460x (cap at C for >50x with unstated flags), and the two sides run at different sizes and very likely different algorithms. Not A (no Haskell flags), not B (unequal workloads, unknown variant).
verification.notes: Downgrade B to C: numbers are on the Boost.Fiber page, but the Haskell row very likely measured the parMap/rpar spark variant (no threads, no channels) against one detached pthread per unit, at different sizes (1M vs 10k) and with Haskell flags unstated. Shortcomings to record: different algorithm (sparks vs kernel threads), unequal workload sizes, Haskell variant/flags/RTS options unstated, 2017 toolchains, C++ fibers on the same page match Haskell so no language-level win. baseline_stdlib set to libstdc++ (gcc-6.3.1 on Linux runs std::thread/std::async from libstdc++).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Haskell (stack-1.4.0/ghc-8.0.1): 0.05-0.06 us per thread (average over 1,000,000) versus pthread 54-73 us and std::thread 52-73 us per thread (average over 10,000): about 900x-1,460x lower cost per unit (derived from page data).
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: C++ side: gcc-6.3.1, Boost.Build variant=release optimization=speed (pthreads created with 8 kB stacks); Haskell side: stack-1.4.0 / ghc-8.0.1, flags not stated
corrected_fields.caveats: The baseline is OS threads (pthread_create, std::thread), not the idiomatic C++ answer for massive concurrency. The same page shows Boost.Fiber (C++ user-space fibers, work stealing, tcmalloc) at 0.05-0.09 us per fiber, which matches or beats Go and Erlang, so this is not a claim that the language beats well-tuned C++. Scale differs: the Go/Haskell/Erlang rows average over 1,000,000 spawned units while the pthread/std::thread rows average over only 10,000 threads because the 1,000,000-thread run exhausted resources (so the ratio compares per-unit cost at different sizes). The numbers come from the Boost.Fiber author's own documentation, ported skynet code for the C++ side (performance/thread/skynet_pthread.cpp: detached pthreads plus a mutex and condition-variable buffered channel) versus the upstream Go source's unbuffered channels; toolchains are from 2017 (go1.8.1, ghc-8.0.1, erts-8.3, gcc-6.3.1). Go/Haskell/Erlang compile flags and runtime options (for example GHC +RTS -N) are not stated on the page. The per-language skynet sources are in https://github.com/atemerev/skynet (MIT, last commit 2023-11-10). Tier B, not A, because the workload sizes differ and the non-C++ flags are unstated; rerunning at an equal unit count would settle it. The repo_url is the GHC compiler mirror because the claim is about the compiler/runtime; the skynet Haskell source is haskell/ in atemerev/skynet. The license file is the Glasgow Haskell Compiler License (BSD-3-Clause text).

name: evio (Go epoll/kqueue event loop; Redis clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis 4.0.2 (C, single-threaded ae event loop on epoll) answering PING_INLINE; the same table also holds Go net/http, fasthttp and a Go net echo server, which are Go baselines and not counted here
workload: redis-benchmark -t ping_inline -q -c 50 -n 1000000 with pipeline depth 1, 8 and 16 against the real redis-server and against the evio example Redis clone (examples/redis-server/main.go), both started with GOMAXPROCS=1 on localhost.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, evio Redis clone vs real Redis 4.0.2 (benchmarks/out/redis{1,8,16}.txt, final redis-benchmark line): pipeline 1: 177,147.92 vs 176,991.14 (parity); pipeline 8: 1,285,347.00 vs 878,734.62 (about 1.46x, derived from page data); pipeline 16: 2,123,142.25 vs 879,507.50 (about 2.41x, derived from page data). The README itself only shows chart images and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go version not recorded (2017 snapshot); bench-redis.sh builds the clone with plain 'go build' and starts both servers with GOMAXPROCS=1. Real Redis is whatever 'redis-server' was on PATH (Redis 4.0.2 per the log, commit=00000000), started with only '--port 6392' (no config file); its build flags are not stated. Redis 4.0.2's own src/Makefile defaults to OPTIMIZATION?=-O2 with jemalloc, so a default build was -O2, not -O3.
hardware: EC2 c4.xlarge instance (CPU model not named in the repo), client and server on localhost over IPv4; run on 2017-11-04 per the log timestamps
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in replacement for Go net or net/http (the README says so). Handlers run inside the event-loop goroutines and must not block. Linux epoll and BSD/macOS kqueue only, with a net-package fallback elsewhere. Calling it from C++ means a separate Go process.
caveats: The two servers do different amounts of work: the evio example is a tiny Redis-protocol clone (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, DEL, FLUSHDB, QUIT, SHUTDOWN, WAKE) over a Go map with a mutex, parsed by redcon.ReadNextCommand (so evio's clone reuses tidwall/redcon's parser), with no persistence, expiry, replication, statistics or full command table; PING is a string switch that appends +PONG. At pipeline depth 1 both are client-bound and equal (177,147.92 vs 176,991.14). Real Redis stays at about 878k-880k requests per second at depth 8 and 16 while the clone keeps climbing; the repo gives no explanation, and the most plausible one is Redis's per-command dispatch path rather than the language or event loop (verifier inference). Only PING_INLINE was benchmarked. One run per cell, no variance, and the redis-benchmark client shares the 4-vCPU instance with the server. Redis 4.0.2 is from 2017; its binary came from PATH with unstated build flags (Redis's Makefile default was -O2) and the log shows THP enabled and somaxconn 128 warnings. The README shows only chart PNGs for pipeline 1 and 8 and states the goal 'performs on par with Redis and Haproxy'; the depth-16 numbers come from benchmarks/out/redis16.txt. The clone at HEAD differs from the 2017 build that was measured (its 'redis server started' log line has since gained a loops field). Latest two commits are README edits (2026-05-12, 2026-05-19) and the one before is from 2022-05-14.
found_via: GitHub: grepped raw READMEs of Go event-loop frameworks (tidwall/evio, panjf2000/gnet) for libuv/Redis/C comparisons; opened tidwall/evio README, benchmarks/README.md, benchmarks/bench-redis.sh, benchmarks/out/redis1.txt, redis8.txt, redis16.txt, examples/redis-server/main.go and the commits page.

verification.tier_reason: First-party raw logs benchmarks/out/redis{1,8,16}.txt from the public script benchmarks/bench-redis.sh show real Redis 4.0.2 and the evio clone (examples/redis-server/main.go) under the same redis-benchmark command, with every number in the record matching the final lines; the Go version, the Redis build and flags, and the CPU model (only 'ec2 c4.xlarge') are not stated, so not A, and no independent run exists, so not B.
verification.notes: Numbers verified exactly in the raw logs; keep at C. Shortcomings: clone vs full Redis (different work per command), PING_INLINE only, single run, client on the same 4-vCPU box, Redis build unknown (default -O2), 2017 snapshot, no mechanism stated; the clone uses redcon's parser, so evio and redcon share code.

corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go version not recorded (2017 snapshot, plain go build in benchmarks/bench-redis.sh). The Redis 4.0.2 build and its flags are not stated; the log shows a default config with transparent-huge-pages and overcommit warnings.
corrected_fields.caveats: The two servers do different amounts of work: the evio example is a tiny Redis-protocol clone (PING, ECHO, GET, SET, DEL, FLUSHDB, QUIT, SHUTDOWN, WAKE) over a Go map with an RWMutex, with no persistence, expiry, replication, statistics or the full command table, so this is not a like-for-like win over Redis. At pipeline depth 1 both are client-bound and equal. Real Redis stays at about 878k requests per second at depth 8 and depth 16 while the clone keeps climbing, and the repo gives no explanation. Only PING_INLINE was benchmarked. One run per cell, no variance, benchmark client shares the 4-vCPU instance with the server. Redis 4.0.2 is from 2017 and the flags and compiler for it are unstated. The README gives no mechanism and no table: it shows chart PNGs, so the numbers here come from the raw benchmarks/out/*.txt files in the repo. Latest two commits are README edits (2026-05-12, 2026-05-19) and the one before is from 2022-05-14.

name: Go net TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is faster than Go
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Go 35.6 s vs libuv 43.6 s wall time for 1000 connections x 5000 echoes (about 1.22x less wall time, derived from page data); Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 1.21x faster than Go (derived from page data). Each value is a single run; the Go value was recorded on 2022-08-25 after the Go server was rewritten (it was 81.0 s before), the libuv value by 2022-07-15. Doc text: 'Go did surprise me: faster than nodejs and libuv!'
compiler_and_flags: libuv server: 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2 -o echo_server_direct' (benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md), linked against an unstated system libuv build. Go server: version and build command not stated; runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1), one goroutine per connection, 1024-byte buffer. Asio server/client: CMake target with C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler and optimisation level not stated.
stars_or_usage: 139.2k stars (golang/go); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Go brings a garbage-collected runtime and goroutine scheduler with its own netpoller; calling Go from C++ goes through cgo or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart on the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' (doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc); the rendered PNG on boostorg.github.io was not viewed. The chart is a composite of single `time` runs recorded on different dates by the Boost.Redis (C++) author on 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms; no CPU model, OS, Go/Rust/compiler versions, no repetitions or variance): libuv 43.568 s was recorded by 2022-07-15 (commit 3fb018c) and never re-run; Tokio moved from 42.2 s/43.2 s to 30.7 s on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime; Go moved from 81.0 s to 35.6 s on 2022-08-25 (commit f11622e) after its server was rewritten from bufio ReadBytes line echo to a raw 1024-byte read loop with GOMAXPROCS(1); Asio was re-measured at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07. Unequal work: the libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example, which mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer (libuv passes 64*1024 as suggested_size, src/unix/stream.c) on every read callback and a write_req_t per echo and frees both after each write, while the Go, Tokio and Asio servers reuse one 1 KiB buffer per connection; the Go server was revised between runs, the libuv one never was. The libuv server is built per benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md with 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2' (not -O3; system libuv build flags unknown). The load generator is the single-threaded Boost.Asio echo_server_client (1000 sessions x 5000 13-byte ping-pong messages) on the same host, which may set a floor near the Asio/Tokio results. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, Tokio current_thread, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. The author gives no explanation for the gap beyond 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio'. The Go server ignores conn.Write's return value (its error check tests the stale read error), harmless for timing. Measured in 2022 (Go about 1.19); the doc page is unchanged since.
found_via: WebSearch: 'tokio vs boost asio benchmark echo server rust faster than C++ github' surfaced the Boost.Redis benchmark page; opened benchmarks.tex, doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc and benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go via raw.githubusercontent.com.

verification.tier_reason: Numbers are real (benchmarks.tex: Asio 29.5 s, Tokio 30.7 s, Go 35.6 s, Libuv 43.6 s, Nodejs 74.2 s) and server code is public (benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go, benchmarks/c/libuv/echo_server_direct.c, benchmarks/cpp/asio/echo_server_client.cpp), but there is no CPU model or Go version, each bar is one run recorded on a different date (libuv by 2022-07-15, Go 2022-08-25 after a server rewrite), and the C side is the libuv docs example that mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer and a write request per message at -O2 while Go reuses one 1 KiB buffer: crippled-baseline and cross-run precedents put the Go-over-C claim at D.
verification.notes: Downgrade C to D: the only C baseline Go beats is the unmodified libuv docs example (per-message 64 KiB malloc plus write-request malloc, -O2) recorded weeks before the revised Go server, one run each; Go loses to the C++ Asio server (29.5 s) in the same table. Shortcomings for decisions.json: composite single-run chart across July-October 2022, no hardware or versions, unequal buffer management, -O2 C build, single-threaded client may cap results.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Go 35.6 s vs libuv 43.6 s for the same echo run (about 1.22x less wall time, derived from page data). Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 1.21x faster than Go (derived from page data). Doc text: 'Go did surprise me: faster than nodejs and libuv!'
corrected_fields.compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Go server (benchmarks/go/echo_server_direct.go) calls runtime.GOMAXPROCS(1), one goroutine per connection, 1024-byte buffer; Go version and build flags not stated. libuv build flags not stated.
corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart that the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' shows; the rendered chart image itself was not viewed. Machine is only described as 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms): no CPU model, no OS, no compiler or Rust/Go versions, no flags, one run, no variance. The author is the Boost.Redis (C++) author, not a maintainer of the tested runtime. The libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example (malloc of a read buffer and of a write request for every message), so it is an untuned C baseline. The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with an unsafe-IO hint, Tokio current_thread runtime, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The doc page says the author expected libuv to perform like Asio and Tokio and was surprised by the Go result; it offers no explanation of the gap. The win is only over libuv (untuned C example); Go loses to Boost.Asio in the same suite.

name: Lingua Franca (reactor language, C++ runtime) on the Savina actor benchmarks vs CAF
language: Lingua Franca (code generator targeting C++ and C)
baseline: CAF (C++ Actor Framework) running the same Savina benchmarks; Akka (JVM) is the second baseline
workload: Savina actor benchmark suite ported to Lingua Franca reactors (micro-benchmarks such as Ping Pong, Thread Ring, Counting, Fork Join, Big, Chameneos plus concurrency and parallelism benchmarks), execution time at a given number of worker threads.
claimed_speedup: Not on any page opened. From the abstract of the ACM TACO 2023 paper 'High-Performance Deterministic Concurrency using Lingua Franca', seen only as web search snippets (arXiv, ACM and mirrors were blocked): LF is about 1.42x faster than CAF and about 1.85-1.86x faster than Akka over the Savina suite at 20 threads, with LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring, ahead on Fork Join and Chameneos, and roughly on par on the parallelism benchmarks.
compiler_and_flags: Paper flags not seen. From the public build sources: the LF C++ benchmarks declare target Cpp { build-type: Release, no-runtime-validation: true, fast: true } (Cpp/Savina/src/micro/PingPong.lf), i.e. CMake Release (-O3 -DNDEBUG); the CAF baseline programs (lf-lang/savina CMakeLists.txt) and CAF 0.16.5 itself both default CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g level) and the README build commands pass no build type, so a build that follows the README compares LF at -O3 against CAF at -O2. Compiler and version not stated.
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (lingua-franca); benchmark repo lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca has 4 stars
tradeoffs: Programs are written in the LF language and compiled by a code generator, so adopting it means a new toolchain; the generated runtime is C or C++, so this is a coordination-language and scheduler claim, not a claim that non-C/C++ machine code is faster. Deterministic semantics restrict some actor patterns (logical time, reactors).
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the TACO 2023 paper and its artifact data were not opened (arXiv, par.nsf.gov, cfaed.tu-dresden.de, ar5iv and deepai unreachable), so tier C; snippets agree on 1.86x over Akka and 1.42x over CAF but give no thread count, CPU or aggregation method, and the '20 threads' setting, CAF 0.17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and i9-10900K details could not be confirmed (the benchmark README names CAF 0.16.5). Snippets also say only 22 of the 30 Savina benchmarks were ported to the LF C++ target: benchmarks needing dynamic actor creation (Fork Join creation, Fibonacci, Quicksort and others), A*-Search and Logistic Map Series (whose CAF version uses a blocking call) are excluded, so the suite average covers only benchmarks LF can express with a static reactor graph. Same-opt-level problem in the public sources: LF benchmarks build with build-type Release (-O3) plus no-runtime-validation, while the lf-lang/savina CAF programs and CAF 0.16.5 default to RelWithDebInfo (-O2) and the README passes no build type; whether the paper overrode this is unknown. The LF ports restructure the Savina programs into reactors with fixed connections (PingPong breaks its causality loop with a logical action), so the work is equivalent but not line-for-line identical to the CAF and Akka versions. The paper's authors built both sides. Both sides are C++ (LF generates C++ against the reactor-cpp runtime), so the win is a runtime and programming-model result, not a code-generation one; the paper also reports LF behind CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and behind Akka on Counting and Big (snippet). The benchmark repo has no LICENSE file; the lingua-franca repo is BSD-2-Clause.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): WebSearch 'actor benchmark Savina Pony vs CAF ...' and 'github Savina actor benchmark CAF Pony Akka comparison' surfaced lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca; WebSearch on the paper title gave the snippet numbers.

verification.tier_reason: The 1.86x (Akka) and 1.42x (CAF) figures of the ACM TACO 2023 paper (DOI 10.1145/3617687, arXiv 2301.02444) were seen only in WebSearch snippets; arXiv, par.nsf.gov, cfaed.tu-dresden.de, ar5iv and deepai were all unreachable, and the public harness (lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca runner/ and Cpp/Savina/src, CAF sources in lf-lang/savina) holds no results, CPU model or compiler, so snippet-only paper numbers stay C.
verification.notes: Kept at C: numbers from TACO 2023 snippets only, benchmark_url set to the arXiv abstract (not opened, egress blocked). Shortcomings to record: snippet-only numbers; only 22 of 30 Savina benchmarks (dynamic-creation ones excluded); public build defaults put CAF at RelWithDebInfo -O2 against LF Release -O3 (same_opt_level false); win comes from the C++ reactor runtime, not the language's codegen.

corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the paper and its artifact data were not opened, so tier C. The public benchmark repo (lf-lang/benchmarks-lingua-franca, last commit 2026-09-20) holds the LF, Akka and CAF sources (README names CAF 0.16.5 and a patched lf-lang/savina fork) and a runner, but no result tables, no CPU model and no compiler flags; one search snippet quoted CAF 17.6, Akka 2.6.17 and an Intel i9-10900K for the paper, which conflicts with the README's CAF 0.16.5 and could not be checked. The paper's own authors built the LF side and the CAF side of the comparison. The runtime behind the win is C++, so a hand-tuned C++ actor program could probably match it; the paper also reports LF losing to CAF on Ping Pong and Thread Ring and to Akka on Counting and Big (snippet).

name: NPB-Rust (NAS Parallel Benchmarks in Rust, sequential and Rayon)
baseline: NPB-CPP, the group's C++ port of NAS Parallel Benchmarks 3.4.1 (sequential NPB-SER, and OpenMP NPB-OMP for the parallel comparison), plus the original Fortran NPB
workload: NAS Parallel Benchmarks kernels EP, CG, MG, IS, FT and pseudo-applications BT, SP, LU in Rust (sequential NPB-RUST and Rayon-parallel NPB-RAYON), compared with the C++ and Fortran versions.
claimed_speedup: From the paper abstract as shown in a search snippet (snippet only): Rust sequential is 5.59% faster than C++ and 1.23% slower than Fortran; Rust with Rayon is slower than both the Fortran and the C++ OpenMP versions.
compiler_and_flags: Repo defaults (paper's actual compilers and flags not seen): Rust 1.85.0+, RUSTFLAGS='--cfg class="X"' cargo build --release with no [profile] section in NPB-RUST/Cargo.toml (opt-level 3, no LTO, no target-cpu); C++ NPB-CPP NPB-SER/config/make.def: g++ -std=c++14 with CFLAGS -O3 -mcmodel=medium; Fortran compiler and flags unknown.
tradeoffs: Rust port of NPB with a sequential variant (NPB-RUST) and a Rayon variant (NPB-RAYON); safety and ergonomics trade-offs are not discussed on the pages that were opened.
caveats: The arXiv page (2502.15536) is blocked in this environment and was not opened; the numbers come from WebSearch snippets of arxiv.org/html/2502.15536v1 (snippet only), so venue, peer-review status, hardware, compiler versions and per-kernel results are unconfirmed; a verifier with paper access should retier. The GitHub repo has no performance numbers. The only win over C++ is the sequential aggregate (5.59%, a small margin); Rayon is slower than C++ OpenMP and Fortran OpenMP, so the concurrency-runtimes category fits poorly (the win is sequential codegen, closer to numerics). The C++ baseline is the same group's NPB-CPP port (FGCS 2021, https://github.com/GMAP/NPB-CPP). Public build defaults are equivalent in optimisation level (-O3 against cargo --release opt-level 3, neither with -march=native), but the C++ default adds -mcmodel=medium; whether that or anything else explains the 5.59% is untested. The latest commit (2026-10-08, 3bb2455 'fix: adjusted tolrsd constants in LU') only assigns the 1.0e-08 tolrsd constants that were previously left at zero; with zero tolerances the early-exit residual check never fired, so the measured LU did the full iteration count and the fix does not inflate the published numbers. NPB-Rust has a --cfg safe="true" switch whose default (unset) reports UNSAFE=true; which mode the paper timed is not stated.

name: Pony actor message ring plus factorisation vs CAF and Charm++
baseline: CAF 0.13 (C++ Actor Framework); Charm++ 6.6.1 (C++) is in the same chart
workload: Mixed case ('Message ring + factorisation') from the CAF benchmark suite: rings of actors pass a token while a worker factorises 86028157 x 329545133 by trial division on each repetition. Pony side: examples/mixed/main.pony (tag 0.1.7; now examples/actors/mixed) with defaults of 20 rings of 50 actors, 10,000 laps and 5 repetitions. CAF side: src/caf/mixed_case.cpp in actor-framework/benchmarks. The run parameters behind the charts are not stated. Plotted as speed relative to Erlang OTP 17 on 1 core against physical cores (1-32) and against 32 physical cores with hyper-threading (up to 64 threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off the charts (approximate, ratios derived from page data): at 1 core Pony 0.1.5 about 2.2 versus CAF 0.13 about 0.5 (about 4x); at 16 physical cores Pony about 29 versus CAF about 8 (about 3.6x); at 32 physical cores Pony about 48 versus CAF about 16 (about 3.0x), with Erlang OTP 17 about 19, Scala/Akka about 13.5 and Charm++ 6.6.1 about 9. With hyper-threading (also Figure 9 of the AGERE! 2015 paper) Pony is about 62 at 64 threads, against CAF at about 26-27 over 56-63 threads and about 30 at its final 64-thread point (about 2.1-2.4x), Erlang about 24 and Akka about 25.
tradeoffs: Pony is a separate language and runtime (actors with per-actor heaps, reference capabilities, no shared mutable state); using it from C++ means FFI or a separate process. Smaller ecosystem and a steeper learning curve than a C++ library such as CAF.
caveats: Unequal work between implementations: in the public Pony program (unchanged from tag 0.1.7 to today) each Ring master builds its ring once and reuses it across all repetitions, spawns a fresh Worker actor per repetition, and computes but never uses the factorisation result (the 'correct' flag is dropped; no message, no check). The CAF suite's mixed_case.cpp (current version; the 2015 CAF 0.13 version could not be retrieved) spawns a new ring of ring_size-1 actors on every repetition while the old links quit, factorises in one detached (own-thread) worker per ring, and sends every factor vector to a supervisor that checks it. Pony therefore skips ring re-creation and the result messages that CAF pays for. Charts only: the website PDF (gnuplot, created 2015-07-06) and the paper have no tables, so figures are approximate. The paper gives 100-run averages but no CPU model (only '32 physical cores with HT'), compiler, flags or variance, and the CAF build type is unknown. Versions are about a decade old (Pony 0.1.5, CAF 0.13, Charm++ 6.6.1, Erlang OTP 17, Scala 2.11.6 Akka). On the physical-core chart Erlang OTP 17 beats CAF at every core count (about 19 versus 16 at 32 cores); with HT, CAF passes Erlang at about 48 threads and ends ahead (about 30 versus 24 at 64). So CAF 0.13 is a weak baseline here, and the Pony gap says more about CAF's scaling and the unequal work than about the language. Both papers are by the Pony authors. The same sources show CAF beating Pony on actor creation beyond about 10 physical cores. The Pony runtime (libponyrt) is written in C. www.ponylang.io and doc.ic.ac.uk/~scb12/pony.html were blocked and are not used.

name: Rayon vs OpenMP (CMU 15-618 project)
baseline: C++ with OpenMP (and GNU parallel-mode sort) for Mandelbrot, matrix multiplication, sorting and reduction; C++ compiled with GCC per the report
workload: Four shared-memory benchmarks written in Rust+Rayon and C++/OpenMP: Mandelbrot (2048 to 8192 square images, 7 views), integer matrix multiplication (1024 and 2048 square, all-ones inputs), stable and unstable sort of 1M, 10M and 100M random elements (Rust: uniform random u64 via par_sort/par_sort_unstable; C++: std::vector<int> via GNU parallel mode, source not committed), and sum/sum-of-squares reduction over 500M, 1B and 2B f64; best of three runs, threads 1 to 16.
claimed_speedup: Mixed; absolute times from data/Data.xlsx (best of three). Matmul 2048x2048, Rayon par_chunks row-dot vs OpenMP: Rust faster at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12 and 16 threads (12 threads 2168.8 vs 2864.5 ms, about 1.32x; 16 threads 2149.1 vs 2264.2 ms, about 1.05x, derived from page data) but slower at 8 threads (2501.7 vs 2277.6 ms) and serially (16277.1 vs 15509.5 ms); the report's 'Rayon performs better for all cases of threads for size 2048' is contradicted by its own 8-thread row, and its 'C++ is faster for all cases of threads for size 1024' by the 12-thread (272.4 vs 362.1 ms) and 16-thread (265.2 vs 285.7 ms) rows. These matmul comparisons are invalid (see caveats). Stable parallel sort, 100M elements: Rayon par_sort 1380 ms vs GNU parallel stable sort 1534.1 ms at 12 threads and 1226 vs 1476.2 ms at 16 threads (about 1.11x and 1.20x, derived from page data); C++ faster at 1 to 8 threads (8 threads 1690.0 vs 1834 ms) and serially (8467.6 vs 10908 ms). Unstable sort: Rust pdqsort/par_sort_unstable is faster in absolute time at every thread count (100M serial 3611 vs 7851.1 ms; 16 threads 684 vs 975.4 ms) although the report says C++ scales better; this is pdqsort vs introsort/multiway mergesort, an algorithm difference. Mandelbrot: C++ faster serially and Rust within about 1% multithreaded; quoted serial view 1 (4096x4096): Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms, Rust 18758.684 ms after removing the num::Complex32 overhead. Reduction: Rust marginally faster serially (500M sum 456.5 vs 460.5 ms), OpenMP faster at every thread count.
compiler_and_flags: C++: g++ -m64 -O3 -Wall -fopenmp (C++/mandelbrot, matrixmultiply, quicksort, reduction Makefiles; no -march); the committed C++ quicksort binary's .comment reads 'GCC: (GNU) 4.8.5 20150623 (Red Hat 4.8.5-36)'. Rust: Cargo.toml files have no [profile] section; build command (release or not) and rustc version not stated; Rayon 1.0.3.
tradeoffs: Rayon work stealing adapts to uneven work but pays split and steal overhead; the report finds OpenMP static scheduling faster on reductions and Mandelbrot. Rust refuses to compile unsafe sharing between threads.
caveats: Student course project (CMU 15-618, 2019): results are graphs inside a PDF plus raw timings in data/Data.xlsx; no hardware stated (threads swept to 16); no license file. Harness defects found in the committed code: (1) the C++ matmul kernels matmul_serial2 and matmul_par_row compute c += A[iOff + k] * B[RM(k, i, size)], indexing B by the row i instead of the column j, so C++ computes a different (wrong) product whose B working set is a single cache-resident column per row, while the Rust kernel correctly walks B[index][col]; the bug is masked because A and B are all ones and the C++ result is never verified, so the matmul comparison is not same-work; (2) the C++ 'par_outer' timing block calls matmul_par_row again and never resets minThread, so the par_outer rows duplicate par_row; (3) the C++ sort source (C++/quicksort/main.cpp) is not committed, only a prebuilt ELF binary whose symbols show std::vector<int> (32-bit keys) sorted with __gnu_parallel multiway mergesort, while the Rust benchmark sorts Vec<u64> (64-bit keys), so element widths differ (against Rust); (4) the committed Rust sort code times stable_sort_par in its 'unstable parallel' loop (unstable_sort_par, typed &mut [u32], is never called) and prints fractional milliseconds, whereas Data.xlsx holds integer-millisecond Rust sort times that differ between stable and unstable, so the Rust sort numbers came from an earlier, uncommitted code version; correctness asserts are commented out; (5) Data.xlsx has copy errors (Rust Mandelbrot view 1 row-parallel row duplicates view 0). The Rayon matmul advantage the report explains (Rust not vectorizing the inner loop and hitting the compute limit later, par_chunks avoiding fork-join overhead) rests on the invalid kernel comparison. Sort compares different library algorithms (Rust stable merge sort and pdqsort vs GNU parallel multiway mergesort and introsort). Old toolchains: GCC 4.8.5 (2015) vs Rayon 1.0.3-era rustc (2019).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/rayon and github.com/topics/openmp?l=rust (repo description 'Comparison of Multi-threading between C++ and Rust (OpenMP vs Rayon)'); opened repo README, project_docs/15618-Project-Final.pdf and commits.
why_faster: Report: Rayon work stealing balances load and its merge sort was tuned (three merge variants benchmarked); for 2048x2048 matmul the unvectorized Rust inner loop keeps scaling longer and par_chunks avoids fork-join overhead.

verification.tier_reason: First-party student report (graphs; the only quoted timings, Mandelbrot view 1 Rust 19319.043 ms vs C++ 18813.754 ms and 18758.684 ms after the Complex32 fix, match) with raw timings in data/Data.xlsx and C++ Makefiles at g++ -m64 -O3 -fopenmp, but no CPU model, no Rust build flags or rustc version, the C++ sort source is not committed, and the matmul baseline kernel computes a different product; C at best.

The only surviving Rayon-over-OpenMP result is stable parallel sort at 12-16 threads (about 1.11-1.20x at 100M, derived). Usability reference (no license), abandoned (last commit 2019-11-01).

name: Redcon (Go Redis-compatible server framework; clone vs real Redis)
baseline: Redis (C, single-threaded, started as 'redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no'; version not stated)
workload: redis-benchmark -t set,get -n 10000000 -q -P 512 -c 512 against real Redis ('redis-server --port 6379 --appendonly no') and against example/clone.go (Go map with an RWMutex; PING, QUIT, SET, GET, SETNX, DEL, PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE/PSUBSCRIBE, DETACH and a blank CONFIG stub that exists only so redis-benchmark runs), Redcon run with GOMAXPROCS=1 and GOMAXPROCS=0. No -r flag is passed, so redis-benchmark uses one fixed key for every SET and GET with its default 3-byte value.
claimed_speedup: Requests per second, README table: SET 2,018,570.88 (Redcon, one thread) vs 941,265.12 (Redis) = about 2.14x (derived from page data); GET 2,403,846.25 vs 1,189,909.50 = about 2.02x (derived from page data). Multi-threaded Redcon: SET 1,944,390.38 (about 2.07x, derived) and GET 3,993,610.25 (about 3.36x, derived).

hardware: MacBook Pro 15-inch, 2.8 GHz Intel Core i7 (README), client and server on one laptop
tradeoffs: Go library, so a C++ project would run it as a separate server or sidecar. The clone in the benchmark has none of Redis's persistence, expiry, data structures or replication. Each connection is served by Go's net package with goroutines.
caveats: First-party README numbers from the Go 1.7 era (2016) with no Redis version, no compiler, no run count and no variance. The Redis command disables the append-only file but not RDB snapshots; because redis-benchmark ran without -r, the dataset is a single key, so any snapshot fork during the 10M-command SET run would be cheap and this is a minor concern. The Go clone implements a handful of commands over a bare map behind an RWMutex, while Redis runs its full command dispatch, so the two servers do different work per command and the gap is mostly per-command overhead, not language (verifier inference). Client, server and OS share one laptop; 512 connections and pipeline depth 512 favour batch throughput over latency. Multi-threaded Redcon SET (1,944,390.38) is slower than single-threaded (2,018,570.88), consistent with every SET taking the global mutex. No latency numbers. The README names no mechanism. The redcon parser has changed since the measurement (it copies each command's raw bytes, and a 2026-07-22 commit reworked number parsing), so the numbers predate the current code. Redis-vs-Go comparison, not a runtime-level language claim. evio's Redis example reuses redcon's parser.

name: Tokio (1M concurrent tasks, peak memory)
baseline: Asio C++20 coroutines (awaitable tasks) and concurrencpp
workload: Spawn N concurrent async tasks that wait on a timer and measure peak memory (port of the Rust '1 million concurrent tasks' memory benchmark to C++ coroutine libraries).
claimed_speedup: Peak memory at 1M tasks: tokio 214,136 KB, concurrencpp 605,972 KB, Asio 853,144 KB (about 2.8x and 4.0x less, derived from page data); at 100k tasks: 23,824 vs 61,460 vs 86,652 KB; at 10k: 6,908 vs 7,840 vs 10,244 KB. At 1 task tokio is the largest (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB). Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M.
compiler_and_flags: C++20, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release set in CMakeLists.txt (-O3 -DNDEBUG with GCC or Clang), compiler not named; Asio and concurrencpp fetched by FetchContent with no GIT_TAG (default-branch HEAD at build time, June 2023), libunifex GIT_TAG main; tokio_bench built by 'cargo build --release' from CMakeLists.txt (opt-level 3), tokio 1.28.2 per Cargo.lock, #[tokio::main] multi-thread runtime.
hardware: Intel i7-8550U (8 threads, about 1.99 GHz), 8 GB RAM, WSL Ubuntu 20.04.6 on Windows 10
tradeoffs: Tokio tasks are stackless futures sized by the compiler, so memory is small per task but not free of heap allocation per spawn; the C++ libraries allocate a coroutine frame per task. The result is about memory only, not throughput or latency.
caveats: Independent hobby replication (4 stars, 6 commits all on 2023-06-24) of the pkolaczk 'How Much Memory Do You Need to Run 1 Million Concurrent Tasks?' benchmark, not the tokio authors' work; the README notes the original methodology was criticised. Memory only (peak RSS from /usr/bin/time), no timing; run count not stated; WSL Ubuntu 20.04 on a laptop i7-8550U with 8 GB. C++ compiler unnamed and Asio/concurrencpp versions unpinned. Workloads match logically (N tasks each awaiting a 10 s timer, all alive at once), but the C++ programs differ in structure: Asio builds a vector of N lazily-started awaitables and then co_spawns each on one io_context thread; concurrencpp copies two shared_ptrs into every coroutine frame and uses one worker_thread_executor plus its timer_queue; tokio spawns each task on the default multi-thread runtime and keeps the JoinHandles. Tokio is the largest at 1 task (3,092 KB vs Asio 1,668 KB) and only pulls ahead from 10k tasks. Libunifex hangs at 100k and 1M. The tokio repo itself makes no comparison to C++ runtimes.

name: Tokio TCP echo server (Boost.Redis echo benchmark, vs libuv)
baseline: libuv TCP echo server (C, epoll event loop, libuv docs tcp-echo-server example); the table also holds a Boost.Asio C++20 coroutine echo server that is slightly faster than Tokio
workload: TCP echo server serving 1000 concurrent client connections on localhost (the Boost.Redis echo_server_client driver, benchmarks.tex comment 'time ./echo_server_client 1000 5000'); metric is the total wall-clock seconds the client run took against each server, one server per language/library, each written from that library's own docs example.
claimed_speedup: Tokio 30.7 s vs libuv 43.6 s wall time for 1000 connections x 5000 echoes (about 1.42x less wall time, derived from page data); Boost.Asio (C++) 29.5 s is about 4% faster than Tokio (derived from page data). Each value is a single run; the Tokio value was recorded on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime (it was 42.2-43.2 s before), the libuv value by 2022-07-15. Go 35.6 s and Node.js 74.2 s are in the same table.
compiler_and_flags: Tokio server: #[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")], tokio = { version = "1.0", features = ["full"] } (benchmarks/rust/echo_server_direct/Cargo.toml has no [profile] section); cargo build profile and rustc version not stated. libuv server: 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2 -o echo_server_direct' (benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md), linked against an unstated system libuv build. Asio server/client: CMake target with C++20 (benchmarks/CMakeLists.txt), compiler and optimisation level not stated.
stars_or_usage: 33.4k stars (tokio); suite repo boostorg/redis has 282 stars
tradeoffs: Rust async needs the Tokio runtime and a Rust toolchain; the benchmark deliberately uses the single-threaded Tokio runtime to match the single-threaded libuv loop. Calling it from C++ needs FFI or a separate process.
caveats: Numbers are the pgfplots source (benchmarks.tex) of the chart on the Boost.Redis doc page 'Echo server benchmark' (doc/modules/ROOT/pages/benchmarks.adoc); the rendered PNG on boostorg.github.io was not viewed. The chart is a composite of single `time` runs recorded on different dates by the Boost.Redis (C++) author on 'my machine' (localhost latency 0.07 ms; no CPU model, OS, Go/Rust/compiler versions, no repetitions or variance): libuv 43.568 s was recorded by 2022-07-15 (commit 3fb018c) and never re-run; Tokio moved from 42.2 s/43.2 s to 30.7 s on 2022-07-16 after switching to a newer Tokio and the current_thread runtime; Go moved from 81.0 s to 35.6 s on 2022-08-25 (commit f11622e) after its server was rewritten from bufio ReadBytes line echo to a raw 1024-byte read loop with GOMAXPROCS(1); Asio was re-measured at 29.5 s on 2022-10-07. Unequal work: the libuv server is the unmodified libuv docs tcp-echo-server example, which mallocs a 64 KiB read buffer (libuv passes 64*1024 as suggested_size, src/unix/stream.c) on every read callback and a write_req_t per echo and frees both after each write, while the Go, Tokio and Asio servers reuse one 1 KiB buffer per connection; the Go server was revised between runs, the libuv one never was. The libuv server is built per benchmarks/c/libuv/README.md with 'gcc echo_server_direct.c -luv -O2' (not -O3; system libuv build flags unknown). The load generator is the single-threaded Boost.Asio echo_server_client (1000 sessions x 5000 13-byte ping-pong messages) on the same host, which may set a floor near the Asio/Tokio results. All servers are single-threaded (Asio io_context with BOOST_ASIO_CONCURRENCY_HINT_UNSAFE_IO, Tokio current_thread, Go GOMAXPROCS(1), one libuv loop). The C++ Boost.Asio coroutine server in the same table is the fastest entry (29.5 s), so this is not a win over the best C++ result. The author gives no explanation for the gap beyond 'I expected Libuv to have similar performance to Asio and Tokio'. Measured in 2022 on a Tokio 1.x release of that time; the Tokio server binds 127.0.0.1 while the others bind 0.0.0.0 (no timing effect expected).

name: Embassy (async Rust executor) vs FreeRTOS
baseline: FreeRTOS (C RTOS, used through the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper in an STM32CubeIDE project) on an STM32F446ZE
workload: Same toy firmware on a NUCLEO-F446ZE at 180 MHz in Embassy, RTIC and FreeRTOS (CMSIS-RTOS v2 over ST HAL): one task blinks an LED every 100 ms, a button task waits on the EXTI13 user-button interrupt and toggles GPIO PG1 (interrupt-to-task latency read on an oscilloscope), formats a 32-byte message and queues it to a UART writer task. Per search-result summaries (blog unreachable), the post compares interrupt latency, program size, static RAM and ease of programming.
claimed_speedup: README quote: 'It obsoletes the need for a traditional RTOS with kernel context switching, and is faster and smaller than one!' No figures appear on any page that was opened; the blog post that carries them (tweedegolf.nl, async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) could not be reached from this environment.
compiler_and_flags: Rust (rust/Cargo.toml): nightly toolchain (feature type_alias_impl_trait), [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1, incremental = false, debug = true (debug info only), embassy and embassy-stm32 from git master of early 2022. C (c/.cproject, STM32CubeIDE 1.8.0, MCU ARM GCC arm-none-eabi-): Release configuration C optimization -O3 with -g0 and no LTO (C++ option -Os, unused by this C project); the Debug configuration leaves the optimization level at the IDE default. The repo does not say which C configuration was measured, and no compiler versions are stated for either side.
hardware: STM32F446ZE (Arm Cortex-M4F) on NUCLEO-F446ZE
stars_or_usage: embassy-rs/embassy: 9.9k stars, 1.7k forks; tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown: 18 stars, 2 forks, 3 commits (2022-01-04 to 2022-02-17)
tradeoffs: Cooperative async tasks, not preemptive threads: a task that does not yield blocks the others, and priorities work through multiple executors/interrupts. Needs Rust nightly features in the 2022 snapshot; no C++ API.
caveats: Tier D because no number could be read from any opened page; the blog post with the figures (tweedegolf.nl/en/blog/65/async-rust-vs-rtos-showdown) was unreachable (DNS ENOTFOUND), as were the zeli.app and hn.svelte.dev mirrors. Secondary search summaries (snippet only) say Embassy used less RAM and flash but FreeRTOS had better interrupt latency, so 'faster' is not established; Reddit r/embedded and Hacker News commenters said worst-case latency was not measured, only the standard deviation, and flagged the C app's static RAM figure. The verifier read the C side and found it does not do the same work as the Rust side: (1) the UART writer uses blocking polled HAL_UART_Transmit, while Embassy writes over DMA asynchronously; (2) the C message formatting uses newlib snprintf (configUSE_NEWLIB_REENTRANT 1), while Rust uses core::fmt into an ArrayString; (3) the C button task's 'only react to falling edges' block sets the same RTSR/FTSR bits as the rising-edge block (EXTI->RTSR |= pin; EXTI->FTSR &= ~pin), so the C firmware waits on two rising edges and never on a falling edge; (4) the EXTI path goes through the ST HAL callback and the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper (osThreadFlagsSet) instead of native FreeRTOS calls. FreeRTOSConfig.h is the untuned CubeMX default: a static 15360-byte heap (configTOTAL_HEAP_SIZE), three 512-byte task stacks, trace facility, software timers, recursive mutexes and generic task selection (configUSE_PORT_OPTIMISED_TASK_SELECTION 0) all on, which inflates the C side's static RAM and flash. Build settings are not equivalent: the Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units = 1 at opt-level 3, the C Release build -O3 without LTO (larger code than -Os), and the repo does not say whether the Debug or Release C build was measured. The showdown repo is a Feb 2022 snapshot built on Embassy master of that date, so the result predates four years of Embassy and FreeRTOS changes. A cooperative executor versus a preemptive RTOS is not a like-for-like scheduling comparison. The only claim in the embassy repo itself is a README sentence linking the blog.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Embassy async rust vs FreeRTOS benchmark latency context switch'; opened github.com/embassy-rs/embassy README, github.com/tweedegolf/async-rtos-showdown (README, rust/Cargo.toml, c/.cproject, commits).
why_faster: README: async tasks compile into cooperatively scheduled state machines that share one stack, need no per-task stack sizing and no dynamic allocation, so no kernel context switch is paid.

Shortcomings to record: no numbers reachable (blog blocked); C baseline is untuned CubeMX FreeRTOS behind the CMSIS-RTOS v2 wrapper and ST HAL with a 15 KB static heap, blocking polled UART vs Embassy DMA, newlib snprintf vs core::fmt, a falling-edge EXTI configuration bug, and no LTO on the C side against LTO plus codegen-units = 1 on the Rust side; worst-case latency not measured; 2022 snapshot. name: CBQN (BQN array language) - CRLF-to-LF conversion versus plain C
language: BQN (implementation in C, SIMD kernels generated with Singeli)
baseline: Plain scalar C loop for the same line-ending conversion (crlf_to_lf), compiled with clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native
workload: Replace every CRLF with LF in a byte buffer of 100 to 1,000,000 bytes with a CRLF about every 100 characters; BQN one-liner (cr!=) with (0 shifted lf!=) filtered by Replicate versus a scalar C loop; the page also reports selection and compiler benchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Page text: BQN breaks even with C at a little under 200 bytes and hits 5x C's speed on inputs of a few thousand bytes or more with AVX-512 disabled, over 10x with AVX-512 until cache becomes a bottleneck. Page timings on a Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (a CRLF every ~100 bytes): C (clang 15.0.7 -O3 -march=native) 0.555 ns/elt from 10k to 1M bytes (0.613 at 100 bytes); CBQN avx2/bmi2/pclmul build 0.893 (100 bytes, slower than C), 0.127 (3k), 0.106 (10k), 0.094 (30k), 0.107 (1M) ns/elt, about 4.4x at 3k and 5.2-5.9x from 10k up (derived from page data); CBQN native build (AVX-512) 0.0526 (10k), 0.0506 (30k), 0.0537 (100k), 0.0787 (1M) ns/elt, about 10.3-11.0x from 10k to 300k and 7.1x at 1M (derived from page data). The page's selection figures (0.04 ns per selection from a table of 32 or fewer 1-byte values via shuffles versus 0.2 ns via gather) are two CBQN code paths, not a C measurement. The compiler benchmark (implementation/bootbench.md) is a separate claim: boot3.bqn in CBQN compiles boot2.bqn in 270.6 us versus 415.5 us for dzaima's comp.c built with clang 15.0 (system values and error handling removed), average of 10,000 runs on a Skylake i5-6200U, i.e. 35% less time (about 1.54x, derived from page data); the two compilers use different algorithms and the C build flags are not stated.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: clang 15.0.7, 'clang -O3 -march=native lineending.c' (gcc 12.2.1 also discussed: branching code, slightly faster at low density, much slower at high). CBQN built at commit 0d2631a2 with FFI, singeli x86-64 avx2 bmi2 pclmul (and a native build)
hardware: Intel Tiger Lake Core i5-1135G7
why_faster: Array primitives are implemented with hand-written SIMD, lookup tables and blocked multi-pass techniques (Replicate compresses with AVX2/AVX-512 mask operations, adapts to sparse inputs), which compilers do not generate from a scalar branching loop (no SIMD scan, movmask or compress idioms from portable C). The page itself says this is a best case: 'Your BQN programs are unlikely to outperform equivalent C programs' and specialized C is always faster.
tradeoffs: Whole-array style only: per-primitive call overhead, benefits grow with array length (hundreds to thousands of elements) and small element types; poor for sequential, data-dependent loops, cryptography with wrapping integer ops, and C++-style object dispatch. Interpreter, so C interop is through an FFI with copying. Licensing is a per-file mix with timsort (MIT) and Ryu (Apache-2.0/Boost) exceptions.
caveats: First-party measurement by the BQN author on one machine; both programs, the C compile line and the CBQN commit and build options are on the page, so it is reproducible (CBQN builds at -O3 with the system cc by default; the compiler used for CBQN is not named). The C baseline is the plain portable scalar loop the author took from his 2017 Dyalog talk; clang 15 makes it branchless and unrolls it 4x, so it is not crippled, but no SIMD-intrinsic or memchr/memcpy-chunk C version was tested and the page says specialized C is always faster. The win is CBQN's hand-written Singeli SIMD Replicate primitive (an adaptive sparse/dense compress) against compiler output for a scalar loop: a best case for BQN primitives, as the page itself says ('combinations of primitives never do so well'); density 1/100 is described as not particularly favourable. Not the same algorithm in the strict sense (data-parallel mask plus Replicate versus a sequential scan), but output is identical. The selection figures (0.04 versus 0.2 ns) compare two CBQN paths, not C. The compiler benchmark side claim (35% faster) ran on different hardware (i5-6200U), compares different compiler designs and states no C flags. The page dates from 2023 (clang 15.0.7, gcc 12.2.1; 'the C compilers of today (2023)') and CBQN has changed since. Licence: most files LGPL-3.0-only OR GPL-3.0-only OR MPL-2.0 at the user's choice; timsort files MIT and Ryu Apache-2.0 or BSL-1.0.
found_via: github.com/mlochbaum/BQN docs/implementation listing, page 'Performance in BQN versus C' (versusc.html); CBQN README for licensing; no WebSearch used

name: TriangularSolve.jl
baseline: Intel MKL (libmkl_rt.so loaded through MKL.jl; MKL version not stated) triangular solve called through Julia LinearAlgebra: rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) and the 3-argument ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) on the Intel run. The M1 run prints no BLAS configuration or versioninfo, so its BLAS is not named.
workload: 100x100 Float64 triangular solves with 100 right-hand sides (rdiv! UpperTriangular, ldiv! LowerTriangular), median of 10000 samples, single and multi-threaded.
claimed_speedup: README medians (BenchmarkTools, 10000 samples, N=100 random dense matrices, 100 right-hand sides). i7-1165G7 single thread (BLAS.set_num_threads(1); TriangularSolve with Val(false)): rdiv! UpperTriangular 17.916 us vs MKL rdiv!(copyto!(C, A), UpperTriangular(B)) 19.852 us (1.11x, derived from page data); ldiv! LowerTriangular 19.694 us vs MKL ldiv!(C, LowerTriangular(B), A) 21.561 us (1.09x, derived from page data). Multithreaded (JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8; the README sets MKL to min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores()) threads, which is 4 on this 4-core/8-thread CPU): rdiv! 8.769 us vs 14.163 us (1.62x, derived from page data); ldiv! 9.871 us vs 15.258 us (1.55x, derived from page data). Apple M1 single thread, BLAS not named: rdiv! 21.624 us vs 46.166 us (2.13x, derived from page data); ldiv! 34.375 us vs 49.124 us (1.43x, derived from page data), and a second ldiv! run of 23.875 us against the same 49.124 us baseline (2.06x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.8.0-DEV.438 (commit 88a6376e99, 2021-08-28), libLLVM 12.0.1 ORCJIT with tigerlake target, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=8, no julia command-line options stated (Julia JIT, no compile flags). BLAS.set_num_threads(1) for the single-thread rows and BLAS.set_num_threads(min(Threads.nthreads(), num_cores())) for the multithreaded rows. MKL, MKL.jl and TriangularSolve versions not stated. The M1 run gives no Julia version or versioninfo.
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1165G7 @ 2.80GHz (Linux); Apple M1 Mac (single-threaded only).
stars_or_usage: 12 stars; part of the JuliaSIMD/LoopVectorization ecosystem
tradeoffs: Only Float32/Float64 with at least two right-hand sides, and the README says only rdiv! with UpperTriangular and ldiv! with LowerTriangular are the supported configurations on the benchmarked paths; vector right-hand sides use pure-Julia sweeps.
caveats: Single matrix size (N=100) from a 2021 author REPL session on a Julia 1.8 development build, on a package version that has since been substantially rewritten (August 2026 kernel changes: native left-upper/right-lower kernels, shortened backward-substitution chains, inlined backward panel kernels), with no re-run; the README still ends with a stale line saying only rdiv!/UpperTriangular and ldiv!/LowerTriangular are supported. The baseline is closed-source, hand-tuned MKL (not a C/C++ -O3 build of the same algorithm), its version is not stated, and the M1 rows compare against an unnamed BLAS with no versioninfo. The single-thread Intel advantage is only about 9-11%; the larger multithreaded and M1 gaps are where small-size threading and call overhead matter most. The README's copy-paste script calls BLAS.set_num_threads(Threads.nthreads()) before the single-thread pair, unlike the REPL session it reproduces. The README gives no mechanism, and the baseline timings include LinearAlgebra's copy of A into C, which is equal work because TriangularSolve's 3-argument form also writes out of place. Not a language-level claim: TriangularSolve is a pure-Julia library (no BLAS call in the matrix path) that beats one vendor library at one small size. Source comments claim the vector right-hand-side path beats BLAS trsv by up to 7x below n=256, but no published harness backs that.

name: D (gdc, ldc2) matmul with std.numeric.dotProduct in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C/gcc 16.1.0 and C/clang 22.1.8 (-O3 -march=native -flto=auto, -std=c23) transposed dot-product matmul of 1500x1500 doubles
workload: Allocate, generate and multiply two 1500x1500 double matrices; the D version transposes b and calls std.numeric.dotProduct per output cell, the C version transposes b and runs one scalar accumulation loop.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks matmul table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): D/gdc 1.505 s, D/ldc2 1.722 s, D/dmd 1.880 s versus C/gcc 3.034 s and C/clang 3.067 s, i.e. gdc about 2.0x, ldc2 about 1.76x and dmd about 1.61x faster than gcc C (derived from page data). Rust 3.067 s, Zig 3.071 s and Nim/gcc 3.091 s tie with C. Not like for like: the D program calls std.numeric.dotProduct (two partial sums) while every tied language runs the single-accumulator loop; in the like-for-like plb2 matmul (same i-k-j loop in D and C, Apple M1) D ldc2 1.35.0 takes 0.57 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, so D is about 5% slower there (derived from page data). BLAS-backed rows (D lubeck 0.042 s, C++ Eigen 0.081 s, NumPy, Arraymancer) are library comparisons and excluded.
compiler_and_flags: From common/commands.mk: C gcc 16.1.0 / clang 22.1.8 '-Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c23'; D ldc2 1.41.0 '-O5 -release -boundscheck=off', gdc 14.2.0 '-O3 -frelease -finline -fbounds-check=off', dmd v2.111.0 '-O -release -inline -boundscheck=off'. The D builds carry no -march=native and no LTO, so the flag difference favours C.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Debian forky/sid Docker image, README updated 2026-07-19
why_faster: Derived by the searcher from the source, not stated by the suite: Phobos std.numeric.dotProduct (std/numeric.d) unrolls 16-wide with two partial sums (sum0, sum1), a different floating-point reduction order; the C loop keeps one strict-FP accumulator and is built without -ffast-math, so the compiler cannot reassociate or vectorize it.
tradeoffs: Gain comes from one standard-library kernel, so a C programmer can match it by writing two or more accumulators or using -ffast-math; D's runtime and GC are not involved in the timed loop.
caveats: Not a language or compiler advantage: the high-level algorithm (transpose plus dot products) is the same, but the timed D path is Phobos' hand-unrolled two-accumulator dotProduct against a naive single-accumulator C loop, so summation order and results differ in the last bits (the harness only checks within 0.1 at n=101). Like for like (plb2, same loop in both languages) D ldc2 is slower than C. The C row is deliberately plain ('written as the average developer would'); C gets -march=native and -flto=auto that the D builds lack. gcc 16.1 and clang 22 are newer than the GCC 14 and LLVM bases of gdc and ldc2. Time includes allocation (D uses GC-allocated jagged arrays, C malloc/calloc rows) and matrix generation.

name: Fortran (gfortran) matmul in plb2
baseline: C (clang 15.0.0, make flags -O3 -fwrapv -flto) 1500x1500 double matmul with the same i-k-j loop order using double** rows
workload: Multiply two 1500x1500 double-precision matrices with triple-nested loops (no BLAS), one of four plb2 tasks. C (src/c/matmul.c) uses row pointers into one contiguous calloc block with i-k-j order (inner loop over j, c[i][j] += a[i][k] * b[k][j]); Fortran (src/fortran/matmul.F90) uses column-major explicit-shape dummy arrays with j-k-i order (inner loop over i), the same unit-stride access pattern and the same work. Elapsed wall time includes matrix generation and process startup.
claimed_speedup: matmul elapsed seconds on Apple M1: Fortran gfortran 13.2.0 0.51 s versus C clang 15.0.0 0.54 s, about 6% faster (derived from page data). Other compiled languages on the same row: Rust 0.56, Zig 0.56, Nim 0.56, Swift 0.56, D ldc2 0.57, V 0.57, Julia 0.76, Mojo 1.12. Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 13.2.0 with FFLAGS=-O3 (src/fortran/Makefile); C: clang 15.0.0 via $(CC) with CFLAGS=-O3 -fwrapv -flto (src/c/Makefile). Neither side passes -march/-mcpu.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (elapsed time, hyperfine)
why_faster: Not stated by the source. Searcher inference only: Fortran dummy arguments may not alias and arrays are contiguous, so gfortran can vectorize the inner loop without alias checks, whereas the C version indexes through double** rows.
tradeoffs: CC0 dedication (no patent grant). Fortran version needs gfortran; plb2 measures a naive triple loop, not tuned BLAS-level matmul.
caveats: Margin is about 6% (0.51 s versus 0.54 s) on one machine, single figures without variance in the table, and the rows were timed on different days (Fortran timing added 2024-01-04 as plb2 grew through January 2024), so this is a near-tie that may sit within run-to-run noise. Different compiler backends (gfortran versus clang), so the language and the compiler are confounded; no gcc-built C row exists. Both sides are at -O3 and neither uses -march; the C side adds -fwrapv and -flto (no effect expected on a one-file program). Fortran is the only language in the table that beats C on matmul; the README notes Clang already hoists the inner-loop invariants that many other languages cannot. Elapsed wall time includes process startup. CC0-1.0 dedication: no patent grant. Repository last changed 2025-01-30.

name: Halide
baseline: Expert hand-tuned C++ (OpenMP + Intel IPP), ARM NEON intrinsics/assembly and CUDA implementations of the same image-processing pipelines used as baselines in the PLDI 2013 paper (local Laplacian filters, bilateral grid, camera pipe, etc.)
workload: Image-processing pipelines written once as an algorithm plus a separate schedule (tiling, fusion, vectorization, parallelism): local Laplacian filters (99 stages) and bilateral grid on quad-core x86, plus camera raw pipe and others on ARM/CUDA, versus the hand-tuned expert code for the same pipelines.
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2013 abstract (search snippet only): Halide programs written in a few hours, with schedules found by stochastic search (autotuning), run up to 5x faster than hand-tuned C, intrinsics and CUDA implementations that experts optimized over weeks or months. Results-table fragments (snippet only; rows could not be matched to applications): '3.7x shorter / 2.1x faster' and '3x shorter / 5.9x faster', against baselines labelled Tuned C++, C++ OpenMP+IPP and hand-written CUDA on a quad-core x86 and a CUDA GPU. Pairing 2.1x with local Laplacian (262-line C++/OpenMP+IPP against 62 algorithm and 7 schedule lines, 335 ms vs 158 ms) and 5.9x with bilateral grid is the search agent's inference and is unconfirmed.
hardware: Quad-core x86 desktop, ARM and CUDA GPU platforms (exact CPU models not confirmed; paper PDF could not be opened)
why_faster: Decouples the algorithm from its schedule: the programmer or autoscheduler explores loop tiling, producer-consumer fusion, recomputation vs storage, vectorization and parallelism without rewriting the algorithm, which finds locality/parallelism trade-offs that were too laborious to hand-code in C++.
tradeoffs: Embedded DSL: requires writing a Halide pipeline and a schedule (C++17 API or Python bindings), ahead-of-time or JIT compiled through LLVM; schedule quality depends on the expert or autoscheduler; image/array pipelines only, not general code. LICENSE.txt is MIT with apps/bgu under Apache-2.0.
caveats: Numbers come only from WebSearch snippets of the PLDI 2013 paper (Ragan-Kelley et al.; the PDF hosts are blocked here, so the table was never opened); the snippet tool said the table text was garbled, so the row attributions (2.1x local Laplacian, 5.9x bilateral grid) are inferred, and the 5.9x row exceeds the abstract's 'up to 5x' without explanation. The baselines are the authors' 2012-13 expert implementations on 2012 hardware with CPU models, compilers and flags unconfirmed. The local Laplacian baseline calls Intel IPP library routines, so part of that comparison is Halide against a vendor library rather than against hand-written C++. The algorithm is the same mathematical pipeline on both sides, but the win comes from a different loop organization (fusion, tiling, recomputation, vectorization and parallelism chosen by the schedule and an autotuner), not from better code generation for the same loop nest. The repo does not carry the paper's baselines or harness; apps/blur/test.cpp does time naive C++, hand-written SSE intrinsics (blur_fast) and Halide side by side but publishes no numbers (enrichment lead). Halide is a C++-embedded DSL compiled through LLVM, so pipelines are callable directly from C++. License is MIT for the core; apps/bgu is Apache-2.0 (both OSI).

name: Fortran (gfortran) in niklas-heer/speed-comparison: Leibniz pi series
baseline: C (gcc 15.2.0, -O3 -flto -march=native with -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math) and the clang / C++ builds of the same Leibniz loop in the same suite
workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run (rounds.txt), timed with hyperfine; this historical run used two warm-up executions, three measured samples (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON) and a separate output execution; median wall time reported. Sources at revision c71e4cd81464b238172605982806c5bf827a70a1 (src/leibniz.f90, src/leibniz.c, src/leibniz.cpp).
claimed_speedup: Published snapshot 2026-09-05T193245, combined_results.csv medians in ms: Fortran 90 (gfortran 14.3.0) 141.67 vs C (gcc 15.2.0) 157.9, about 1.11x (derived from page data); vs C++ (g++) 158.78, about 1.12x (derived); vs C (clang 21.1.2) 146.07, about 1.03x (derived); vs C++ (clang++) 143.32, about 1.01x (derived). Min-max ranges: Fortran 141.04-144.35 ms, C++ clang++ 142.74-144.96 ms, C (clang) 143.63-150.61 ms, C (gcc) 155.46-160.78 ms, so the lead over the clang builds is inside the sample range.
compiler_and_flags: Fortran: gfortran 14.3.0 `gfortran leibniz.f90 -o leibniz -Ofast -flto -ffast-math -march=native -mtune=native`. C: gcc 15.2.0 `gcc -O3 -s -flto -march=native -mtune=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math -o leibniz leibniz.c -lm`. C++ clang++ 21.1.2 and C clang 21.1.2 use the same flag set (from docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json).
hardware: AMD EPYC-Genoa Processor, 4 threads, shared x86-64 VM (runner homelab-argo), kernel 6.18.38-talos
tradeoffs: The suite compares single implementations of one arithmetic loop, not Fortran as a whole. The Fortran loop is written differently from the C loop: it is unrolled by hand to four terms per iteration (src/leibniz.f90), while C/C++ use a one-term loop with an `i & 1` sign trick written to allow vectorisation (src/leibniz.c).
caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public for both sides) but no mechanism is established, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast -ffast-math (adds -freciprocal-math, -ffinite-math-only, -fno-math-errno) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the backends differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The sources are not line-for-line equivalent: the Fortran loop is hand-unrolled by four with compile-time signs (do i=1,rounds,4: pi = pi + x/(2i+1) - x/(2i+3) + x/(2i+5) - x/(2i+7), signed 32-bit counter), while the C and C++ loops compute each term's sign from the index parity (x = -1.0 + 2.0*(i & 1)) in unsigned arithmetic; both sum the same 1e9 terms with one division each. The CalculatedPi values differ by about 1.5e-10 (Fortran 3.141592654730, C 3.1415926545850823), so the lower accuracy column (9.440 vs 9.499 digits) reflects both the 12-digit printout and a different summation order. Nim (142.43 ms), Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) and Objective-C (142.95 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and C++ (g++) 226.37 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable, and in that snapshot g++-built C++ beat gcc-built C by 1.12x on the same loop, which shows how much of the gap is run-to-run and build variation. The HEAD pipeline pins different compiler versions than the snapshot (not re-checked); the snapshot's per-target JSON was used here.

name: Julia Base sort! in LilithHafner/InterLanguageSortingComparisons
baseline: C++ std::sort on std::vector<double> (src/script.cpp, Apple clang 13 under the g++ name) and C qsort with a comparator callback (src/script.c), same suite
workload: Sorting-dominated workload: fill a vector of 3^i uniform random Float64 values, sort it, compute a dot product; the sorting time is inferred by subtracting a no-sort control run; ns per element for 3 to 3^15 elements.
claimed_speedup: data.txt at 3^14 = 4,782,969 elements, ns per element of sorting: Julia 1.9.0-beta3 35.1, Julia 1.8.5 92.5, C++ 207.6, C gcc 307.2, so Julia 1.9 is 5.9x and Julia 1.8 2.2x faster than C++ (derived from page data). README: 'Julia and Rust outperform other languages'.
compiler_and_flags: Commands recorded in data.txt: C 'gcc script.c' and C++ 'g++ -std=c++11 script.cpp', both Apple LLVM 13.0.0 (clang-1300.0.27.3) with no -O flag (-O0); Julia 1.9.0-beta3 and 1.8.5 with default settings; Rust 1.67.0 'cargo run --release'.
hardware: 2019 MacBook Air, 1.6 GHz dual-core Intel Core i5, 8 GB
tradeoffs: Algorithm difference: the AcceleratedKernels.jl README calls Julia's Base CPU sort a radix sort, unlike std::sort's introsort and the C qsort comparator version; Julia JIT warm-up is not in the per-element numbers.
caveats: Crippled baseline: the C and C++ programs were compiled without any optimization flag (-O0) while Rust used --release, so std::sort's templated comparisons run unoptimized and the 5.9x (Julia 1.9 vs C++) and 8.8x (Julia 1.9 vs C) figures are mostly a build artifact. The C++ figure is not a sort time: script.cpp prints total runtime (vector allocation, generation, sort and dot product) times a fixed 0.85 (comment says 0.8, label says 80%) instead of subtracting the no-sort control, and it stops at 3^14 (N = 14) while the other languages run to 3^15. script.cpp also constructs a fresh default-seeded std::default_random_engine for every vector, so all repetitions of one size sort identical data. The C row is qsort with a function-pointer comparator, a different algorithm from std::sort and from Julia's sort!. Each data point is a single trial (README says so). claimed_speedup: 2026-10-05 run, CLBG::Fannkuchredux runtime in s: Nim/Clang 0.918 vs C/Gcc (prod, -O2) 1.036, about 1.13x (derived from page data); C/Clang 1.174; C++/Clang++ 1.128; C/Gcc/Fast 1.364; C/Clang/Fast 1.278; best -O3 row C++/Clang++/Unsafe 1.137, about 1.24x (derived from page data). Other Nim rows: Nim/Clang/ARC 0.934, Nim/NLVM 0.944, but Nim/Clang/Danger 1.114 and Nim/Clang/Max 1.231. The hobby compiler row C/mycc/LLVM/Default ran 1.026. Nim/Clang was 0.918-0.933 s in all six monthly runs from 2026-05-17 to 2026-10-05 against 1.020-1.047 s for C/Gcc prod, the best gcc or clang C/C++ build in every one of those runs.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2.12 `nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang` (system clang 22.1.8; no project nim.cfg or config.nims, so Nim's stock speed options apply, without -march=native; -d:release keeps runtime checks). C baseline rows (c/Makefile): prod = cc -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (gcc 16.0.1 trunk r16-8246 or clang 22.1.8); Fast = -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops, with -flto=thin passed only at link time (no -flto at compile time, so LTO is inert); Unsafe = -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math, with -flto=full only at link time. C++ rows use the same modes from cpp/Makefile. Versions and build commands from the build-cmd and version fields of results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js.
tradeoffs: Nim compiles to C and then to native code via the system C compiler, so the claim is about the C that Nim emits (garbage collection mode, bounds checks and overflow checks follow -d:release defaults).
caveats: Flags are not matched: C `prod` is -O2 with hardening and the Nim row is built for generic x86-64 with runtime checks on, but the -O3 Fast and -ffast-math C/C++ builds are also slower on this test (1.137-1.364 s). Nim emits C, so the gap is Nim-generated C versus hand-written C compiled by the same clang. The Nim source matches the C source loop for loop, except that Nim's int arrays are 64-bit where C uses 32-bit int. The result is fragile to build settings: Nim's own unchecked -d:danger clang build (1.114 s) and -Ofast -march=native LTO build (1.231 s) are slower than the checked default build (0.918 s), and C at -O3 with -funroll-loops (1.278-1.364 s) is slower than C at -O2 (1.036-1.174 s), which suggests the tiny loops (trip counts of at most 8) are hurt by aggressive unrolling or vectorisation and that the Nim/Clang default build happens to avoid it (inference, assembly not inspected). No mechanism, so the tier is capped at C. A hobby C compiler row (C/mycc/LLVM/Default) reached 1.026 s and 1.006 s in the 2026-08-14 run. One benchmark only: Nim/Clang is slower than C on CLBG::Nbody (1.73 s vs C/Gcc 1.465 s) and Matmul::Single (8.788 s vs 5.019 s). Single measurement per configuration per run; subjective AI-assisted suite. The C Fast and Unsafe LTO flags are link-only and inert.
