name: Yao.jl (Julia quantum circuit simulator) in Roger-luo/quantum-benchmarks
baseline: Qulacs 0.1.9 (C++ library driven from Python through pybind11, one Python call per gate or circuit) and QuEST via pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 (C library driven from Python through cffi, one Python call per gate), single-thread full-amplitude state-vector simulation
workload: Minimum time per gate application for X, H, CNOT and T gates on 4 to 25 qubits, and minimum time for a parameterized QCBM circuit (layers of per-qubit Rx/Rz rotations with ring CNOT entanglers) on 4 to 25 qubits, single thread (OMP/MKL/JULIA threads set to 1), Yao v0.6.1 per RESULTS.md (yao/Manifest.toml at the May 2020 refactor pins Yao 0.6.2 and YaoBlocks 0.10.3) against qulacs, QuEST (pyquest-cffi), qiskit-aer, ProjectQ, Cirq and PennyLane.
claimed_speedup: Read off the repo's 'relative to Yao' chart images images/gates_relative.png and images/pcircuit_relative.png (log scale, no tables; ratios approximate; bin/plot uses the minimum time for every package). Parameterized circuit (QCBM) at 25 qubits: qulacs about 1.9x and pyquest-cffi (QuEST) about 8x Yao's time; below about 11 qubits qulacs is faster than Yao (about 0.34x of Yao's time at 4 qubits). This circuit does unequal work: Yao makes 19n state-vector passes (each qubit's rotation chain fused into one 2x2 matrix, 8 mid layers, 9 entanglers) while qulacs and QuEST apply 41n separate gates (9 mid layers, 10 entanglers), a 2.16x pass ratio (derived from the benchmark scripts) that covers the whole qulacs gap. Single gates at 25 qubits (same work, one pass each): pyquest-cffi about 2.4x (X), 1.8x (H) and 2.5x (CNOT) Yao's time but about 0.75x on T (QuEST faster); qulacs about 1.0x on X, CNOT and T and about 0.6x on H (qulacs faster), and qulacs is faster than or equal to Yao on all four gates at most sizes between about 11 and 20 qubits (down to about 0.3x on H).
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.3.0 (LLVM 6.0.1 ORCJIT, skylake target, run without -O flags so Julia's default -O2), BLAS Intel MKL, Python 3.7.3 (from RESULTS.md). Not stated on the results page, derived from package sources: qulacs 0.1.9 exists on PyPI only as an sdist, built by pip through its CMake Release config (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG plus -march=native -mtune=native -mfpmath=both, AVX2 SIMD kernels enabled by default, OpenMP limited to 1 thread by OMP_NUM_THREADS=1); pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 is an sdist that builds QuEST through QuEST's own CMake, which sets -O2 (QuEST v3.2.0 CMakeLists; the exact QuEST version bundled by pyquest-cffi 0.1.1 was not checked). GCC version not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6230 @ 2.10GHz (single thread); Tesla V100 for the CUDA rows
stars_or_usage: 1.0k stars and 131 forks (Yao.jl); the benchmark repo, now yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks (old Roger-luo URL redirects), has 129 stars
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and compilation time is not part of the per-gate timings. Qulacs is faster on small circuits and the advantage of Yao appears only at 20 or more qubits.
caveats: First-party: the suite is written by Yao's author (reviewed by maintainers of several competitors per its acknowledgements). Results are marked 'only up to date till 2020'; the chart images were last regenerated on 2020-05-29 and the benchmark repo's last commit is 2022-05-17, with old package versions (qulacs 0.1.9, Julia 1.3.0). RESULTS.md and the README give only chart images, so every ratio is read off a log-scale chart. Unequal work in the parameterized circuit: YaoBlocks 0.10.3 PutBlock apply! calls instruct!(r, mat_matchreg(r, content), locs), so Yao's put(i=>chain(Rz, Rx, Rz)) is one dense 2x2 pass per qubit per layer, and Yao's build_circuit(k, 9, ...) has 8 mid layers and 9 entanglers where qulacs/QuEST build_circuit(n, 9, ...) has 9 and 10, giving 19n Yao passes against 41n qulacs/QuEST gate passes (2.16x); the reported 1.9x over qulacs is therefore not a per-gate or language win (qulacs' QuantumCircuitOptimizer gate fusion was not used). Single gates use different target qubits (Yao qubit 2 one-based, qulacs and QuEST qubit 3 zero-based) and Yao starts from rand_state while qulacs/QuEST start from |0>. qulacs and QuEST are timed through Python (pybind11 and cffi), so below about 10 qubits their numbers are dominated by Python call overhead; pyquest-cffi's QCBM function also calls np.random.rand inside the timed region. QuEST is built at -O2 (QuEST's CMake default) rather than -O3; qulacs is built at -O3 -march=native with AVX2 kernels and matches or beats Yao on single gates at large sizes. RESULTS.md's text calls panel d 'Toffolli' but the chart and bin/plot show the T gate; the relative charts label their y axis 'ns' though they plot ratios. The current quest/ directory holds a newer C++ google-benchmark harness (QFT only) that did not produce these charts. The baseline is not a C or C++ program at a stated -O3.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/Roger-luo/quantum-benchmarks (found while checking Julia packages with C or C++ competitors); opened README, RESULTS.md, images/gates_relative.png and images/pcircuit_relative.png

verification.notes: Chart readings in the record match images/gates_relative.png and images/pcircuit_relative.png, but the headline 1.9x over qulacs on the parameterized circuit is explained by unequal work (Yao fuses per-qubit rotation chains and runs one fewer layer: 19n vs 41n state passes, verified in yao/benchmarks.jl, qulacs/benchmarks.py, pyquest/benchmarks.py and YaoBlocks 0.10.3 put_block.jl/chain.jl). The only same-work win is 1.8-2.5x on X/H/CNOT against QuEST at -O2 through pyquest-cffi (QuEST faster on T); against qulacs at -O3 -march=native Yao is equal or slower on single gates at 11-25 qubits. Keep at C with these shortcomings; benchmark repo moved to yardstiq/quantum-benchmarks.

caveats: Small margin on one benchmark (1.04-1.07x over the best C row across five monthly runs), stable rather than noise, but from codegen differences between equivalent loops, not a Zig language mechanism. Zig's production row targets the native CPU (b.standardTargetOptions default) while the C prod rows are generic x86-64 -O2 with hardening, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe C/C++ rows are slower (1.137-1.364 s), so flags do not explain the gap; on this test every -O3 C/C++ row is slower than the -O2 C/Gcc row. The Zig loop is written differently from the C loop (decrementing j against the C k2 count) and uses @memcpy. Zig is slower than C on Matmul and several other numeric rows in the same file. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run. LangArena's README calls it a subjective, not peer-reviewed suite whose translations were AI-assisted and reviewed by the author.

name: Futhark
baseline: Hand-written OpenCL reference implementations from Rodinia 3.1 (CUDA for Myocyte on NVIDIA), Parboil 2.5 (MRI-Q) and FinPar (LocVolCalib, OptionPricing); the four Accelerate benchmarks (Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body) were compared against Accelerate 0.15.1 (a Haskell DSL with a CUDA backend), not C/C++.
workload: 16 GPU benchmarks manually translated to Futhark (Rodinia Backprop, CFD, HotSpot, K-means, LavaMD, Myocyte, NN, Pathfinder, SRAD; FinPar LocVolCalib, OptionPricing; Parboil MRI-Q; Accelerate Crystal, Fluid, Mandelbrot, N-body), datasets in the paper's Table 2; runtime averaged over 10 runs, excluding input upload, result readback and OpenCL context creation and kernel build on both sides (Rodinia timing patched to match).
claimed_speedup: PLDI 2017 paper: from about 0.6x (slower, FinPar LocVolCalib on AMD W8100) to 16x (Rodinia NN on GTX 780 Ti) against hand-written OpenCL/CUDA reference implementations; geometric mean 1.81x over the 12 benchmarks that have a low-level CUDA/OpenCL implementation; Futhark slower on 4 of those 12 (geometric mean 0.79x on them). Table 1 runtimes on GTX 780 Ti, reference vs Futhark in ms: NN 178.9 vs 11.0, Backprop 46.9 vs 20.7, K-means 1597.7 vs 572.2, Myocyte 2733.6 vs 555.4 (CUDA reference), Pathfinder 18.4 vs 7.4, SRAD 19.9 vs 16.1, MRI-Q 20.2 vs 15.5, OptionPricing 136.0 vs 106.8; slower: CFD 1878.2 vs 2235.9, HotSpot 35.9 vs 45.3, LavaMD 5.1 vs 6.7, LocVolCalib 1211.1 vs 1293.2. Artifact W8100 speedup files: srad 5.60, nn 5.14, hotspot 3.58, backprop 3.21, pathfinder 2.77, lavaMD 1.25, mri-q 1.24, OptionPricing 1.19, cfd 0.86, kmeans 0.79, LocVolCalib 0.62.
compiler_and_flags: Futhark compiler git 78c956ba58057ca6773cefb466efef2fa65c1386 with the OpenCL backend and no benchmark-specific flags; references built by their own suite Makefiles with gcc/g++ (-lOpenCL) and nvcc (CUDA 8.0 on NVIDIA). The paper and artifact state no host compiler versions or optimisation flags; Rodinia OpenCL Makefiles in the yuhc/gpu-rodinia mirror use g++ -g -O2 (backprop) and -g -O3 (nn). GPU kernels on both sides are compiled by the vendor OpenCL driver.
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 780 Ti with CUDA 8.0 and AMD FirePro W8100 (OpenCL benchmarks only); host CPU not stated.
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars, 210 forks; futhark-benchmarks 48 stars; futhark-pldi17 artifact 8 stars
tradeoffs: Purely functional ML-family language; programs are rewritten in Futhark and called from C, Python or other hosts through generated code; sequential/irregular code does not fit.
caveats: The wins are mostly not a language-level effect: the paper attributes them to the hand-written references leaving work unoptimised, namely Rodinia NN leaving 100 reduce operations sequential on the CPU, Backprop leaving a reduction sequential, K-means not parallelising the cluster-centre update, and Myocyte/MRI-Q lacking coalescing or locality optimisation; the authors say the 0.79x geometric mean on the 4 slower benchmarks is 'a better estimation of where Futhark stands in relation to hand-optimised GPU code'. HotSpot and Pathfinder references use time tiling that Futhark lacks. Same benchmarks but different parallelisation strategies, so same_algorithm is false for the large speedups (NN 16x, Backprop, K-means, Myocyte). Accelerate rows compare against a Haskell DSL, not C. Timings exclude transfer and kernel build on both sides. Numbers are from 2017 Futhark on 2013-2014 GPUs; the C and multicore CPU backends are not compared against C here, and futhark-benchmarks itself publishes no results. futhark-website performance.md compares against Thrust and Rodinia HotSpot only as graphs, without numbers or hardware in the text. A 2026 arXiv snippet (seen only by the search agent) reports big-integer multiplication about 1.35x slower than hand-coded CUDA. Paper PDF: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diku-dk/futhark-website/HEAD/publications/pldi17.pdf.

name: .NET 11 preview JIT (C#): benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: C# (.NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7) 0.931 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.08x faster than C and 1.23x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins, run_benchmarks.sh). C#: .NET SDK 11.0.100-preview.7, built as a file-based app with dotnet build -c Release -o out Program.cs (no .csproj in the repo) and run as dotnet out/Program.dll (default tiered JIT and default GC, no Native AOT).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 122.1 MiB for C# vs 33.3 MiB for C; Fibonacci(45) takes 3.793 s vs 1.694 s for C.
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs are naive per-node malloc/free (new/delete in C++) and walk every tree a second time to free it inside the timer, while the .NET GC never traces dead trees; an arena or pool allocator in C would beat the runtimes here. The native malloc-based rows for the same algorithm already spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) through 1.010 s (C), 1.033 s (Rust), 1.109 s (Ada) and 1.119 s (Zig) to 1.147 s (C++), so the 8% C# margin over C lies inside the run-to-run and implementation spread of one algorithm; the 1.23x figure is against the slowest of those rows. Several runtimes beat C on this workload in the same table (Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s, OCaml and Dart 0.865 s), which points at glibc per-node malloc/free rather than a .NET-specific code-generation win. The benchmark is 1 of 5 workloads, and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs Java 13.536 s, C# 11.914 s, OCaml 16.233 s; C is faster than C# on Fibonacci 1.694 s vs 3.793 s, strings 2.132 s vs 2.235 s and Mandelbrot 2.201 s vs 2.229 s). Managed runtimes keep default settings with JIT warm-up inside the timed region and may use extra GC and JIT threads, so wall time is not CPU time; .NET 11 was a preview SDK.

name: Bun (JavaScriptCore JIT 1.3.13): benchLANG binary trees
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, malloc and free per node, 1.010 s) and C++ (GCC 16.2.0, new and delete per node, 1.147 s)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees in one process after four other workloads: a stretch tree of depth 19, a long-lived tree of depth 18, then 2^(22-d) short-lived trees for each even depth d from 4 to 18, each built and checked; C and C++ free every tree with a recursive free pass (malloc/free or new/delete per node) inside the timer, the JS version just drops the references (no free pass).
claimed_speedup: JS (Bun) 0.816 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.24x faster than C and 1.41x faster than C++ (derived from page data). JS (Node v26.8.1) is slower at 1.444 s. Peak RSS 336.1 MiB for Bun vs 33.3 MiB for C.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s (GCC 16.2.0); C++: g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags. JS (Bun) 1.3.13: bun run directly, JIT default (no flags).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (performance governor), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux with i3-wm; results dated 3 September 2026, one run per language
why_faster: Stated by the suite's methodology: 'Binary trees: ... Allocator + GC + pointer chase, native code frees inside the timer, GC runtimes collect when they like'. Agent inference: per-node malloc/free (C, C++) against bump-pointer allocation and deferred or concurrent collection in a managed runtime; the C/C++ programs do not use an arena.
tradeoffs: 10x the peak memory of C; other columns are much slower than C (fib 7.735 s vs 1.694 s).
caveats: One run per language ('1 run/lang'), no variance. In-program wall times from a monotonic clock: JIT warm-up is inside the managed runtimes' timed region, but their garbage collection can run partly after the timer stops ('GC runtimes collect when they like'), while C/C++ pay an extra recursive free traversal inside the timer. The column is an allocator benchmark, not a codegen one: Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Dart AOT 0.865 s, OCaml 0.865 s, C# 0.931 s and Fortran 0.986 s also beat C's 1.010 s, so per-node glibc malloc/free is the bottleneck and an arena or pool allocator in C/C++ would likely beat every managed runtime (compare the Arena variant in LangArena, where C wins by about 6x). compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk GCC_CPP_BUILD); clang++ 22.1.8 row uses the same flags plus -stdlib=libc++; C rows -std=c23. C# (Staged): .NET 10.0.100, dotnet build -c Release, root Directory.Build.props sets TieredCompilation=false (every method JIT-compiled once at full optimisation, no tier-0 or dynamic PGO), ServerGarbageCollection=true, ConcurrentGarbageCollection=true; RyuJIT targets the host CPU at run time.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: Run-time compile inside the process: needs the .NET JIT and about 36 MiB resident versus about 3.4 MiB for the C++ interpreter; wins only for programs long enough to amortize compilation.
caveats: Different algorithm: the C++ baseline (brainfuck/bf.cpp) interprets a vector<Op> AST instruction by instruction, as brainfuck/README.md requires of every implementation ('interprets all bf instructions, one by one, without any squash or other hacks'), while the staged C# variant compiles the Brainfuck program to native code at run time (type construction and JIT inside the timed region), so it is listed as a separate '(Staged)' row. No C++ counterpart that also specializes on the program (template staging, LLVM ORC or asmjit, a BF-to-C compiler) was benchmarked, so the result shows runtime specialization beating an interpreter, not the .NET runtime beating C++ at the same work. The plain C# interpreter in the same suite is slower than C++/g++. The staged tape is a byte array with != 0 loop tests, the C++ tape a vector<int> with > 0 tests (outputs agree by checksum). The staged variant was contributed by hez2010 in PR #511 (merged 2025-11-17). It uses about 11x the memory of the C++ row (36.9 vs 3.38 MiB). Results are medians from one suite run on one machine (Xeon E-2324G), timed between libnotify start and stop messages, so process start-up is excluded for every language.
found_via: Suite-repo check after WebSearch for Julia/Java/.NET beating C++ returned only blog and forum threads; opened github.com/kostya/benchmarks README, brainfuck/ Makefile and staged sources via raw.githubusercontent.com.
why_faster: Runtime specialization on the input program (first Futamura-style staging): the JIT sees the whole Brainfuck program as types and removes interpretation overhead (derived from reading brainfuck/bf-staged.cs; the README gives no explanation).

verification.tier_reason: The measurement itself is reproducible (README bench.b table, brainfuck/bf-staged.cs vs brainfuck/bf.cpp, flags in common/commands.mk and Directory.Build.props, Xeon E-2324G), but the staged C# row runs a different algorithm (a run-time compiler) against the suite's C++ interpreter, so it cannot stand at A as a language-level win; capped at C like a tuned variant measured in place of the comparable program (Topaz precedent).
verification.notes: Numbers match the README row exactly; repo metadata (MIT, 2.9k stars, last commit 2026-07-19) checks out. Shortcoming: staged C# compiles the Brainfuck program at run time while the C++ baseline interprets it (the suite's brainfuck README requires interpretation), no C++ staged or JIT counterpart exists in the suite, and the plain C# interpreter is slower than C++ (1.280 vs 1.097 s); the win is runtime specialization, not the language. name: ClangJIT (Clang with JIT extensions for C++ templates)
baseline: The same Eigen expression (m = Ones + 0.00005*(m + m*m)) compiled ahead of time with runtime-sized Matrix<T,Dynamic,Dynamic> and float/double/long double dispatch, by the same Clang at -march=native -ffast-math -O3; the wiki also reports an AoT build specialized for one fixed size, which matches the JIT.
workload: Eigen bench/benchmark.cpp adapted: 40,000,000 repeats of small dense matrix operations; AoT runtime-sized matrices versus JIT-instantiated fixed-size matrices for sizes 3, 7 and 16, JIT compile time excluded from the runtime rows.
claimed_speedup: Runtime, double, 40,000,000 repeats, times reported by the code (JIT compile time excluded): size 3 JIT 1.0 s vs AoT dynamic-size 8.05 s vs AoT single fixed-size specialization 1.01 s; size 7 JIT 8.34 s vs AoT 20 s vs single specialization 8.45 s; size 16 JIT 35.3 s vs AoT 36.2 s vs single specialization 35.1 s (about 8x, 2.4x and 1.03x over dynamic-size AoT and parity with size-specialized AoT, derived from page data). Compile time (user): JIT only 3.5 s vs AoT double only 5.3 s and AoT float/double/long double with dispatch 9.7 s; one fixed-size specialization 2.95-4.95 s; includes and main only 2.58 s.
compiler_and_flags: ClangJIT (Clang fork, -fjit, [[clang::jit]] attribute) with -march=native -ffast-math -O3 on both sides per the wiki; the Clang used was built with GCC 8.2.0 in CMake RelWithDebInfo mode. Eigen version, ClangJIT commit and the benchmark's main() are not given.
hardware: Xeon E5-2699 (exact variant not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs a custom Clang/LLVM fork (not upstream); the program links the compiler infrastructure and compiles templates at run time (JIT start-up cost, memory, requires source or serialized AST available at run time); restrictions on decltype(auto), explicit specializations and pointer arguments listed on the wiki; the WG21 proposal P1609 for [[jit]] has not been adopted.
caveats: The run-time win is over Eigen's dynamic-size code path; the wiki's 'single specialization' AoT rows (1.01 s, 8.45 s, 35.1 s) equal the JIT rows, so JIT code is no faster than AoT C++ -O3 code that knows the size; the real advantage is lower compile time than instantiating many sizes or types ahead of time. JIT compile time is excluded from the runtime rows. First-party wiki, single runs without variance, CPU generation of the Xeon E5-2699 not stated, Eigen version not stated, main() omitted from the listings. The SC19 P3HPC paper (arXiv 1904.08555) was not reachable (arxiv.org, open-std.org P1609R0 and deepai blocked), so only the wiki was checked. Clang fork, last commit 2019-12-30. It is C++ with a JIT extension rather than another language, so it could also sit beside Easy::jit in wave 12 jits.
found_via: WebSearch: 'Clang-JIT C++ template instantiation at runtime speedup over ahead-of-time compiled code paper github' surfaced arXiv 1904.08555 and P1609; repo wiki then opened on github.com.
why_faster: Runtime values (matrix dimensions) become template arguments instantiated at run time, so the optimizer sees fixed sizes and can unroll and vectorize; only the sizes actually used are compiled (wiki: 'performance benefits of many AoT specializations, sometimes better, at a low compile-time cost').

verification.tier_reason: First-party wiki by the author with code listings for the timed functions, flags (-march=native -ffast-math -O3) and CPU family, but no main(), Eigen version, ClangJIT commit, CPU generation (E5-2699 v3 or v4) or run count, so not A; the peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 1904.08555, SC19 P3HPC workshop) could not be opened and its snippets give no numbers. The wiki's own size-specialized AoT rows match the JIT, so the win holds only against dynamic-size code.
verification.notes: Numbers match the wiki exactly; license Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (llvm/LICENSE.TXT, legacy NCSA appended), 237 stars, 25 forks, last commit 2019-12-30 (abandoned) all check out. Shortcoming: the JIT beats only dynamic-size AoT Eigen; AoT code specialized to the same size ties it (1.01 vs 1.0 s, 8.45 vs 8.34 s, 35.1 vs 35.3 s), win shrinks to 1.03x at size 16, first-party wiki with partial methodology, paper unreachable. Not yet catalogued anywhere (wave 12 leads.md lists it as a lead); related to the wave 12 Easy::jit entry but not a duplicate.

Compile time (user): JIT build 3.5s total vs AoT double-only 5.3s and AoT three-float-types-with-dispatch 9.7s.

name: dotnet JIT (C# on .NET 11): LangArena Distance::NGram
baseline: C++ using std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> for 4-gram counts (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s
workload: Count 4-gram frequencies of many generated string pairs in two hash maps and compute the n-gram overlap score.
claimed_speedup: C#/JIT 0.516 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s and C++/Clang++ 0.877 s (prod, -O2). The best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s (C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.85 s), so C# is about 1.67x faster than C++/G++ prod and 1.59x faster than the best row (derived from page data). Other .NET rows also win, including NativeAOT builds with no JIT: C#/SC-JIT 0.475 s, C#/R2R 0.526 s, C#/AOT 0.609 s. F#/JIT 0.534 s and Julia/Default 0.58 s also win. Java/OpenJDK at 2.072 s is slower, and the C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still: best C/Clang/Fast 1.789 s, C/Clang prod 1.811 s. The timed loop is 100 iterations over 10 string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet), after 20 untimed warm-up iterations.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). 'prod' (headline rows): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 for C++. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) are passed only on the link line (LDFLAGS) while objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place. Managed side: dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128, 'dotnet build -c Release' (Optimize=true) run as 'dotnet Benchmark.dll' with default tiered JIT; the C#/AOT rows are NativeAOT with IlcInstructionSet=native and IlcOptimizationPreference=Speed; Julia 1.13.1 run as 'julia --project=. --threads=16 benchmark.jl' (Julia/Max adds -O3 --check-bounds=no --math-mode=fast); Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar'. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count) before the timed loop.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Inferred from the sources, not stated by the suite: .NET Dictionary<uint,int> keeps entries in flat arrays, while libstdc++ std::unordered_map allocates a node per distinct key, and each string pair builds two maps. This is a container-implementation effect rather than JIT code quality.
tradeoffs: C# peak RSS about 41 MB. .NET 11 is a release candidate (11.0.100-rc.1) in this run.
caveats: This is a container comparison more than a JIT one. .NET NativeAOT builds with no JIT (C#/AOT 0.609 s, C#/SC-AOT 0.61 s) also beat every C/C++ row, so the runtime-jit-beats-aot category fits poorly. The C++ side uses node-based std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int>, reserved to the string length, with the default identity hash and prime-modulo buckets. An open-addressing map would likely close the gap. The C version (uthash with one malloc per distinct gram) is about 2x slower than the C++ one. The C# side does slightly more work: Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes copies both strings on every call. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). Java does not share the win, so this is not a general JIT property. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README links to LangArena; parsed results/2026-10-05-kostya-ms7c37.js for tests where a Java, C# or Julia row is faster than every Clang/GCC C and C++ row

why_faster: Author cannot fully explain it and lists hypotheses: HotSpot inlines aggressively after profiling, C math functions come from a library and cannot be inlined, and Java's % operator on doubles may map to better machine code.

name: Julia 1.13: LangArena Sort::Self (built-in sort vs std::sort)
baseline: std::sort on std::vector<int32_t> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ configuration is C++/G++ prod at 0.982 s
workload: Copy a large array of random 32-bit integers and sort it with each language's built-in sort (std::sort, Arrays.sort, Julia sort!).
claimed_speedup: Julia/Default 0.116 s vs C++/G++ 0.982 s (prod -O2, also the best of the 16 gcc/clang C and C++ configurations), C++/G++/Fast at -O3 0.998 s and C++/Clang++ 1.022 s: about 8.5x (derived from page data). Java/OpenJDK at 0.187 s is about 5.3x faster than std::sort (derived). C# Array.Sort at 1.057 s is slightly slower. The C rows use qsort with a comparison callback (best C/mycc/LLVM/Default 1.957 s, C/Gcc/Fast 1.964 s). The timed loop is 50 sorts of a copied 400,000-element array after 10 untimed warm-up sorts. The suite's same-algorithm sorts show no managed-runtime win: Sort::Quick Julia/Default 1.307 s vs C/Gcc 1.15 s, and Sort::Merge Julia/Default 1.602 s vs C/Clang 1.09 s.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). 'prod' (headline rows): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 for C++. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) are passed only on the link line (LDFLAGS) while objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place. Managed side: dotnet 11.0.100-rc.1.26425.128, 'dotnet build -c Release' (Optimize=true) run as 'dotnet Benchmark.dll' with default tiered JIT; the C#/AOT rows are NativeAOT with IlcInstructionSet=native and IlcOptimizationPreference=Speed; Julia 1.13.1 run as 'julia --project=. --threads=16 benchmark.jl' (Julia/Max adds -O3 --check-bounds=no --math-mode=fast); Temurin OpenJDK 27+35 run as 'java -Xmx2g -jar'. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count) before the timed loop.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: The suite's own docs/ai_analysis.js says Julia specializes sort! on Int32 at run time and picks a radix or counting sort (O(n)), and docs/ai_critic.js says this is the standard library choosing a better algorithm for the data type, not the language being faster ('You're comparing algorithms, not languages').
tradeoffs: Julia peak RSS about 405 MB; JIT latency excluded by the warm-up phase.
caveats: Not the same algorithm. std::sort is a comparison introsort. Julia's default sort! for Int32 runs ComputeExtrema and skips counting sort because the range (about 1,000,000) exceeds half the length. It then picks its stable LSD RadixSort, because 20 bits + 70 < 22 ln(399,999), which is about 284 (base/sort.jl ConsiderRadixSort). The suite's own docs/ai_critic.js says 'You're comparing algorithms, not languages'. A radix sort in C++ would be expected to match or beat it. The Java row is probably not a JIT win either. OpenJDK ships an AVX2 sort intrinsic (libsimdsort, avx2-32bit-qsort.hpp, C++ based on Intel x86-simd-sort) that Arrays.sort(int[]) can use on AVX2 CPUs such as this Ryzen; whether it ran here was not checked. Every language, C and C++ included, runs untimed warm-up iterations (20 percent of the timed count, cpp/src/benchmark.cpp and csharp/BenchmarkBase.cs) before the timed loop, so steady state is compared on both sides; the record's statement that only JIT languages get a warm-up was wrong. -flto appears only on the link line in cpp/Makefile, so the 'Fast' and 'Unsafe' rows get no actual LTO (the hot code sits in one translation unit, so this is probably immaterial). One measurement per test and configuration (no variance). LangArena's README calls it 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. Rows were selected as tests where a managed-runtime row beats every C/C++ row; most tests go the other way (for example Sort::Quick, Sort::Merge and Binarytrees::Arena). Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

name: OCaml 5.4.1: benchLANG binary trees vs C and C++ at -O3
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0: gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off) and C++ (g++ -std=c++20 with the same flags) binary-trees programs that allocate every node with malloc/free (C) or new/delete (C++)
workload: CLBG-style binary trees, depths 4 to 18: allocate, traverse and (in native code) free complete binary trees of individually allocated nodes; the README says the workload measures allocator plus GC plus pointer chasing, with native frees inside the timer and GC runtimes collecting when they like.
claimed_speedup: OCaml 5.4.1 0.865 s vs C 1.010 s and C++ 1.147 s: about 1.17x faster than C and 1.33x faster than C++ (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 16.2.0 -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s; C++: g++ 16.2.0 -std=c++20 with the same flags (nixpkgs-unstable pins, run_benchmarks.sh). OCaml 5.4.1: ocamlopt -O3 -unsafe -inline 200 -nodynlink monotonic.c bench.ml -o bench -ccopt -s. flake.nix installs the plain nixpkgs `ocaml` package, and nixpkgs' pkgs/development/compilers/ocaml/generic.nix defaults flambdaSupport to false, so -O3 has no effect and the OCaml side is a non-flambda (closure-mode) build.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz (cpupower performance governor, min and max 3500 MHz), 48 GB DDR4-3600 CL16, Arch Linux
why_faster: Source (README workload note): native code frees every node inside the timed region while GC runtimes collect when they like. Likely mechanism (inference): bump-pointer allocation in the runtime and deferred or concurrent reclamation against glibc malloc and free per node.
tradeoffs: Whole-process peak RSS 89.7 MiB for OCaml vs 33.3 MiB for C; OCaml is slower than C on primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s) and strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s).
caveats: One run per language (no variance) from a single machine on 2026-09-03. The C and C++ programs allocate every node with malloc/new and walk every tree a second time to free it inside the timer (languages/C/bench.c make_tree/free_tree), while OCaml just drops the references and its minor GC never traces dead young trees; an arena or pool allocator in C would likely beat the runtimes here. The column is an allocator benchmark, not a codegen one: the malloc-based native rows spread from 0.986 s (Fortran) through 1.010 s (C), 1.033 s (Rust), 1.109 s (Ada) and 1.119 s (Zig) to 1.147 s (C++), and Java 0.347 s, Nim 0.809 s, Bun 0.816 s, Dart AOT 0.865 s and C# 0.931 s also beat C. ocamlopt is an ahead-of-time compiler, so the win comes from the OCaml GC runtime, not from a JIT. Binary trees is 1 of 5 workloads and C wins overall (total 9.762 s vs OCaml 16.233 s); OCaml loses primes (3.200 s vs 2.725 s), Fibonacci (4.897 s vs 1.694 s), strings (5.000 s vs 2.132 s) and Mandelbrot (2.271 s vs 2.201 s). OCaml peak RSS 89.7 MiB vs 33.3 MiB for C. OCaml uses 63-bit tagged ints where C uses long long; the analyzer checks that checksums agree. The -O3 flag is ignored because the nixpkgs OCaml is built without flambda.

name: Racket (Staged): Brainfuck bench.b in kostya/benchmarks
baseline: C++/g++ brainfuck (brainfuck/bf.cpp): an AST-walking interpreter with std::vector ops, g++ -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Run the bench.b Brainfuck program; the staged Racket version generates a lambda from the program with syntax objects and calls eval (compiled by Racket CS / Chez Scheme) inside the timed region, with unsafe fixnum and vector operations.
claimed_speedup: bench.b: Racket (Staged) 0.885s (MAD 0.000) vs C++/g++ 1.097s, C/gcc 1.112s, C++/clang++ 1.167s (about 1.24x vs g++, derived from page data); memory 101.37 + 0.06 MiB vs 3.38 + 0.00 MiB. On mandel.b the staged Racket version is slower than C++/g++ (15.722s vs 10.143s). The same-algorithm (non-staged) Racket interpreter is slower than C++/g++ on both (1.761s and 35.373s).
compiler_and_flags: C++ baseline: g++ 16.1.0 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -Wcast-align -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -std=c++23 (common/commands.mk GCC_CPP_BUILD, libstdc++); clang++ 22.1.8 row uses the same flags with -stdlib=libc++. Racket 9.2 (Racket CS) run as PLT_CS_COMPILE_LIMIT=100000 racket bf-staged.rkt (common/commands.mk RACKET_RUN), so the large eval'd form is compiled to machine code rather than interpreted.
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2324G (README Environment section); Debian forky/sid Docker image
tradeoffs: About 100 MiB resident versus 3.4 MiB; uses unsafe ops (#%declare #:unsafe) so no bounds checking, the same as the C++ baseline's unchecked indexing.
caveats: Not the same algorithm: the C++/g++ baseline (brainfuck/bf.cpp) is a tree-walking interpreter that dispatches every Brainfuck instruction at run time, while the staged variant compiles the Brainfuck program to native code at run time; the suite's own brainfuck/README.md says implementations interpret every instruction one by one, so the staged rows deviate from the suite rule. The repository has no C or C++ staged/JIT counterpart, so the result shows runtime compilation beating an interpreter, not the language beating C++ at equal work. The timed region (between the notify calls) includes parsing and the run-time compile on both sides, but verify() runs one staged compile of a hello-world program before timing, warming the compiler machinery. Measurements run with QUIET=1 (analyze.rb, 10 attempts, median with MAD), so output flushing does not matter. Single machine (Xeon E-2324G), single suite. Wins only on bench.b (1.24x) and loses on mandel.b (15.722s vs 10.143s, 1.55x slower), so the bench.b win does not generalise; the bench.b margin is well outside the reported MADs on this machine. On bench.b C++/g++ is not the fastest AOT interpreter either (V/gcc 0.985s, Rust 1.008s, D/ldc2 1.078s). The generated code uses unsafe fixnum and vector operations (#%declare #:unsafe); bf.cpp also indexes std::vector without bounds checks, so safety checks are comparable.

name: Bun (JavaScriptCore JIT 1.4.2): alya-lang/benchmarks binary trees
baseline: C (gcc 13.3.0 -O2, malloc and free per node, binary_trees.c)
workload: Binary trees at depth 14: stretch tree, long-lived tree, then repeated pairs of short-lived trees built, checked and (in C) freed.
claimed_speedup: Bun 98.3 ms vs C 126.3 ms (median of 10 timed runs after 1 warm-up): about 1.28x faster (derived from page data). Of the 14 benchmarks in the same table, Bun beats C only on this one.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0 invoked by cross_lang/runner.ts as 'gcc -O2 binary_trees.c -o binary_trees_c' (no -march, no LTO); Bun 1.4.2 run as 'bun run binary_trees.js' (installed by oven-sh/setup-bun@v2 at CI time); Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS x64 on a GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner (.github/workflows/benchmark.yml).
tradeoffs: Bun process start (about 24 ms cold start per the README) is inside the measured time; Bun peak RSS about 36 MB vs about 3 MB for C.
caveats: This suite exists to compare the new Alya language; the Bun-versus-C row is incidental, first-party to Alya, and the repo gives no mechanism for Bun. C is built at -O2, not -O3. Runs happen on a shared GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest VM (CPU model not stated, noisy neighbours) and the README is rewritten by CI on each dispatch, so the numbers drift between commits. The work differs in memory management: the C version calls glibc malloc per node and walks every tree again with a recursive free_tree inside the timed region, while the JS version never frees and leaves dead trees to the GC (possibly never collected before exit). Bun beats C on only this 1 of 14 rows; C wins the other 13 by 1.9x to 9x. The README's start-up, binary-size and RSS table rows for Bun and C are hard-coded strings in runner.ts, not measurements.

name: Julia (no BLAS) matmul with @fastmath @simd ivdep in kostya/benchmarks

The C inner loop is a scalar floating-point reduction (t += p[k] * r[k]) that gcc and clang at -O3 may not reorder or vectorise without -ffast-math, so it runs as one serial dependency chain; the Julia inner loop uses the other loop order (c[m,n] += a[m,k] * b[k,n] down a column-major column), whose iterations are independent and vectorise without reassociation, plus @simd ivdep (no alias checks), @fastmath (FMA contraction and reassociation allowed) and @inbounds. The README's Julia version (1.11.6) disagrees with the Dockerfile at HEAD (1.12.6), so the version behind the published row is uncertain. workload: 100,000 random walks of 3,000 coin flips each, accumulating a histogram of final displacements.
claimed_speedup: C++-11 3.88 s vs Julia v0.3 1.27 s and Julia v0.4 1.68 s: about 3.1x and 2.3x faster (derived from page data); the README says 'The Julia code runs three times faster than the C++ code'.

name: Node.js (V8 Irregexp JIT) regex-dna in kostya/jit-benchmarks
baseline: C regex-dna (regexdna/test.c, Mike Pall's 2009-era Benchmarks Game program) using libpcre (PCRE1) with pcre_study(re, 0, ...), so PCRE's JIT is not enabled and every match runs in PCRE's interpreter; gcc 12.2.0 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops, linked with -lpcre
workload: Benchmarks Game regex-dna on a fasta file generated by regexdna/helper.c with n=3,500,000 (ONE 7M, TWO 10.5M and THREE 17.5M bases): nine case-insensitive variant-count regexes and eleven IUB-code substitutions after stripping headers and newlines; single thread, one process run, timed externally from the 'started' message (after input reading and line stripping) to process exit.
claimed_speedup: regexdna: Node 1.06s vs C 5.6s (about 5.3x, derived from page data), one measured run per row (Runs 1); memory 622.4 MB vs 86.7 MB. PHP (PCRE2 via preg_*) takes 1.39s (JIT) and 1.40s on the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions.
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -funroll-loops -Wno-unused-result -Wno-implicit-function-declaration ... -lpcre (tools/languages.rb c build_cmd plus tools/benchmarks.rb build_flags for regexdna); gcc 12.2.0 per README Versions; libpcre version not stated. Node.js 19.7.0 run as node test.js with default flags.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
tradeoffs: Node uses 622 MB vs 86.7 MB for the C program.
caveats: Crippled baseline: the C program calls pcre_study with flags 0, so libpcre runs its interpreter, while V8's Irregexp compiles each regex to native code; the comparison measures regex-engine mode (interpreted PCRE1 vs compiled Irregexp), not JavaScript against C. The PHP rows, which drive PCRE2 through preg_* with the same nine caseless counts and eleven substitutions (PHP's pcre.jit setting defaults to on), take 1.39s and 1.40s, 4x faster than the C row, so a C build with PCRE or PCRE2 JIT would likely land near Node. The Crystal row (0.34s) is not the same work: its test.cr does all eleven substitutions in one gsub pass with an alternation and a hash, uses case-sensitive variant regexes and maps S to (c|t), so it is no evidence for what JIT-enabled C would reach. The C program dates from before PCRE gained a JIT (PCRE 8.20, 2011). Single measured run per row (Runs 1). Numbers are from round 1 (2023-02-28) with node 19.7.0 and were not rerun; the only 2026 commit adds a README link. The README states no mechanism. The win belongs to V8's Irregexp engine (C++), not the JavaScript language.

name: OrdinaryDiffEq.jl (DifferentialEquations.jl) ODE solvers vs Sundials, ODEPACK and Hairer codes
baseline: Sundials CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (C), ODEPACK lsoda (Fortran) and Hairer dopri5/dop853/odex (Fortran), called through Julia wrappers
workload: Work-precision diagrams (wall time versus error at tolerances 1e-6 to 1e-13) for non-stiff ODEs: Lotka-Volterra, Pleiades and Three-Body.
claimed_speedup: SciMLBenchmarks README summary (no numbers): non-stiff 'OrdinaryDiffEq.jl's methods are the most efficient by a good amount', the Vern methods do best, ARKODE and Hairer dopri5/dop853 are 'far less efficient than the Vern methods', CVODE_Adams and lsoda 'tend to not do very well'; stiff: ARKODE is inconsistent and KenCarp4 is 'much more efficient in most cases'. Rigid Body work-precision plot (RigidBody_wpd_5_1, 3 equations, AMD EPYC 7502): Vern7/Vern8 take about 2e-5 to 1e-4 s while CVODE_Adams and ARKODE (explicit, order 6) take about 1e-4 to 1e-3 s over the same error range, roughly 5-10x at matched error (read off the plot, derived from page data). On the stiff Pollution page (20 equations) FBDF is only modestly ahead of CVODE_BDF in the high-tolerance plot, and the page's own conclusion reads 'Sundials CVODE_BDF the best here'.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.11.9 (LLVM 16.0.6, znver2) for OrdinaryDiffEq; Sundials C library via Sundials.jl v6.7.1 and Sundials_jll v7.5.0+0 (BinaryBuilder build, compiler and flags not stated); ODEInterface_jll v0.0.2 and LSODA_jll v0.1.2 for the secondary baselines
hardware: AMD EPYC 7502 32-Core (128 threads), Linux; Julia 1.11.9, LLVM 16.0.6 (znver2), per the RigidBody and Pollution page appendices
tradeoffs: Julia JIT start-up and package precompilation; wins depend on the Verner high-order Runge-Kutta methods and algorithm-specific interpolation that the C and Fortran codes do not provide.
caveats: First-party suite run by the SciML project on its own solvers. Algorithm versus algorithm: Vern7/8/9 and Tsit5 against Dormand-Prince, Adams and ARKODE methods, so the win is not the language's (same_algorithm false). In this harness the Sundials C solvers are driven through Sundials.jl wrappers with a Julia right-hand side called back across the C boundary on every function evaluation, and each timed solve includes wrapper setup; on 3-equation problems solved in 20 microseconds to 1 ms this fixed overhead weighs heavily, and the Julia methods also get a StaticArrays out-of-place variant (prob_choice 2) that the C library cannot use. Numbers exist only as plots; the RigidBody page notes that some of the gap depends on each library's error norm. The win is not universal: on the stiff Pollution problem the page's conclusion names Sundials CVODE_BDF the best, and FBDF is only modestly ahead in its high-tolerance plot. Fortran baselines (dopri5, dop853, radau, ODEInterface) are out of scope for a C/C++ baseline.

why_faster: Pages credit the Verner methods and algorithm-specific interpolants; Julia specialization of the user's ODE function (FullSpecialize, StaticArrays) is implied by the setup but not argued as the cause.

name: Go: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ row is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s, the C rows use uthash with a strdup per word at about 1.99 s
workload: Split a generated text of 50,000 space-separated words (3 to 8 lowercase letters, about 325 KB) into words, count frequencies in a hash map, then report the most frequent word and the vocabulary size; 360 timed iterations after 72 untimed warm-up iterations (run.js). A verifier simulation of the suite's LCG gives 18,623 distinct words and a unique top word ('tea', 9 times), reproducing run.js's checksum 1998586832 over 432 runs, so all languages do the same work.
claimed_speedup: Go 1.129 s vs C++/G++ 1.638 s and C++/Clang++ 1.707 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s (-O3 -march=native), best of the 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ configurations C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s, C/Clang 1.988 s: about 1.41x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.45x faster than C++/G++ prod (derived from page data). Go/Opt (static, stripped) 1.11 s. Peak RSS 11.3 MB vs 7.5-7.9 MB for the C++ rows.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions and build commands from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu snapshot package), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections; C++ adds -std=c++20. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use -fprofile-correction (GCC). The Makefiles pass -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only on the link line while the objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place (inference from the Makefiles). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Go 1.27.1 'go build -buildvcs=false' (default gc compiler, no PGO). Go harness runs 20 percent untimed warm-up iterations and runtime.GC() before the timed loop; the C++ harness also runs the same warm-up count.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Go uses strings.Fields (substrings share the text's backing array, no copies) and a built-in map[string]int; C++ copies each word out of an istringstream into std::string keys (this agent's reading of the sources).
tradeoffs: Zero-copy word keys; the Go and Rust versions keep a reference to the whole text while the map is alive.
caveats: Mostly a standard-library and idiom comparison (tokenizing and hashing containers), so the result is about istringstream and node-based unordered_map, not code generation; a C++ version with string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close the gap (inference, not measured). Other languages also beat every C/C++ row: Crystal 0.88 s, Zig 0.91 s, Rust 1.021 s, Java/OpenJDK 1.272 s (the Java row is a separate verified record of the same test). The C version (strdup of the whole text every iteration, strtok_r, uthash with a strdup per new key) is slower still at 1.963-2.084 s. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 Fast, Unsafe and PGO variants were also compared and Go still wins; the Makefiles' -flto flags are link-only, so the 'LTO' builds probably get no LTO. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, which is a tie).

name: regex (Rust regex crate)
baseline: PCRE2 (interpreter and JIT) and RE2 (C/C++ regex engines); Hyperscan also measured
workload: rebar curated barometer: about 38 regex search benchmarks (literals, alternations, dates, Unicode classes, bounded repeats, dictionaries, ReDoS-style patterns, noseyparker rules) across many engines; corroborated by the LangArena Etc::LogParser task (13 log-grep patterns over generated web-server log lines).
claimed_speedup: rebar README summary of search-time benchmarks (geometric mean of per-benchmark speed ratios to the best engine, lower is better): hyperscan 2.37 (28 benchmarks), rust/regex 1.12.2 3.08 (38), pcre2/jit 10.47 6.00 (34), re2 10.39 (31), pcre2 interpreter 114.75 (33). The compile-time summary goes the other way: pcre2 1.41, pcre2/jit 6.20, rust/regex 11.85, re2 12.28. Intersection derived from the repo's recorded CSVs record/curated/2025-12-19/*.csv (median search times; derived from page data, re-computed by the verifier): vs PCRE2 JIT rust/regex is faster in 21 of 34 benchmarks, geometric-mean time ratio 2.13x; vs RE2 faster in 27 of 31, 4.3x; vs the PCRE2 interpreter faster in 32 of 33, 44x; vs Hyperscan faster in only 12 of 28 (Hyperscan about 1.45x faster overall). LangArena results 2026-10-05, Etc::LogParser (13 patterns, count all matches): Rust 0.302 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 0.485 s (clang -O2), 0.488 s (gcc -O2) and 0.486 s (gcc -O3 -march=native 'Fast' build), about 1.6x; vs the C++ version, which uses RE2, 0.993-0.998 s (about 3.3x). In the same file, Template::Regex ({{(.*?)}} replacement): Rust 3.699 s vs C with PCRE2 JIT 1.155-1.173 s, so PCRE2 JIT is about 3.2x faster there; vs C++ RE2 4.84-4.90 s, Rust is about 1.3x faster.
compiler_and_flags: rebar: engine versions only (rust/regex 1.12.2, pcre2 10.47, re2 2025-11-05). PCRE2 (with SUPPORT_JIT) and RE2 are compiled from vendored source by the cc crate inside each engine's Cargo release profile (lto = fat, codegen-units = 1, default opt-level 3, so -O3 by the cc crate's default). This is derived from engines/pcre2/build.rs, engines/re2/build.rs and their Cargo.toml files; no compiler version is stated. LangArena: rustc 1.99.0, 'cargo build --release' with regex 1.12. C: clang 22.1.8 and gcc 16.0.1, prod flags -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, Fast flags -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -funroll-loops with -flto=thin, linked against the system libpcre2-8. C++ is linked against the system libre2. The system PCRE2 and RE2 versions and build flags are not recorded in the results file.
hardware: rebar does not state the machine. LangArena results file: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB, x86_64 Linux.
why_faster: rebar analysis: finite-automata engines (lazy DFA, one-pass DFA) with SIMD literal prefilters (memchr, Teddy) avoid backtracking and give DFA-speed matching on most patterns; PCRE2 JIT stays faster where JIT-compiled backtracking is cheap (small anchored patterns, capture-heavy cases).
stars_or_usage: 4.0k stars; the regex engine behind ripgrep and much of the Rust ecosystem
tradeoffs: No backreferences or look-around (linear-time guarantee in exchange). Pattern compilation is slower than PCRE2 and RE2. Unicode tables add binary size. Rust API; C++ needs the rure C binding or FFI.
caveats: rebar's summary geometric means cover different benchmark subsets per engine (28 to 38), so only the intersection numbers compare like for like; the verifier re-computed them from the repo's recorded CSVs and they match. rebar is written by the regex crate's author, and its README says the analysis is biased towards that crate (BIAS.md). rebar states no CPU or compiler version. Hyperscan beats regex overall, and PCRE2 JIT wins 13 of the 34 shared benchmarks. LangArena is independent, with public code, compilers, flags and CPU. Its C LogParser time is the same at -O2 and at -O3 -march=native (0.486 s), so the opt level does not explain the gap. The PCRE2 and RE2 it measures are system libraries whose versions and build flags are not recorded. The C++ LangArena rows use RE2, not PCRE2. LangArena's Template::Regex task shows a 3.2x loss to PCRE2 JIT. The win is a library and engine-design effect (lazy DFA plus SIMD literal prefilters), not a language effect.

name: Rust: LangArena Distance::NGram
baseline: C++ using std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> for 4-gram counts (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ row is C++/Clang++/PGO at 0.822 s, C/Clang is 1.811 s
workload: For 10 generated string pairs (lengths 4 to 20,003 over a 10-letter alphabet, so at most 10,000 distinct 4-grams), count 4-gram frequencies of each string in two hash maps (reserved to the string length) and compute the n-gram overlap score; 100 timed iterations after 20 untimed warm-up iterations (run.js).
claimed_speedup: Rust 0.533 s vs C++/G++ 0.863 s and C++/Clang++ 0.877 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 0.85 s (-O3 -march=native), best of the 16 Clang/GCC C and C++ configurations C++/Clang++/PGO 0.822 s, C/Clang 1.811 s: about 1.54x faster than the best C/C++ row and 1.62x faster than C++/G++ prod (derived from page data). Rust/WMO (codegen-units 1) 0.388 s. Peak RSS 4.3 MB vs 6.6-7.1 MB for the C++ rows.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (cpp/Makefile, c/Makefile; versions and build commands from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu snapshot package), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag). Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections; C++ adds -std=c++20. 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math -fvisibility=hidden -fno-common -fstrict-overflow -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use -fprofile-correction (GCC). The Makefiles pass -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) only on the link line while the objects are compiled without -flto, so no link-time optimisation actually takes place (inference from the Makefiles). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Rust: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release' (default release profile from rust/Cargo.toml: opt-level 3, 16 codegen units, no LTO, no target-cpu). hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Rust's std HashMap (hashbrown SwissTable) is flat open addressing, while C++ std::unordered_map<uint32_t,int> allocates a node per distinct 4-gram, and the test builds two maps per string pair (this agent's inference from the containers used).
tradeoffs: Flat hash tables use less memory per entry than node-based std::unordered_map.
caveats: Container comparison: a C++ open-addressing map (absl::flat_hash_map, boost::unordered_flat_map) would likely close the gap (inference, not measured), and the suite only uses std::unordered_map. The C version (uthash, one malloc per distinct gram) is slower still at 1.789-1.844 s for the non-instrumented Clang/GCC rows. LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. The suite publishes one measurement per test and configuration (no variance). baseline: samtools faidx 1.24 with HTSlib 1.24 (C); also measured: fastahack, SeqKit (Go), noodles and rust-bio (Rust), pyfaidx (Python).
workload: Build a samtools-compatible .fai index (`z-fasta index --emit-fai`) of uncompressed FASTA (human genome ~2.9 GiB, transcriptome ~459 MiB, proteome ~13 MiB), and fetch one 1 kbp region through an existing index; warm cache.
claimed_speedup: README (v0.3.5, measured 2026-10-10) and bench/index/REPORT.md Table 5, .fai index build, z-fasta `index --emit-fai` vs samtools faidx: human genome 0.3824 s vs 8.1614 s (21.3x), transcriptome 0.1546 s vs 1.7112 s (11.1x), proteome 0.0113 s vs 0.0650 s (5.8x); fastahack (C++) 20.8901 s on the genome (54.6x, REPORT.md only). One 1 kbp positional GET through an existing index: human genome 2.3 ms vs 8.2 ms, transcriptome 8.2 ms (.zfi) or 28.3 ms (.fai) vs 301.8 ms, proteome 2.7 ms (.zfi) vs 17.9 ms. Stats is compared with noodles and SeqKit only, not samtools.
compiler_and_flags: z-fasta 0.3.5 built with Zig 0.16.0, `zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dstrip=true`; build.zig uses standardTargetOptions and no -Dtarget/-Dcpu is passed, so the binary targets the host (native) CPU. samtools 1.24 and HTSlib 1.24 built from source by tools/install.sh with plain `./configure` and `make`, i.e. package-default flags (htslib Makefile `-g -Wall -O2 -fvisibility=hidden`, samtools Makefile `-g -Wall -O2`) for generic x86-64; C compiler not named.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3950X (README Performance section); Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.43 target in the report provenance); zebrac 0.6.2, 5 measured samples after 3 warmups, 5000 ms budget per command, warm cache.
stars_or_usage: 9 stars, 0 forks (GitHub repo page, 2026-10-11); new project (v0.3.5, 244 commits).
tradeoffs: Uncompressed FASTA only; own .zfi index plus samtools-compatible .fai for representable FASTA; one static executable (about 800 KiB) with no runtime dependencies; scope limited to index, get, validate and stats.
caveats: First-party benchmark with the author's own runner and reports. Both sides are single-threaded (no threads in src/indexer.zig; HTSlib's fai_build_core is a per-character bgzf_getc loop), so the gap is algorithmic: z-fasta validates fixed-width line blocks with SIMD whitespace counts over 256 KiB reads. The cross-tool `--emit-fai` lane constructs the .fai bytes but discards the emitted stream while samtools writes a .fai sidecar file, so output destinations differ (REPORT.md says so). z-fasta is built for the native CPU while samtools uses its package-default -O2 generic build; the C compiler is unnamed. The 7.9 GiB/s genome throughput is a warm page-cache figure. The rust-bio lane is a custom FAI writer, not a rust-bio command. v0.3.5 indexing is 10-40% slower than v0.3.4 on 15 of 30 cases (genome .fai 382.4 ms vs 321.2 ms) after whitespace validation was added. FAI parity with samtools passed 20/20 structural edge cases.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/simd?l=zig (listed as 'z-fasta, 9 stars').

Not a language-level claim.

name: Zig (csv-zero): LangArena CSV::Parse
baseline: C and C++ CSV parsing: best C/C++ row is C/Clang prod at 2.223 s, a hand-written scalar quote-tracking byte loop (c/src/csv.c) that copies each numeric field into a stack buffer and calls glibc strtod; the C++ test (cpp/src/csv_parse.cpp) uses the header-only lazycsv parser and calls std::stod on a std::string copy of each trimmed cell.
workload: Parse a generated 100,000-row CSV (70 timed iterations, generation untimed) whose quoted text columns contain commas, doubled quotes and a literal backslash-n character pair (no embedded line breaks), extract three unquoted float columns per row (fields 1, 3 and 5) and average them.
claimed_speedup: Zig 0.974 s (ReleaseSafe) vs C/Clang 2.223 s, C++/Clang++ 2.348 s, C++/G++ 2.543 s and C/Gcc 2.572 s (prod, -O2): about 2.3x faster than the best C/C++ row (derived from page data). The -O3 -march=native rows are no faster (C/Gcc/Unsafe 2.378 s, C++/Clang++/Fast 2.396 s, C/Clang/Fast 2.422 s, C++/G++/Fast 2.645 s), so Zig leads the best -O3 row by about 2.4x (derived). Zig/Unchecked (ReleaseFast) is 0.585 s; Rust (simd-csv) 0.881 s and Odin/Default 1.789 s also beat every C/C++ row. Earlier monthly runs show a similar lead: 2.24x on 2026-08-14, 2.18x on 2026-09-03, 1.96x on 2026-09-18 (Zig 0.16.0; derived from the results files).
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ (c/Makefile, cpp/Makefile; versions from the results file): Clang 22.1.8 and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk r16-8246, Ubuntu package build), libstdc++ (no -stdlib flag), -std=c++20 for C++. Headline 'prod' rows (make -j prod): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3, no -march). 'Fast': -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -DNDEBUG -pipe -fstack-protector -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops. 'Unsafe': -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -fno-stack-protector -fomit-frame-pointer -fvisibility=hidden -fno-trapping-math. 'PGO': -O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use (Clang) or -fprofile-use (GCC). -flto=thin (Fast) and -flto=full (Unsafe) appear only in LDFLAGS while objects are compiled without -flto, so those builds probably get no LTO (inference from cpp/Makefile). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO rows were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows excluded). Zig: 0.17.0, 'zig build build-zig', which zig/build.zig maps to optimize = .ReleaseSafe (LLVM optimisation with runtime safety checks kept); the target comes from standardTargetOptions with no -Dtarget or -Dcpu in the build command, so it presumably builds for the host CPU (inference from zig/build.zig). The Zig/Unchecked row is ReleaseFast. csv-zero is pinned by commit a687d508 in zig/build.zig.zon.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78 GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37; the run's change note says the host moved from Ubuntu to Arch Linux)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The Zig test uses the csv-zero iterator and std.fmt.parseFloat (an Eisel-Lemire style parser), while the C++ test calls std::stod on a std::string copy of each cell, which goes through libc strtod; much of the gap is plausibly float parsing rather than CSV splitting (this agent's inference from reading the sources, not measured).
tradeoffs: Peak RSS about 13 MB, similar to C. Depends on the third-party csv-zero package.
caveats: Library comparison: the suite pins a different CSV parser per language (README: 'for library-based (JSON, Base64, CSV), I use the best practical option for each language'), SIMD csv-zero for Zig against a scalar hand-written C loop and lazycsv for C++, with different float parsers, so the result says nothing about Zig code generation; a C/C++ build with a SIMD CSV scanner and fast_float would be the fair comparison. The workload has no multi-line fields (the '\\n' in the generator is a literal backslash and n). The Zig prod build is ReleaseSafe with safety checks on and presumably host-CPU code generation (inference), against generic x86-64 C/C++ prod builds; the -march=native C/C++ rows still lose. The sibling Rust row of this test is in the wave sys file (batch-29, tier C). LangArena calls itself 'a subjective benchmark' and says AI tools helped translate the tests between languages. One measurement per test and configuration (no variance reported), although the harness checks each run's checksum against run.js. The headline C/C++ 'prod' rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows also lose. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked as text tests where a non-C row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests go the other way (Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust; Distance::Jaro is a tie).

name: Zig: LangArena Etc::Words
baseline: C++ splitting with std::istringstream and counting in std::unordered_map<std::string,int> (g++ 16, clang++ 22); best C/C++ row is C++/G++/PGO at 1.587 s, the C rows use uthash with a strdup per word at about 1.99 s
workload: Split a large generated text into words and count word frequencies, then report the most frequent word and the vocabulary size.
claimed_speedup: Zig (ReleaseSafe) 0.91 s vs C++/G++ 1.638 s (prod, -O2), C++/G++/Fast 1.651 s and C++/G++/Unsafe 1.631 s (-O3 -march=native), and the best of all 16 C/C++ rows C++/G++/PGO 1.587 s: about 1.74x faster than the best C/C++ row (derived from page data). The C rows (uthash, strdup per key) are slower still: C/Gcc/Fast 1.963 s, C/Clang 1.988 s. Zig/Unchecked (ReleaseFast) runs 0.57 s, about 2.8x faster than the best C/C++ row (derived). Rust (1.021 s) and Go (1.129 s) also beat every C/C++ row. Peak RSS 4.2 MB for Zig vs 7.8 MB for C++/G++. The lead is stable across the five monthly runs checked: 1.71x on 2026-07-14 (Zig 0.941 s vs C++/G++ 1.611 s), 1.72x on 2026-08-14 and 2026-09-03, 1.71x on 2026-09-18 and 1.74x on 2026-10-05 (all derived from page data; Zig 0.16.0 before 2026-10-05).
compiler_and_flags: C/C++: Clang 22.1.8 (official LLVM release tarball; docker/base_clang points cc, c++, gcc and g++ at clang via update-alternatives and sets no -stdlib flag, so the clang rows link the system libstdc++) and GCC 16.0.1 20260322 (trunk, Ubuntu build), -std=c++20, glibc malloc. Headline 'prod' build (cpp/Makefile CXXFLAGS_PROD, c/Makefile CFLAGS_PROD): -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, linked with -Wl,-z,relro,-z,now -Wl,--gc-sections (not -O3). The same suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -pipe ..., -flto=thin at link), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math ..., -flto=full at link) and 'PGO' (-O2 plus -fprofile-instr-use or -fprofile-use) variants; the LTO flags appear only in LDFLAGS, so those builds probably get no real LTO (inference from the Makefiles). All 16 Clang/GCC x C/C++ x prod/Fast/Unsafe/PGO configurations were compared (instrumented PGO/Gen rows and the author's mycc/cproc compilers excluded; they are slower anyway). Zig 0.17.0 'zig build build-zig': zig/build.zig builds this 'Zig' row with optimize = .ReleaseSafe (LLVM release optimisation with runtime safety checks kept) and b.standardTargetOptions(.{}), which defaults to the native host CPU, so it is closer to -O3 -march=native with bounds checks than to the generic -O2 prod C/C++ build; 'Zig/Unchecked' is the same source at .ReleaseFast. Go 1.27.1 (go.mod says go 1.24.0) 'go build -buildvcs=false' with default settings (no opt levels in Go); 'Go/Opt' adds -trimpath and a static link. Rust: rustc 1.99.0 'cargo build --release'. Versions and build/run commands from the results file's version, build-cmd and run-cmd fields.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (results file 2026-10-05, host kostya-ms7c37; the run notes say the host moved from Ubuntu to Arch Linux for this run)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Zig splits with std.mem.splitScalar and keys a std.StringHashMap with slices into the original text inside an arena allocator, so no per-word allocation or copy happens; the C++ test reads with istringstream >> std::string and copies each key into std::unordered_map (this agent's reading of the sources).
tradeoffs: Zero-copy word keys and arena allocation; the map and its keys die with the arena.
caveats: Standard-library and idiom comparison, not code generation: Zig keys a flat hash map with zero-copy slices into the text inside an arena, while the C++ test uses istringstream plus a node-based unordered_map with copied keys and the C test strdup()s the text and every key; a C++ version with std::string_view keys and a flat hash map would likely close most of the gap (inference, not measured). Both sides do the same split, count and max-scan over the same text and the suite checks the checksum. Zig's production row is ReleaseSafe built for the native CPU (b.standardTargetOptions default), while the prod C/C++ rows are generic x86-64 -O2 with hardening flags; the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows were also compared and still lose, and the Makefiles pass the LTO flags only at link time, so no C/C++ row had real LTO. The same test is catalogued for Java (lang:java/kostya/langarena#etc-words), where the same C++ weakness drives the result. LangArena's README calls it not an objective, peer-reviewed or industry-standard suite (rules and library choices are the author's judgment) and says AI tools helped translate the tests from Crystal, with the author reviewing them. name: Sassy (SIMD approximate string matching)
baseline: Edlib (C++ Myers bit-vector aligner); parasail (C) and SWOffinder also compared in the paper
workload: Searching short DNA/ASCII patterns (up to about 1000 characters) in long texts allowing k edit errors, synthetic data and a human genome search.
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract (Bioinformatics, May 2026; repo copy in doc/abstract.md): Sassy1 is 4-15x faster than Edlib for patterns up to 1000 bp and reaches a text throughput up to 2 Gbp/s; for CRISPR off-target detection of 61 guides in a human genome it is 100x faster than SWOffinder and only slightly slower than the index-based CHOPOFF. 'Over 100x faster than parasail' appears in the published abstract only as quoted by a WebSearch snippet (snippet only; not in the repo copy). Sassy2 (bioRxiv, March 2026) is an additional 10-50x faster than Sassy1 for short (<200 bp) texts and 2.5-4.5x for long (>8 kbp) texts; README: Sassy2 2x faster with AVX-512 and pre-encoded patterns 10-20x faster for short texts (internal comparisons).
compiler_and_flags: Sassy: Rust >= 1.91, release profile opt-level 3 (debug info on; dist profile adds LTO and one codegen unit) with .cargo/config.toml target-cpu=native; the Edlib eval is built with 'cargo build --release -p evals'. Edlib (C++) is called through edlib-rs, whose build.rs uses the cmake crate; the cmake crate derives CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE from the Cargo profile, and with sassy's release profile (debug = true) that is RelWithDebInfo (CMake default -O2 -g), with no -march=native; edlib-rs's .cflag("-D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release") only adds a C preprocessor define and Edlib's CMakeLists sets no build type. Parasail built from its CMake (flags unstated, striped SSE4.1/AVX2 kernels tried); Ish built with ISH_SIMD_TARGET=sse.
why_faster: Bit-packing with SIMD (AVX2/NEON) where the bit-vectors run along the text direction ('tiling in the text direction'), with the text split into 4 parts searched in parallel; complexity O(k ceil(n/W)) with W=256.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 18 forks; crates.io 6101 downloads (2287 recent, v0.2.6); also on bioconda and PyPI (sassy-rs); third-party DuckDB/R bindings (ducksassy)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or NEON; supports ASCII, DNA and IUPAC alphabets; best for patterns up to about 1000; C bindings, Python bindings and a CLI exist.
caveats: Edlib numbers come from the peer-reviewed paper's abstract (repo copy doc/abstract.md); the full paper, its hardware and the eval CSVs were not opened (bioRxiv, doi.org and the KIT library PDF host were unreachable). The win is algorithmic, not a language effect: Sassy tiles bit-vectors along the text with 256-bit AVX2 lanes over 4 text chunks, while Edlib runs scalar 64-bit Myers/Hyyro bit-vectors. In the public evals harness Edlib is probably compiled at RelWithDebInfo (-O2 -g, generic x86-64) while Sassy gets opt-level 3 plus target-cpu=native, so optimisation levels are not matched (not a crippled -O0 build). The parasail >100x figure is snippet only. Requires AVX2 or NEON at compile time (scalar feature is slower).

name: cuniq (Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: GNU coreutils 8.32 `sort -u | wc -l` and `sort | uniq -c`, and GNU awk 5.3.2 (`a[$0]++`), all C programs.
workload: Count distinct lines (and per-line occurrence counts) of a 32 GiB preprocessed Wikipedia text dump with 6,028,206,370 lines, 78,035,032 of them unique; also a 4,000,000-line random-number file in criterion benches.
claimed_speedup: PERFORMANCE.md, 32 GiB Wikipedia test (bash time, one run each): count, `sort -u huge.txt | wc -l` (GNU 8.32, 8 threads) 14m11.935s vs `cuniq --memmap --threads=1` 2m47.462s (5.1x, derived from page data) and `cuniq --memmap --mode=near-exact` (16 threads, stores hashes only) 59.387 s (14.3x, derived from page data); `--mode=estimate` (HyperLogLog, 0.74% error, 16 threads) 9.038 s. Report: `sort huge.txt | uniq -c` 28m46.811s and gawk 5.3.2 `a[$0]++` 25m03.082s vs unsorted `cuniq --memmap -c` 3m07.817s (9.2x and 8.0x, derived from page data); like-for-like sorted report `cuniq --memmap -cs` 3m26.898s vs `sort | uniq -c` (8.3x, derived from page data). README: 'For counting cuniq reliably outperforms GNU sort in all cases', with one stated exception for sorted reports on inputs with almost no duplicates.
compiler_and_flags: Build used for the 32 GiB table not stated. PERFORMANCE.md gives `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo +nightly bench -Z build-std=std ... --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` for the criterion benches and a `release-optimized-debug` profile build for profiling; README mentions profile-guided optimization and recommends `-C target-cpu=native` installs. GNU coreutils 8.32 and gawk 5.3.2 are Git Bash (Windows) binaries, build flags and locale unknown.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (16 threads), 5200 MT/s memory, 6950 MB/s sequential disk read, Windows 11 24H2
why_faster: PERFORMANCE.md optimization list: hash table instead of sorting (O(n)), memory-mapped input, memchr newline search, no UTF-8 validation, ahash, leaking large structures instead of freeing, multithreaded hashing and HyperLogLog for the estimate mode.
stars_or_usage: 4 stars, 1 fork (GitHub repo page, 2026-10-11); crates.io cuniq 2.0.0 (2025-10-14), 4,635 downloads; AUR package per README.
tradeoffs: Exact mode keeps every distinct line in memory; near-exact mode ignores 64-bit hash collisions; estimate mode is approximate; -c output is unsorted unless -s; hashing loses to sorting when nearly every line is unique.
caveats: First-party, Windows-only harness: GNU coreutils 8.32 and gawk 5.3.2 run under Git Bash with unknown build flags and unstated locale (GNU sort in a UTF-8 locale collates far slower than LC_ALL=C), and the 32 GiB input file is not published; single bash `time` runs. The 9.2x report figure compares an unsorted cuniq report with a sorted `sort | uniq -c`; the sorted `cuniq -cs` row gives 8.3x. why_faster: Not stated by the suite. The loop is nearly identical in Go and C++; the Go key is a zero-copy substring plus strings.TrimSpace, while the C++ test copies the key with substr and trim (this agent's reading of the sources, small effect).

Go's harness calls runtime.GC() after warm-up so the timed loop starts with a clean heap, but collections during the loop (a new output buffer of about 1.5x the template per iteration) are timed; Go uses 75 MB peak RSS against 41 MB for C. The C/C++ prod rows are -O2 with hardening flags, but the -O3 -march=native Fast and Unsafe rows and the PGO rows were also compared and lose, and the Makefiles pass the LTO flags only at link time. Go also loses badly on other text tests in the same suite (Etc::LogParser 30.9 s). LangArena's README calls it not an objective, peer-reviewed or industry-standard suite (rules and library choices are the author's judgment) and says AI tools helped translate the tests from Crystal, with the author reviewing them. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run (no repeats or variance within a run); every language, C and C++ included, runs 20% of the iterations as untimed warm-up and checksums are verified. The per-benchmark ratios are derived from the results files, not stated by the suite. Rows were picked by the search agent as text tests where a Rust, Zig or Go production row beats every C and C++ row; most other text tests in the suite go the other way (for example Base64::Encode and Base64::Decode, where C is about 3x faster than Rust, and Distance::Jaro, a tie).

name: jumprope (Rust rope)
baseline: librope (C skip-list rope by the same author)
