README also says jumprope is about 3x faster than ropey (a Rust rope) on real editing operations, and its JumpRopeBuf wrapper (merges runs of edits before applying them) is claimed about 10x faster again.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. Workspace Cargo.toml release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (Rust side). rope_benches/build.rs compiles a vendored rope.c with cc::Build defaults (no explicit flags, no NDEBUG; cc follows Cargo's release opt-level), linked as a static library with no cross-language LTO, so every C call crosses an FFI boundary. Run with 'cargo run --release -- --bench' in rope_benches.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 5800X, single core
why_faster: README: jumprope is a skip list whose leaf nodes each contain a gap buffer, versus librope's plain skip list.
license: ISC (LICENSE.txt and README); Cargo.toml declares ISC OR Apache-2.0
tradeoffs: Fewer features than ropey (no line/column conversion). Meant for large documents; the README recommends std String for strings under about 100 bytes.
caveats: First-party numbers from the author, who also wrote the C baseline. The README table was last updated on 2021-10-05/06 (README commit history), before jumprope 1.0 (2022), so it does not reflect the current code. Benchmark code is public (rope_benches/src/main.rs, criterion 'realworld' group) but loads traces from a hard-coded /home/seph/src/diamond-types/benchmark_data path; compiler versions and C flags are unstated. Harness asymmetry: the C column ('C-JumpRope' in the code) is a vendored copy of librope's rope.c built by the cc crate without NDEBUG and driven through FFI with a CString allocation and copy per insert inside the timed loop, while Jumprope takes &str directly inside the same LTO-built Rust binary; this inflates the 2.4-2.7x gap by an unmeasured amount. The realworld check compares only the final char_len, not the content. Algorithms differ (gap-buffer leaves vs plain skip-list nodes), so the win is data-structure design rather than language. librope itself is already catalogued (wave 1, https://github.com/josephg/librope) from the same table; this record is its Rust successor, not a duplicate. The linked criterion report host (home.seph.codes) does not resolve (ENOTFOUND). No commits since 2023-05-20.

name: Vibrato (Rust MeCab reimplementation)
baseline: MeCab (C++ Japanese morphological analyzer), 2020-09-14 build
workload: Tokenize all 2,346 lines (158.8 characters on average) of 'I Am a Cat' (Aozora Bunko). Each tool reads the lines into memory, then times only the tokenization loop with a steady clock, single-threaded. run_all.sh runs 101 iterations, each a fresh process, and iteration 0 is a warm-up. MeCab uses mecab-ipadic 2.7.0 or unidic-cwj 3.1.1, and Vibrato uses its v0.5.0 precompiled dictionaries built from the same sources. The MeCab driver calls tagger->parse() with -Owakati, which builds a space-separated output string. The Vibrato driver calls worker.tokenize() and only counts tokens.
claimed_speedup: Wiki Speed-Comparison table: Vibrato 0.5.0 ipadic 42 ms vs MeCab ipadic 87 ms (about 2.1x, derived from page data); Vibrato unidic-cwj 75 ms vs MeCab unidic-cwj 179 ms (about 2.4x, derived from page data); the Vibrato raw-connector variant takes 1364 ms (7.6x slower than MeCab) and dual-connector 170 ms (about equal).
compiler_and_flags: From tokenizer-speed-bench compile_all.sh (tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark): MeCab (taku910/mecab submodule) is built with its own ./configure, whose configure.in sets CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS to '-O3 -Wall' under GCC. The MeCab driver is built with 'g++ -std=c++11 -O3 ./main.cc -lmecab'. The Vibrato 0.5.0 crate is built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+avx2' cargo build --release (release profile, opt-level 3). No gcc or rustc version is stated, and MeCab gets no -march, so only the Rust side is built for AVX2.
hardware: Intel Core i9-12900K, 64 GB DDR5, Ubuntu 22.04
why_faster: README: reimplementation of the MeCab algorithm simplified and optimised; for dictionaries with a large connection matrix (unidic-cwj, 459 MiB) cache-efficient id mappings make it faster.
tradeoffs: Rust library, C++ needs FFI or the CLI. Uses its own compiled dictionary format (zstd compressed system.dic.zst), converted from MeCab dictionaries; MeCab-compatible output options exist.
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the authors' organisation (LegalForce / daac-tools): one corpus (one novel) on one machine. Compiler versions are not stated. The two sides do not do equal work. (1) MeCab's parse() with -Owakati formats an output string, while Vibrato only builds the lattice and counts tokens. (2) Vibrato runs with default settings, not the MeCab-compatible -S -M 24 options, so its tokens can differ from MeCab's (README 'MeCab-compatible options'), and outputs were not compared. (3) Only Vibrato is compiled with AVX2 (+avx2); MeCab uses generic x86-64 -O3. (4) MeCab mmaps its dictionary and 459 MiB unidic matrix, so the timed loop likely pays page faults that Vibrato, which reads the whole dictionary into memory before timing, does not. This is an inference from the harness, not a measurement. The raw-connector compact model (1364 ms) is 7.6x slower than MeCab, and the dual-connector model (170 ms) is roughly level with it. The speedup is largest with the large-matrix unidic dictionary. The numbers are for Vibrato 0.5.0 (early 2023) and have not been re-run for later releases.
found_via: Searched for Rust reimplementations with a C++ baseline (tokenizers); opened vibrato README and its Speed-Comparison wiki page.

verification.tier_reason: The wiki Speed-Comparison page (last edited 2023-03-01) has first-party times for Vibrato 0.5.0 and MeCab 2020-09-14 on an i9-12900K. The harness is public (legalforce-research/tokenizer-speed-bench, tag vibrato-0.5.0-benchmark: compile_all.sh, run_all.sh, bench/mecab-unidic-3_1_1-bench/main.cc, bench/vibrato-bench/src/main.rs) and its flags are visible, but neither the g++ nor the rustc version is stated anywhere. Under the project's precedent a missing compiler version keeps it out of A, and the authors' own run is not B, so it stays C.
verification.notes: Numbers match the wiki exactly: ipadic 42 vs 87 ms (2.07x) and unidic 75 vs 179 ms (2.39x), derived from page data. The baseline is MeCab built at -O3 by its own configure, so the C++ side is not crippled. The gain is a reimplementation with a different data layout (cache-efficient id mapping of the connection matrix) plus a lighter timed path, not a Rust codegen effect. Shortcomings to record: no compiler versions, AVX2 only on the Vibrato side, MeCab formats -Owakati output while Vibrato only counts tokens, outputs not checked equal (non-compatible default mode), and likely mmap page faults inside MeCab's timed loop (inference).

name: Zig (benchLANG strings workload, 19x19 word equality)
baseline: C (GCC 16.2.0, `-O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops`, glibc memcmp per equal-length pair) and C++ (g++ same flags, std::string_view ==, libstdc++).
workload: benchLANG 'Strings': 5M iterations of comparing every pair of the 19 words of a constant sentence for equality (19x19 pairs per iteration).
claimed_speedup: README results table (3 September 2026, one run per language), String Operations column: Zig 1.504 s, C 2.132 s, C++ 2.190 s, C# 2.235 s, D 2.351 s, Go 2.532 s, Ada 2.603 s, Rust 2.621 s, Nim 2.804 s. Zig is 1.42x faster than C and 1.46x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Zig is not faster overall: Fibonacci Zig 3.181 s vs C 1.694 s, and C ranks first on total runtime (9.762 s vs Zig 10.737 s, Zig factor 1.10x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 `zig build-exe -OReleaseFast -mcpu=native -fstrip -lc`; C `gcc -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -ffp-contract=off -s` and C++ `g++ -std=c++20` with the same flags, GCC 16.2.0 from nixpkgs-unstable.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz, 48 GB DDR4-3600, Arch Linux; one run per language, 3 September 2026
tradeoffs: ReleaseFast removes Zig's safety checks. The Nix flake pins every toolchain, and the analyzer marks the ranking invalid if checksums differ between languages (README).
caveats: One run per language (the runner supports --runs 3 but the published table is a single run); the CPU is locked at 3.5 GHz and the gap is 42%, so noise alone is unlikely to explain it. The win belongs to the Zig standard library's equality routine, not to Zig codegen: std.mem.eql inlines a branch-light short-slice compare (three byte XORs below 4 bytes, four overlapping 4-byte loads up to 16 bytes) and returns early when both slices share a pointer, which skips the byte compare on the 19 diagonal pairs of each iteration; the C and C++ versions call out-of-line glibc memcmp (variable length, so GCC presumably does not inline it; disassembly not checked) for each of the 103 equal-length pairs of the 361 per iteration. A C version with an inlined compare would likely close the gap (inference). The input is a compile-time constant 19-word sentence (README says constant folding counts as a result); C tokenises a strdup copy with strtok at run time while Zig tokenises the constant slice, so LLVM may specialise more (not checked). Zig 0.16.0's lib/std/mem.zig was not readable (the tag is not on the GitHub mirror); the eqlBytes code was read at 0.15.1 and master. Rust and Go are also slower than C on this task, and C ranks first overall in the same repository.

claimed_speedup: Nim/Clang (prod row, default ORC) 1.55 s and Nim/GCC/ARC 1.193 s vs C++/G++/Fast 2.098 s (the best of the C and C++ prod, Fast, Unsafe and PGO configurations; only the instrumented C++/Clang++/PGO/Gen build is lower, at 2.081 s), C++/G++ 2.101 s and C/Clang 2.482 s. That is about 1.35x faster at default and 1.76x with ARC than the best C/C++ configuration (derived from page data). The lead held in the three previous runs (2026-08-14 to 2026-09-18: Nim/Clang 1.51-1.55 s vs best C/C++ 2.02-2.15 s). Memory: Nim/Clang 102 MB and Nim/GCC/ARC 69 MB vs C++/G++ 70 MB.
compiler_and_flags: C/C++ 'prod' build: make -j prod with -O2 -DNDEBUG -fstack-protector-strong -fno-omit-frame-pointer, -std=c++20 (clang 22.1.8, g++ 16.0.1 20260322 trunk), glibc malloc. The suite also builds 'Fast' (-O3 -march=native -mtune=native -ftree-vectorize -funroll-loops, -flto=thin passed only at link), 'Unsafe' (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math, -flto=full at link) and PGO variants of every C and C++ test, all in the results file. Nim 2.2.12: Nim/Clang (the suite's 'prod' Nim row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:clang; Nim/GCC/ARC (a 'hack' row) is nim c --threads:on -d:release --cc:gcc --gc:arc. In Nim's config/nim.cfg, -d:release turns on opt:speed, so the generated C is compiled at clang -O3 or gcc -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno, both with -fno-strict-aliasing. Nim/Clang uses the default ORC memory manager (Nim doc/mm.md). No build passes -d:useMalloc, so Nim's own allocator is used.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X 8-Core Processor, 78GB RAM, x86_64 Linux (host kostya-ms7c37, results dated 2026-10-05)
why_faster: Not stated by the suite. Unverified inference: Nim's ref objects are allocated by Nim's own allocator and released by reference counting (ARC or ORC) at scope end, so the per-node allocate and free path avoids glibc malloc and free that the C and C++ tests hit once per node. The suite's own index-based Arena variant of this test removes the per-node allocation.
tradeoffs: About 45 percent more memory than C++ in this test; reference counting adds a count word per object.
caveats: The win is allocation-strategy specific: an arena or pool allocator in C or C++ beats it, and the suite's Binarytrees::Arena rows go the other way (C/Gcc/Fast 0.255 s, C++/G++/Fast 0.53 s, Nim/Clang 1.049 s). The 1.76x figure is the non-default ARC 'hack' configuration; the default ORC 'prod' row gives 1.35x and uses 46% more memory than C++ (102 vs 70 MB). Nim's generated C is compiled at -O3, while the headline C/C++ prod rows are -O2; the -O3 Fast and Unsafe rows also lose. Nim's node carries a 64-bit int item, where C and C++ use a 32-bit int. ORC as the default and the -O3 mapping were checked in Nim's doc/mm.md and config/nim.cfg on the devel branch, not in the 2.2.12 tag. V (Clang) 0.806 s, Crystal 1.175 s and Java also beat C++ on this test; Rust (2.62 s), Zig (6.31 s) and C3 (3.4 s) are slower. LangArena calls itself a subjective benchmark, and its README says AI tools helped translate the tests. Each configuration is timed once per monthly run with no variance reported, though four monthly runs agree. Rows were selected by the search agent as tests where the language beats every C/C++ configuration; most other tests in the suite go the other way. Ratios are derived from the results file, not stated by the suite.

why_faster: Not stated by the suite. name: D dmd compile throughput (nordlow/compiler-benchmark) vs clang, gcc, clang++ and g++
baseline: clang 23.1.1, gcc 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C) and clang++ 23.1.1, g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1 (C++) compiling the same generated arithmetic translation unit
workload: nordlow/compiler-benchmark: compile (and run) a single massive synthetic translation unit of arithmetic call chains, reported as microseconds per generated function for check, compile and Total=Build+Run, untemplated and templated variants.
claimed_speedup: README table (Ryzen AI 7 350, 2026-09): D (dmd 2.113.0) Total=Build+Run 13 us/f untemplated (19 templated), Compile 10.3 us/f (17.9 templated), Check 4.5 us/f, against C (clang 23.1.1) Total 118 us/f and Compile 77.9, C++ (clang++ 23.1.1) Total 236 (107 templated) and Compile 82.4 (128.7), C++ (g++-15 15.3.0) Total 303 (600) and Compile 269.6 (665.0), C (gcc-15 15.3.0) Total 392 and Compile 193.8, C (gcc 16.2.1) Total 454, C++ (g++ 16.2.1) Total 486. About 9x faster than clang C and 23x faster than g++-15 on Total, and about 7.6x (clang C) to 26x (g++-15) on the link-free Compile column (derived from page data). The README's '6x-38x' headline is dmd against the other D compilers (ldmd2 1.43.0 Total 95 us/f, gdc 16.2.1 Total 527 us/f), not against C. The C compiler tcc 0.9.28rc is faster than dmd (Total 4 us/f, Compile 2.0 us/f).
compiler_and_flags: From cbench: C/C++ via gcc, g++, clang, clang++ with -Wall -Wextra (C) or -Wno-c++11-extensions (C++) and no -O flag (default -O0); check uses -fsyntax-only, compile uses -c, build links with the compiler's default system linker. dmd and ldmd2 use -betterC; check -o-, compile -c, build adds -Xcc=-fuse-ld=lld (or gold) when available; gdc gets no extra flags. Versions: dmd 2.113.0-95551bb, ldmd2 1.43.0, gdc 16.2.1, clang/clang++ 23.1.1, gcc/g++ 15.3.0 and 16.2.1. Minimum of --run-count=10 repetitions (capped to 3 or 2 for slow steps), workers pinned to cores in a multiprocessing pool.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8 cores) at 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, sample run as of 2026-09
why_faster: README: dmd's custom backend and front end do little optimization work; comparing dmd with LLVM-based ldmd2 and GCC-based gdc on the same D source isolates backend cost (dmd about 6x faster than ldmd2 and about 38x faster than gdc).
stars_or_usage: 3.3k stars (dlang/dmd); benchmark repo nordlow/compiler-benchmark 167 stars, 17 forks, MIT
tradeoffs: dmd generates less optimized code than LDC or GCC; this claim is about build time, not run time. In the README's table Zig (110 us/f) is on par with clang C (118) and Odin (147), C3 (153) and Rust (187) are slower than dmd but not faster than clang, so only dmd is a clear compile-time win.
caveats: Compile-time claim, not run-time: both sides build unoptimized code (gcc/clang default -O0, dmd without -O), so the -O3 rule for run-time baselines does not apply. Not a language-level win: the C compiler tcc compiles the same generated program faster than dmd (Total 4 vs 13 us/f) and cuik and cproc are close (76 and 86 us/f), so the gap is dmd's implementation against GCC and Clang, as the dmd vs ldmd2 vs gdc rows show. Harness asymmetries: D builds link with lld via -Xcc=-fuse-ld=lld while gcc and clang use the default system linker, and D uses -betterC (no druntime), which favours D in the Total=Build+Run column; the link-free Compile column still shows 7.6x to 26x. C adds -Wall -Wextra. Synthetic arithmetic call chains in one translation unit, no headers, standard library or modules; the README says real builds differ. Noisy cells: clang++ templated Total 107 is below its own Compile 128.7, and clang++ untemplated Total 236 is nearly 3x its Compile 82.4; the README prose (dmd 11.5, ldmd2 70.3, gdc 433.2, clang 87 us/f) comes from a different run than the tables. Single machine, single sample run by a D community developer (nordlow).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts): WebSearch 'programming language benchmark repository results Rust Zig Nim Odin D C++ C same algorithm' surfaced nordlow/compiler-benchmark; README opened on github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ixy network driver in Rust (C2Rust-transpiled unsafe build versus C)
baseline: ixy C user-space network driver packet forwarder (gcc, and clang with the same LLVM version)
workload: CPU cycles and instructions per forwarded 64-byte packet by the ixy forwarder at batch sizes 32 and 8 on an Intel 82599-class NIC, measured with CPU performance counters (paper: The Case for Writing Network Drivers in High-Level Programming Languages, ANCS 2019).
claimed_speedup: Rust-vs-C-performance.md: the C2Rust-transpiled, fully unsafe Rust driver forwards a packet in 91 cycles with 121 instructions, 'faster than the original code', also when C is compiled with clang on the same LLVM version. The C rows in the same document are 94 cycles and 127 instructions at batch 32 (108 and 139 at batch 8), so about 3% fewer cycles than C at batch 32 (derived from page data; the document does not state the batch size of the C2Rust run). The idiomatic safe Rust driver is slower: 100 vs 94 cycles at batch 32 and 120 vs 108 at batch 8, executing 65% more instructions.
compiler_and_flags: C baseline: emmericp/ixy CMakeLists.txt compiles with -g -O2 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer (current HEAD; the file was last changed in November 2019). ixy.rs Cargo.toml sets no profile overrides (cargo release default opt-level 3, no target-cpu). Compiler versions and the C2Rust build's flags are not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon E3-1230 v3 per the Rust-vs-C document (the repo README names an E3-1230 v2 at 3.3 GHz for the throughput graphs)
tradeoffs: Faster variant is entirely unsafe transpiled Rust without bounds checks; the safe idiomatic driver pays about 65% more instructions that out-of-order execution mostly hides.
caveats: The C2Rust claim is a tongue-in-cheek addendum added to the repository on 2019-10-30, after the ANCS 2019 paper; whether the paper contains it could not be checked (arXiv and net.in.tum.de blocked here). name: mosdepth (Nim BAM/CRAM depth calculator)
baseline: samtools depth (C, htslib); README table also lists bedtools genomecov (C++) and sambamba depth (D)
workload: Per-base depth on a 30X whole-genome BAM/CRAM with one thread, 500-base window mean depth with three threads, and an exome BAM against 1,195,764 exons.
claimed_speedup: Per-base depth about 2x as fast as samtools depth (BAM: mosdepth 25:23 vs samtools 50:12, relative 1.98; CRAM samtools 1.79x slower); sambamba 5.71x and bedtools 5.31x slower; window depth genome-wide in under 9 minutes of user time with 3 threads (8:44, relative 0.34); exome in 1 minute 38 seconds on one CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Nim with --mm:refc (nim.cfg) and -d:release; nim.cfg comment: nim c -a -d:static -d:release mosdepth.nim with htslib configured --with-libdeflate --disable-libcurl. Nim's release build passes -O3 -fno-ident -fno-math-errno to gcc (nim-lang/Nim config/nim.cfg gcc.options.speed). samtools' default Makefile uses CFLAGS -g -Wall -O2; the flags of the samtools, bedtools and sambamba builds actually timed are not stated.
tradeoffs: Memory is about 32 bits times the longest chromosome (about 1 GB for chr1, against 27 MB for samtools); slower than samtools for small one-off regional queries; no gain past about 4 threads; links htslib (C) for decoding.
caveats: The README table lists no hardware, tool versions or commands; tier B would rest on the Bioinformatics 2018 paper, which was not opened (publisher, PMC and bioRxiv blocked; a search snippet confirms the comparison but gives no numbers). Results date from 2017 samtools and htslib. Both mosdepth and samtools decode BAM/CRAM with htslib (C); mosdepth's documented build links htslib with libdeflate, and the htslib build used by samtools in the table is not stated, so part of the gap may be decompression rather than mosdepth's code. By default mosdepth corrects mate overlaps and walks CIGAR operations; --fast-mode (-x) skips both; the README does not say which mode the timing table used, and its accuracy check compared samtools depth defaults with mosdepth without overlap detection. The speedup is algorithmic (difference array against samtools' pileup), not a Nim-versus-C effect; mosdepth uses far more memory (1196 MB vs 27 MB for samtools). Opt levels are not matched if default builds were used (Nim release -O3, samtools Makefile -O2).

Timers have 1 ms resolution on both sides, so the 5k-post margin (10.50 vs 12.20 ms) is near the timer granularity. Community-written implementations; no plain C solution.

name: fd
baseline: GNU find (findutils, C)
workload: Search the author's home folder (about 750,000 subdirectories and about 4 million files) for names ending in [0-9].jpg with a warm disk cache, timed with hyperfine. The commands were find ~ -iregex '.*[0-9]\.jpg$', find ~ -iname '*[0-9].jpg' and fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' ~ (fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh uses fd -HI, 5 warm-up runs, and diffs the outputs). Both tools returned the same 546 files.
claimed_speedup: fd -u '[0-9]\.jpg$' 854.8 ms vs find -iregex 19.922 s (README: approximately 23 times faster) and vs find -iname 11.226 s (about 13 times faster).
tradeoffs: Respects .gitignore and skips hidden files by default (the benchmark needs -u to match find's work); regex search by default instead of glob; parallel traversal uses all cores.
caveats: First-party benchmark on one unnamed machine against the author's own home directory. The README says 'one particular benchmark on one particular machine'. fd, find and compiler versions are not stated, and nor is GNU find's build (distribution packages are usually -O2). fd walks directories in parallel with one thread per core by default, while GNU find is single-threaded. The task is dominated by pattern matching: find -iregex uses gnulib regex on the full path, and -iname uses case-folding fnmatch. Without a pattern the gap disappears. In sharkdp/fd issue #304 (2018, fd 7.0-7.1, Linux source tree, warm cache, no hardware stated), multi-threaded fd -HI -t f only reached parity with 'find . -type f' (69.1 ms vs 68.9 ms after commit 50a2bab), and fd -j1 was 1.49x slower than find. In the reporter's home-directory runs find was 2.15x (warm) and 1.85x (cold) faster than fd 7.0.0. So the README's 13-23x is a parallelism plus regex-engine win on a filtering query, not a codegen win, and single-threaded fd is slower than find on plain traversal. The README credits the regex and ignore crates (shared with ripgrep).
found_via: Checked READMEs of widely used Rust command-line replacements for C tools
GitHub: README of sharkdp/fd (Rust rewrites of C command-line tools); not in KNOWN_LIST.
why_faster: Parallelized directory traversal (README feature list: 'Very fast due to parallelized directory traversal').

verification.tier_reason: The README Benchmark section gives first-party hyperfine results against GNU find (19.922 s, 11.226 s and 854.8 ms; '23 times' and '13 times'). The scripts are public (sharkdp/fd-benchmarks warm-cache-simple-pattern.sh, config.sh, prelude.sh). There is no CPU, no fd or find version, no build flags, and the dataset is the author's own home folder, so it is not reproducible: C. WebSearch found no independent suite.
verification.notes: Numbers and the 546-file equality check match the README verbatim. Metadata is confirmed: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 44.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-06, not archived. Shortcomings to record: first-party, no hardware or versions, private dataset, a parallel versus single-threaded comparison, and issue #304 shows find matching or beating fd on unfiltered listing and fd -j1 1.49x slower than find.

corrected_fields.workload: Search a home directory (about 750,000 subdirectories and 4 million files, warm disk cache) for the 546 files matching [0-9].jpg; hyperfine means; fd runs with -u so it does the same work as find.
corrected_fields.caveats: README itself says this is one particular benchmark on one particular machine. CPU model, find version, filesystem and build flags are not stated, so tier A is not met. The speedup mixes multithreading (fd parallelizes traversal, find is single-threaded) with regex-vs-glob matching, so it is not a per-core efficiency win. Benchmark scripts are in sharkdp/fd-benchmarks (opened: README only, scripts not read or run). GNU find was not confirmed to be built at -O3.

name: Lightpanda
baseline: Headless Google Chrome 143 (Chromium, C++) driven over CDP
workload: Crawler: a Go chromedp program crawls the Amiibo demo site (933 URLs) over the live internet. Chrome runs 1-100 tabs in one browser, while Lightpanda runs 1-100 separate processes (--fork --lpd-path), because Lightpanda cannot open multiple tabs. Each configuration ran once with /usr/bin/time -v, and smem PSS and ps CPU were sampled every 100 ms (watch -n0.1) for peak memory. Campfire: a homemade fake e-commerce page that loads two JSON XHRs, served locally, loaded 100 times via Puppeteer over CDP.
claimed_speedup: README: '16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium'. Its table is labelled '(100 pages)', but its numbers (123MB vs 2GB, 5s vs 46s) match the BENCHMARKS.md 25-way rows: Lightpanda 25 processes 4.81 s, 123.0M versus Chrome 25 tabs 46.70 s, 2.0G (about 9.7x faster, 16x less memory, derived from page data). Other rows from the same table: 1 process versus 1 tab, 51.68 s, 27.2M versus 1:22.83, 1.3G (1.6x faster, derived from page data). 100 processes versus 100 tabs, 5.23 s, 410.2M versus 1:09.37, 4.2G (about 13x, derived from page data). Best versus best is 4.81 s versus 45.62 s for Chrome at 10 tabs (about 9.5x, derived from page data). Campfire page, 100 local loads via Puppeteer: average 16 ms versus 185 ms (total 1,698 ms versus 18,551 ms, about 11x), peak memory 21.2M versus 402.1M, peak CPU 4.6% versus 158.6%.
compiler_and_flags: Lightpanda commit 7b1f157cf8ccbdded7db6ab47e94577495ee87e4. The build mode is not stated; the README says Zig 0.15.2 and the Campfire section points to the nightly release binary. The baseline is the official Google Chrome binary, 143.0.7499.169 for the crawler and 143.0.7499.109 for Campfire, started with --headless=new --remote-debugging-port=9222 (crawler also --user-data-dir=/tmp/bench_chrome).
hardware: AWS m5.xlarge (x86_64), fresh Ubuntu install, per BENCHMARKS.md; the CPU model appears only in a neofetch screenshot that was not read. The README calls the same crawler benchmark an m5.large.
tradeoffs: A new browser written from scratch for automation, not a Chromium fork; it is not a full rendering browser, so page-compatibility and Web API coverage are narrower. AGPL-3.0 licence.
caveats: Vendor benchmark (Lightpanda sells a cloud service), so first-party. The two browsers do unequal work: Lightpanda has 'No graphical rendering engine' (README), so it skips style, layout, paint, compositing and Chrome's GPU and renderer processes. The JavaScript runs on V8 (C++) in both browsers; Lightpanda also uses libcurl (C) for HTTP and html5ever (Rust) for HTML parsing. So the gap comes from doing less work, not from Zig codegen. The authors chose a homemade page because Lightpanda 'is not yet fully compliant'. The crawler fetches pages over the internet, so its single-process runs are network-bound (6-11% CPU). The concurrency models differ (N processes versus N tabs). There is one run per configuration with no variance. The README's '(100 pages)' label does not match the 25-way rows its numbers come from. The summary table has a typo (1:09:37 for 1:09.37). The instance size is m5.xlarge in BENCHMARKS.md but m5.large in the README. No independent reproduction was found; a Wavect write-up (WebSearch, snippet only) notes it was not reproduced. The category is a poor fit for a language-level claim.

why_faster: Source gives no language mechanism; README only says it is built from scratch for AI agents and automation (the speed comes from doing less work than a rendering browser).

name: Rewrite it in Rust: A Computational Physics Case Study (Veytsman, Zhai, Ding, Sefkow)

A snippet also mentions a comparison with an interpreted-language (MATLAB) version.
claimed_speedup: Per search snippets of the arXiv paper (paper not opened): Rust was at least 1.6x as fast as the C++ version in the smaller cases, and up to 5.6x faster on the large mesh on the EPYC machine; a parallel Rust version improved performance further. No per-case runtimes were seen.
hardware: Includes an AMD EPYC machine (model not seen; snippet only)

tradeoffs: Unknown; the study also reports a parallel Rust version.

All three are the same naive tree-walking interpreter (no run-length folding), but the op representations differ: Rust uses an enum with separate Inc/Dec variants and boxed child slices and reads the tape with unsafe get_unchecked, C uses a 16-byte tagged union with an offset field and a tape_get that truncates the int cell to char, and C++ uses a 32-byte Op struct that embeds a std::vector in every op. V/gcc, which emits C and compiles it with gcc, is faster than the C row, which points to data-layout and codegen variance rather than a language advantage. The suite reports median with median absolute deviation from a ~1 s run; no mechanism is given by the source.

name: Rust (related_post_gen suite)
claimed_speedup: Single-core table on AWS c7a.xlarge, measuring processing time without JSON I/O: Rust 9.84 ms, 124.59 ms and 1.10 s (5k/20k/60k posts, total 1.23 s) versus C++ 12.20 ms, 164.33 ms and 1.39 s (total 1.57 s). That is about 1.28x on the total and 1.26x at 60k posts (derived from page data). D (v2) is fastest at 1.10 s total and C3 takes 1.28 s. In the multicore table C++ Concurrent (402.33 ms total) beats Rust Concurrent (489.91 ms), so the Rust lead holds only on a single core. The raw files results/raw_results_rust.md and raw_results_cpp.md match the table. At 60k posts their whole-process wall times, including JSON I/O, are 1.27-1.32 s for Rust and 3.35-3.40 s for C++.
compiler_and_flags: C++: clang++ -O3 -std=c++20 -I./include main.cpp (run.sh run_cpp). It is a single translation unit with header-only nlohmann/json, so the missing -flto changes little. Neither side uses -march; the suite rules forbid hardware targeting. Rust: cargo build --release with the rust/Cargo.toml release profile lto = "fat", codegen-units = 1, panic = "abort" (default opt-level 3), plus hashbrown 0.14.3, aligned-vec 0.5 and serde_json. Compiler versions are not stated: the Docker image is archlinux:base with an unpinned pacman clang and rustup stable (dockerfiles/base.Dockerfile, dockerfiles/rust.Dockerfile).
caveats: The suite gives no mechanism. The timed region ('Processing time (w/o IO)') excludes JSON parsing and writing on both sides, so nlohmann/json versus serde_json does not affect the table. It does dominate whole-process time: C++ 3.35 s versus Rust 1.27 s at 60k posts, with 460 MB versus 29 MB RSS. Inside the timed region both programs run the same algorithm: per-tag lists of post indices, uint8 shared-tag counters, a scan in 64-entry chunks with a running minimum, and 5-slot top-k insertion. The tuning differs. Rust zeroes each 64-byte chunk right after scanning it, on a 64-byte-aligned counter buffer padded to a multiple of 64. C++ memsets the whole counter array before each post and uses bounds-checked std::vector::at() for every counter access in the hot loops. The tag index is hashbrown in Rust and std::unordered_map<std::string, unique_ptr<vector<int>>> in C++; Rust re-hashes each tag string per post, while C++ caches per-post pointers. The suite has no C solution. The solutions are community-written and were run on a cloud VM (10 runs at 5k posts, 3 at 20k and 60k) with compiler versions and CPU model unstated. Zig (1.93 s) and Odin (2.00 s) are slower than C++. The Rust HO row (51.55 ms) uses specialised data structures and is excluded. The repository now lives at zupat/related_post_gen, and the jinyus URL redirects there.

name: skani
baseline: FastANI 1.33 (C++) and Mash 2.3 (C++), bioconda builds pinned in skani-test/env.yml
workload: Average nucleotide identity computation between prokaryotic genomes and against a database of more than 65,000 genomes.
claimed_speedup: README: sketching about 3x faster than Mash, querying about 25x faster than FastANI but slower than Mash; v0.4.0 (October 2026) claims about 2x faster than v0.3. Paper abstract (snippet only): >20x faster than FastANI on fragmented, incomplete MAGs. Paper benchmark repo skani-test, /bin/time outputs at 50 threads (derived from page data): all-vs-all on 195 MAGs, skani triangle 3.30 s vs FastANI 2:58.96 (54x wall; 154.75 s vs 7142.43 s user, 46x); E. coli D3 database query, skani search 4.17 s (plus 3.55 s sketching) vs FastANI 2:44.50 (39x query-only, 21x including sketching); RefSeq all-vs-all, skani sketch 3.10 s plus triangle 11.38 s vs FastANI 3:02:24 (about 750x). Against Mash: skani sketching 3.55 s vs 18.19 s on D3 and 3.10 s vs 14.79 s on RefSeq (about 5x), but Mash dist on D3 takes 0.26 s vs skani search 4.17 s (skani 16x slower), and Mash triangle on the 195 MAGs takes 0.55 s vs 3.30 s.
compiler_and_flags: skani: prebuilt binary checked into skani-test (cargo release build; flags not stated). FastANI 1.33 (fastani=1.33=h0fdf51a_1) and Mash 2.3 (mash=2.3=ha9a2dd8_3) from bioconda, build flags those of the bioconda recipes.
hardware: CPU model not stated; 50 threads (/bin/time reports 3500-4950% CPU)
stars_or_usage: 265 stars, 15 forks; Nature Methods 2023 paper (doi 10.1038/s41592-023-02018-3); bioconda package; pyskani Python bindings by a third party
tradeoffs: Approximate ANI without base-level alignment; accuracy is 'almost as accurate' as BLAST-based methods per README.
caveats: The speedup is algorithmic, not a language effect: skani does approximate mapping with sparse chaining of k-mer seeds and no base-level alignment, while FastANI uses Mashmap-style mapping of 3 kb fragments, so same_algorithm is false and the Rust-vs-C++ question is not answered. skani is slower than Mash at querying (16x on D3, 6x on the 195-MAG triangle) and only beats it at sketching. The timings come from the paper-era binary in skani-test, not the current v0.4.0. No CPU model is given, and the FastANI and Mash builds are bioconda defaults. The RefSeq row compares outputs filtered differently (skani -E edge list vs FastANI full output), so the ~750x figure is indicative only. The skani README says a C compiler is needed to build (C dependency). The README's 25x figure has no raw numbers on the README page itself. The wave-14 category is a poor fit, since the win comes from the method, not the language.

why_faster: README: approximate mapping with sparse chaining of seed matches instead of base-level alignment.

name: SPARKNaCl
baseline: TweetNaCl (C), compiled into the same binary with the same GNAT compiler at the same -O level
workload: CPU cycles for one Ed25519 Sign operation on a 256-byte message on a SiFive HiFive1 Revision B (32-bit RISC-V); also Curve25519 and SHA512 analysed.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (two WebSearch result summaries; no page opened): in the February 2021 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl' post, one Ed25519 Sign of a 256-byte message on a HiFive1 Rev B took SPARK 198.03 vs C TweetNaCl 241.83 million cycles at -O0, 98.03 vs 97.65 at -O1 and 93.86 vs 84.99 at -O2 (SPARK slower at -O1 and -O2). After tuning, 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)' reports SPARK at 181.74 (-O0), 69.96 (-O1) and 57.82 then 34.94 (-O2) million cycles. A slide deck summary gives final SPARK 24.37 million cycles at -O2 against 84.99 for the original TweetNaCl C and 51.00 for a revised C version, i.e. about 3.5x vs original and about 2.1x vs the revised C (derived from snippet data). The FOSDEM 2022 abstract claims SPARKNaCl outperforms TweetNaCl on Sign by a factor of 3 at all optimization levels. README itself gives no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GNAT Community 2020/2021 riscv64-elf cross compiler (CE 2019 GCC 8.3.1, CE 2021 GCC 10.3.1 based). perf/perf.gpr applies the same Opt_Switch to both the C TweetNaCl and the Ada code (debug = -g -O0, O1, O2, O3, Os, Og) plus -march=rv32im -ffunction-sections -fdata-sections; the Ada side also gets -gnatp (all run-time checks suppressed). perf/tsign.mk builds with SPARKNACL_RUNTIME_MODE=zfp, RUNTIME_CHECKS=disabled, CONTRACTS=disabled and, as committed, SPARKNACL_BUILD_MODE=debug (-O0); other levels are chosen by editing that variable.
hardware: SiFive HiFive1 Revision B board (FE310 32-bit RISC-V SoC, code built for rv32im), cycles read from the mcycle CSR
stars_or_usage: 139 stars, 14 forks; published in the Alire package index
tradeoffs: Full SPARK proof of absence of run-time exceptions (needs CVC4 and Z3), TweetNaCl-compatible API, readable constant-time code; results are for a small RISC-V core and do not transfer to x86.
caveats: Numbers are snippet-only: blog.adacore.com, www.adacore.com and www.slideshare.net returned ENOTFOUND here and archive.fosdem.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED for the search agent, so no cycle table was seen; a verifier with access should read 'Performance analysis and tuning of SPARKNaCl', 'Doubling the Performance of SPARKNaCl (again...)', 'SPARKNaCl with GNAT and SPARK Community 2021' and the FOSDEM 2022 talk. The win is not a language-level codegen effect: both sides run with run-time checks off (-gnatp), and the speedup comes from reworked field arithmetic that the SPARK proofs made safe (Normal_GF limbs bounded to 0..65535, '*' rewritten as a product-scanning multiply on 32-bit limb products U32NL with the carry folded in, fewer carry passes, loop fusion in '+' and '-'), while the C baseline in perf/tweetnacl.c still multiplies i64 limbs (costly on rv32im) followed by two car25519 passes, although it has been given the WireGuard carry and an unrolled inner loop 'as per SPARKNaCl'. The same restructuring could be written in C, so this is a library-versus-library result. Results swing strongly with -O level (SPARK was behind at -O1/-O2 before tuning; README notes the new '*' is slower at -O0). Not an x86 or -O3 measurement; only one embedded 32-bit RISC-V board. README says the latest results are still to be documented.
found_via: GitHub: rod-chapman/SPARKNaCl README; WebSearch snippets of AdaCore blog posts.
why_faster: Per search snippets only ('formal is fast'): the proof of absence of run-time errors lets the code run without run-time checks; README keeps TweetNaCl's constant-time algorithms.

name: Supersnappy
baseline: Google Snappy (C++), called through its C API (snappy_compress, snappy_uncompress, snappy_validate_compressed_buffer) from a prebuilt libsnappy.dll loaded by the nimsnappy wrapper (version and build flags unknown; the wrapper says it tracks 1.1.3). Also Andi Kleen's snappy-c (C), compiled from source into the benchmark through the nimsnappyc wrapper's {.compile.} pragma. The pure-Nim status-im/nim-snappy is the fourth column.
workload: Snappy benchmark corpus (alice29.txt, asyoulik.txt, fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata, html, html_x_4, kppkn.gtb, lcet10.txt, paper-100k.pdf, plrabn12.txt, urls.10K). tests/bench.nim times one compress plus one uncompress of the whole file per benchy timeIt sample, with 1000 samples (x1000). The README header's '100 compress-uncompress cycles' does not match the current code.
claimed_speedup: README: 'performs significantly better in all cases than alternatives'. Table, avg ms per compress-plus-uncompress round trip (derived ratios from page data). Against Google Snappy via nimsnappy: alice29.txt 0.513 vs 0.599 (1.17x), asyoulik.txt 0.451 vs 0.529 (1.17x), html_x_4 0.534 vs 0.559 (1.05x), kppkn.gtb 0.435 vs 0.523 (1.20x), lcet10.txt 1.380 vs 1.599 (1.16x), plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.237 (1.18x), urls.10K 1.574 vs 1.842 (1.17x); slower on fireworks.jpg 0.015 vs 0.011, geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.101 and paper-100k.pdf 0.041 vs 0.017, html 0.128 vs 0.127 (tie). Against snappy-c via nimsnappyc, faster on all 11 files by 1.10x (plrabn12.txt 1.898 vs 2.092) to 1.42x (geo.protodata 0.106 vs 0.150). Against status-im/nim-snappy it is slower on fireworks.jpg (0.015 vs 0.011) and paper-100k.pdf (0.041 vs 0.020). So 'all cases' holds only against snappy-c.
compiler_and_flags: nim c --gc:arc -d:release -r tests/bench.nim (README still says tests/benchmark.nim, which is now 404). Nim's release config compiles both its generated C and the {.compile.}'d snappy-c with the same backend C compiler (gcc/clang -O3, vcc /O2 per Nim's config/nim.cfg), and supersnappy turns checks off in release builds. The backend compiler and version are not stated, and the build of the libsnappy.dll used for Google Snappy is unknown.
hardware: Not stated (a Windows machine, judging by the .\tests path and libsnappy.dll)
tradeoffs: Pure Nim, dependency free, usable at compile time; outputs checked for compatibility with other Snappy implementations.
caveats: Weak entry. Nim compiles to C, so this is a C-versus-C comparison and no language effect. The cleanest comparison is against snappy-c, built by the same C compiler at the same flags, which supersnappy beats on all 11 files by 1.10-1.42x; but the nimsnappyc wrapper calls snappy_init_env/snappy_free_env (allocating the hash table) on every compress, which inflates small-file times. Against Google Snappy the nimsnappy wrapper runs a full snappy_validate_compressed_buffer pass before every uncompress, and newString zero-fills both output buffers, so the C++ baseline does extra work; even so supersnappy wins only 16-20 percent on text, ties html and loses on fireworks.jpg, geo.protodata and paper-100k.pdf (2.4x slower on paper-100k.pdf). The libsnappy.dll version and flags are unknown (the wrapper says it tracks snappy 1.1.3, a 2015 release), no hardware is stated, and the README's 'all cases' claim is contradicted by its own table. The code credits snappy-c as its main influence.

name: Usuba (bitslicing language and compiler to C with SIMD intrinsics)
baseline: Hand-tuned reference implementations in SUPERCOP, compiled with the same C compilers at -O3: Kwan's bitsliced DES (C), Kasper-Schwabe SSSE3 AES-CTR and Kivilinna's AVX AES-CTR (assembly), Dolbeau AVX2, moon AVX/SSSE3 and e/ref ChaCha20, Linux C and avx2-16way/avx-8way/sse2-8way Serpent-CTR, and the Rectangle reference. Secondary: BSC 0.1 (Thomas Pornin's prototype bitslicing compiler, which emits C) on DES in results.org.
metric: throughput (units not stated in the log, probably cycles per byte)
workload: Usuba-generated bitsliced or m-sliced ciphers (DES, AES-CTR, ChaCha20, Serpent-CTR, Rectangle) against hand-tuned references in SUPERCOP crypto_stream (xor_cycles over 4096-byte messages), plus bitsliced DES generated by Usuba against DES generated by BSC 0.1 in experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc (rdtscp cycles per byte, 15 runs).
claimed_speedup: bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex (cycles per byte; SUPERCOP xor_cycles on 4096-byte messages, lower half of samples averaged; speedup = (ref - usuba)/ref). Usuba faster: Rectangle SSE 11.18 vs 14.51 (+22.95%), AVX 4.21 vs 4.92 (+14.43%), AVX2 2.10 vs 2.45 (+14.29%), GP 25.88 vs 28.61 (+9.54%); Serpent GP 25.78 vs 30.37 Linux C (+15.11%), SSE 11.29 vs 11.48 (+1.66%); ChaCha20 SSE 2.31 vs 2.72 moon SSSE3 (+15.07%), AVX2 1.02 vs 1.03, AVX 2.07 vs 2.09; DES GP 11.47 vs 12.01 Kwan (+4.50%). Usuba slower: AES 7.92 vs 7.77 Kasper-Schwabe (-1.93%) and 5.71 vs 5.59 Kivilinna AVX assembly (-2.15%); Serpent AVX2 4.53 vs 4.33 (-4.62%) and AVX 8.66 vs 8.36 (-3.59%); ChaCha20 GP 5.65 vs 5.64. ciphers/des/results.txt also has Usuba behind Kwan on SSE (6.64 vs 6.50) and AVX (3.74 vs 3.63). results.org (main branch): des-usuba 17.086 +-0.121 vs des-bsc 17.419 +-0.142 cycles/byte, about 1.9 percent faster (derived from page data). PLDI 2019 abstract: 'on par with hand-tuned reference implementations' (search snippet only); WPMVP 2018 quoted as about 15 percent faster on DES with 64-bit general-purpose registers depending on the C compiler (search snippet only).
compiler_and_flags: Usuba emits C that is compiled by the same C compilers as the references. DES (ciphers/des/compile.pl): clang -O3 -march=native for both Usuba and Kwan. SUPERCOP rows (bench/ua-vs-human/run.pl): icc or clang with -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv -std=gnu11 plus -march=native, -mssse3, -xSSSE3, -xSSE2 or -msse4.2; several rows pair different compilers or ISA flags per side (Serpent GP: Usuba clang -march=native vs Linux C icc -msse4.2; Serpent AVX: Usuba clang vs reference icc; ChaCha20 GP: Usuba icc -msse4.2 vs e/ref icc -march=native). usuba-vs-bsc (experimentations/usuba-vs-bsc/run.pl): clang -O3 -Wall -Wextra for both, Usuba flags -no-arr -inline-all -no-precalc-tbl -check-tbl -B. Compiler versions not stated.
hardware: Not stated; SUPERCOP data paths name an amd64 host 'dadaubuntu', CPU model unknown.
tradeoffs: Domain-specific language for bitsliced and vector-sliced ciphers; targets x86 SIMD and the generated code is only as good as the C compiler used.
caveats: Win is mixed and small: faster on Rectangle (9.5-23%), Serpent GP (15%), ChaCha20 SSE (15%) and DES GP (4.5%); slower on AES (about 2%), Serpent AVX/AVX2 (3.6-4.6%) and DES SSE/AVX; the paper itself claims 'on par'. The results.org DES comparison is against BSC 0.1, which the experiment's own Readme calls a prototype 'not meant to be an optimizing compiler', so it is not a hand-tuned baseline. The hand-tuned comparison lives only on the old master branch (bench/ua-vs-human/human.tex, ciphers/des/results.txt); the default main branch was restructured and no longer carries bench/, ciphers/ or experimentations/. Numbers are undated author runs on an unstated CPU, and some rows use different compilers or ISA flags for each side. Usuba output is C compiled by the same C compiler, so the gain comes from the Usubac compiler's transformations (scheduling, interleaving, inlining), not from a different backend. results.org also logs broken runs ('No supercop', 'C compilation goes wrong', a stack overflow, 0.00 AVX-512 results). Papers not opened (snippet only).
found_via: WebSearch 'Usuba bitslicing compiler faster than hand-written C ciphers PLDI github usubalang'
why_faster: Compiler-level optimizations specific to bitslicing (inlining, scheduling, interleaving; the repo has bench directories for each).

Shortcomings to record: claim is 'on par' with mixed wins, CPU model unstated, some rows use different compilers per side, master-branch-only data, papers unreachable (snippet only), repo stale since 2024-09-04.

name: verztable
baseline: absl::flat_hash_map/flat_hash_set, boost::unordered_flat_map/unordered_flat_set and ankerl::unordered_dense::map/set (src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp); integer keys use each library's default hash, string keys use std::string_view with a shared wyhash. The 'std' column is Zig's std.AutoHashMap/StringHashMap, not std::unordered_map.
workload: u32, u64 and random-length (8-64 char) string keys with void, 4-byte and 64-byte values, at 100, 3K and 100K elements (1M appears only in the memory table); 16 operation mixes (random and sequential insert, reserved insert, update, random lookup, high load, lookup miss, tombstone, delete, iteration, churn, mixed, read-heavy, write-heavy, update-heavy, zipfian); ns per operation, 15 iterations; C++ tables called from Zig through per-operation extern "C" wrappers.
claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms Google's Abseil, Boost, and Ankerl on mixed workloads'. BENCHMARKS.md, 100-element u32 set: Reserved Ins. 5 ns vs Abseil 13 / Boost 14 / Ankerl 9 (but the C++ tables are never reserved, see caveats); Delete 4 vs 13 / 6 / 6; Lookup Miss 1 vs 5 / 2 / 3; Tombstone 5 vs 16 / 6 / 8; losses in the same table: Rand. Lookup 3 vs Boost 2, Write-Heavy 12 vs Ankerl 8. Across all 432 per-configuration rows verztable beats the best of the three C++ tables in 156, ties 37 and loses 239; geometric-mean time ratio C++/verztable is about 1.03 vs Boost, 1.33 vs Abseil and 1.46 vs Ankerl (derived from page data). At 100K integer keys it loses nearly every row to Abseil and Boost (u32 set: 0 wins of 16; geomean 0.61x of Boost's speed); its clearest wins are on string keys (8-10 of 16 rows per configuration) and on 100-element tables. The page's 27-configuration average table shows verztable ahead on 10 of 16 operations and behind on random/sequential insert, lookup miss, iteration and write-heavy.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2+ with -O ReleaseFast for verztable and the Zig std maps; the C++ wrapper and Abseil sources are compiled by Zig's bundled clang with -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (build.zig); native target by default; no LTO configured, so C++ calls are not inlined into the Zig benchmark loop.
tradeoffs: Uses about 25% more memory than the C++ tables (12.0 KB vs 8.0 KB for 1K u32 keys, 12.0 MB vs 8.0 MB at 1M); Zig only.
caveats: Own harness, no CPU model or OS stated. Harness asymmetries: (1) 'Reserved Ins.' calls ensureTotalCapacity for verztable and Zig std, but benchCpp's setup for .insert_reserved does nothing and the wrapper has no reserve function, so the C++ columns in that row are plain un-reserved inserts (verztable 'wins' 22 of 27 such rows); (2) every C++ operation goes through a non-inlined extern "C" call (insert also memcpys the value into a temporary), which adds roughly a call's cost to 1-5 ns operations, the size range where verztable wins most; the README's argument that Ankerl's 0 ns iteration shows minimal FFI overhead does not hold because iteration is a single wrapper call that counts inside C++. The string fast path (keys up to 8 bytes packed into a u64) and stored 64-bit hashes are design features the competitors do not use. Uses about 25% more memory than the competitors by the README's own trade-off note (string sets 3.3 MB vs 1.9-2.0 MB at 100K). Verstable (C) is the algorithmic inspiration, not a benchmark target. 15 stars, single author.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/performance?l=zig description 'faster than the top C++ hash tables'; README and BENCHMARKS.md of ThobiasKnudsen/verztable.
why_faster: README: hash-fragment filtering skips non-matches without touching bucket data; fast path for strings of 8 bytes or fewer; stores full 64-bit hashes for string keys to skip memcmp.

verification.tier_reason: First-party harness is public (src/benchmark.zig, src/cpp_hashtables_wrapper.cpp, C++ flags in build.zig) and BENCHMARKS.md has the quoted numbers, but no CPU model or machine is stated, so not A; tier stays C, and the claim is downgraded because the headline rows are partly harness artifacts and verztable loses most integer-key rows at 3K and 100K elements.
verification.notes: Real table with a public harness, but the claim is overstated: the cited Reserved Ins. win compares reserved verztable against un-reserved C++ tables, all C++ operations pay a non-inlined FFI call, and verztable loses 239 of 432 rows to the best C++ table (beats Boost by only about 3% geomean, loses most integer rows at 3K/100K). Record shortcomings: harness asymmetry (no reserve for C++, per-op FFI), no CPU model, not faster than Boost on integer keys at scale, higher memory use.

name: Zig (kostya/benchmarks base64)
baseline: Hand-written scalar C base64 (no library), gcc and clang, -O3 -march=native -flto
workload: Base64 encode and decode of a 131072-byte string, 8192 tries, into newly allocated buffers; seconds.
claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks base64 table (median, Xeon E-2324G, README updated 2026-07-19): Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, about 1.31x and 1.59x faster (derived from page data); Rust 0.842 s also beats both. The same table has C/clang (aklomp) 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7.4x faster than Zig, and PHP 0.065 s (its C base64) fastest overall; C++ with libcrypto takes 3.664 s.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (std.base64); C and C++: gcc/g++ 16.1.0 or clang/clang++ 22.1.8 with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto -std=c23 / c++23 -Wa,-mbranches-within-32B-boundaries (common/commands.mk)
caveats: Not the same algorithm: Zig uses std.base64 (checked in lib/std/base64.zig at the 0.15.2 tag and master on the GitHub mirror; the 0.16.0 tag is not on GitHub), whose decoder ORs four 256-entry u32 tables pre-shifted per character position, checks validity once per 4 characters and writes 16 bytes per u128 store, and whose encoder reads 16 bytes as a u128 and emits 16 characters per 12 input bytes; base64/test-nolib.c uses one decode table, branches on every character, scans for \n and \r before each quantum (MIME tolerance Zig's standard decoder does not provide) and stores byte by byte. So the win is a library implementation difference; the SIMD C library (aklomp) is about 7x faster than Zig, and the same four-table technique is available in C (e.g. Chromium modp_b64). Buffers: Zig uses a FixedBufferAllocator and C uses stack VLAs, so 'newly allocated buffers' cost nothing on either side; the Zig input is a comptime constant ("a" ** 131072) and the C input a memset stack array. Zig is built with zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -lc (native CPU by default), C with -O3 -march=native -flto=auto. Medians with MAD from one machine; the README states no flags in prose (they are in common/commands.mk).
found_via: GitHub: kostya/benchmarks README tables (cross-language suite named in QUEUE.md section E).
tradeoffs: Single task microbenchmark; Zig std.base64 is scalar.

verification.tier_reason: The kostya/benchmarks README (UPDATE 2026-07-19, Intel Xeon E-2324G, Zig 0.16.0, gcc 16.1.0, clang 22.1.8) shows Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s, with code (base64/test.zig, base64/test-nolib.c) and flags (common/commands.mk, base64/Makefile) public, so the harness is A-grade; capped at C because it is not like for like: Zig calls std.base64, which decodes 16 characters per step through four pre-shifted lookup tables with one validity check and a 16-byte store and encodes 12 bytes per u128 load, while the C program is a hand-written per-character decoder with a branch per character and newline skipping (same asymmetric-kernel cap as the kostya matmul D entry in batch-02).
verification.notes: Numbers verified on the README; harness is reproducible (code, flags, CPU, versions) but the win comes from Zig's std.base64 algorithm against a naive hand-written C loop, so it stays C with same_algorithm false; the best C (aklomp/base64, SIMD) is about 7x faster than Zig. Record shortcoming: different algorithm on each side, not a language effect.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Zig 0.703 s vs C/clang 0.918 s and C/gcc 1.117 s (about 1.3x and 1.6x faster, derived from page data). Rust 0.842 s is also faster than both. The same table has C/clang with aklomp/base64 at 0.095 s and C/gcc (aklomp) 0.097 s, about 7x faster than Zig.
corrected_fields.caveats: No mechanism is given by the source, which caps the tier at C. Zig uses its standard-library base64 while C is a separate hand-written table-driven implementation, so this compares two implementations, and the best C implementation (aklomp SIMD library) is far faster than Zig. The README states no compiler flags in prose; flags were read from common/commands.mk and the base64 Makefile. Values are medians with MAD from one machine.

name: C# NativeAOT minima-sync (HttpArena entry)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG) and libreactorng (C, io_uring, gcc -O3 -march=native) implementing the same HttpArena endpoints
workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), 16x pipelined and limited-conn profiles for a synchronous single-issuer io_uring HTTP/1.1 server written in C# and compiled with NativeAOT: one pinned reactor thread per core, multishot accept, parse-in-place, responses serialized straight into the send buffer. Code lives in frameworks/minima-sync of the HttpArena repo.
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,386,544 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.34x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.20x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.18x), libioma 4,255,834 (1.03x), libreactorng 4,377,377 (1.00x, parity) and Drogon 2,022,710 (2.17x); the Zig io_uring entry zeemo is ahead at 4,422,489 and libxev (Zig) ties at 4,381,919, all at the roughly 4.4M req/s baseline ceiling the suite itself names in scripts/lib/profiles.sh. pipelined-4096 (reference-only): 57,140,640 vs libreactorng 43,424,448 (1.32x), h2o 4,938,603 (11.6x), nginx 4,037,345 (14.2x); libioma and mongoose have no pipelined result. limited-conn-4096: 2,687,059 vs libioma 2,707,029 (0.99x), mongoose 2,701,933 (0.99x), libreactorng 2,685,717 (1.00x), h2o 2,651,569 (1.01x), nginx 2,626,297 (1.02x). Ordinary .NET servers in the same suite: Kestrel 1,320,795 and ASP.NET Core minimal 1,305,946 req/s at baseline-4096.
compiler_and_flags: C#: mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:10.0 image, 'dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64 -p:PublishAot=true' with clang and zlib1g-dev for the native link; csproj sets PublishAot, Optimize, ServerGarbageCollection, InvariantGlobalization and AllowUnsafeBlocks, and no IlcInstructionSet, so the binary targets generic x86-64. The io_uring bindings are C# (raw io_uring_setup/enter/register through libc syscall(), mmap'd rings), not liburing. C side: libreactorng at pinned commit 7a65f8b plus a connection-close patch, library configured with CFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' and server.c built with gcc -O3 -march=native (ubuntu:24.04 build-essential, compiler version not stated); nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' (debian:trixie build-essential, version not stated); libioma and mongoose -O3 -march=native with LTO, h2o CMake Release with clang -march=native, Drogon handler only against the prebuilt drogonframework/drogon:latest image.
hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine per site/data/current.json: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX 64-Cores (64 cores, 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), CPU governor performance; each entry runs in a container. current.json is undated and may differ from the machine state of the run behind a given results file.
stars_or_usage: HttpArena repo has 128 stars; the Minima io_uring bindings it reuses live in a separate HttpArena entry whose own repository was not found
tradeoffs: Benchmark-only synchronous reactor that blocks the core on slow handlers (the README says so); does not run the async-db, crud or TLS profiles; Linux io_uring only; NativeAOT drops reflection-based .NET features.
caveats: Parity, not a win, against the C server with the same design: 1.00x libreactorng at baseline-4096 and limited-conn-4096, below libioma and mongoose at limited-conn, and the top baseline entries (zeemo, minima-sync, libxev, libreactorng) sit within 4% at the roughly 4.4M req/s ceiling that scripts/lib/profiles.sh names, with the gcannon load generator pinned to the other half of the machine (CPUs 32-63,96-127). The gains over nginx (1.34x), h2o and mongoose compare a minimal io_uring server against epoll servers and different response sizes (62.9 bytes per response vs nginx 135.4, Drogon 134.4, libreactorng 108.7, libioma 85.8, mongoose 72.5; derived from bandwidth divided by req/s), so same_algorithm is false. The pipelined profile (16x batched) is reference-only in HttpArena's composite score. The contender was written by the suite owner MDA2AV (PR #824, 2026-06-07) and exists only inside the HttpArena repo (meta.json repo is empty), modelled on the Zig zeemo architecture; the same-owner ioxide entry was tiered C in this wave while suite-owner entries such as kestrel kept A. Results are best of 3 runs of 5 s each (RUNS=3 in scripts/lib/common.sh), not one run, but the JSON files are undated and rows come from different runs on the same machine: minima-sync.json was last re-measured on or before 2026-08-29 (later commits only dropped profiles), libreactorng.json on 2026-09-07 and nginx.json in August. C/C++ entries are built -O3 -march=native (libioma and mongoose with LTO) or CMake Release with clang -march=native (h2o), while the C# binary targets generic x86-64, so the flags favour the C side; Drogon compiles only its handler against the prebuilt drogonframework/drogon:latest image, so the Drogon ratios are weaker evidence. The C competitor handlers are minimal hand-written servers by the suite maintainers or contributors, not tuned production configurations. tradeoffs: V is a young language (default GC, built from master, 77 open issues on the repo); memory use is high (about 640 MiB to 990 MiB in the entries above versus about 100 MiB for C entries); the io_uring backend has no TLS (TLS runs on the epoll backend).
caveats: The json-comp ratios (9.6x over userver, 22x over Drogon) time a response cache: write_json_gzip in main.v keeps complete gzipped responses keyed by (count, m), compresses once on the first miss and appends the cached bytes on every hit, while HttpArena's json-comp rules forbid pre-compressed caches for standard and tuned entries (vanilla is an 'engine' entry, which has no rules) and the C++ rows compress per request. vanilla's rate there is 2.7x the next entry (zix, which compresses per request). No C engine or nginx runs json-comp. The json-tls body is partly pre-serialized: each item's JSON except total is rendered once at startup into a prefix string, so per request vanilla formats one integer per item and copies prefixes, whereas nginx's infrastructure rules require full per-request serialization; TLS is Mbed TLS (C, patched to cache the RSA signing context) with kTLS record offload in the kernel. static-tls and pipelined are reference-only profiles. At baseline-4096 the entry trails libreactorng (0.98x) and is level with libioma (1.01x) and at limited-conn it ties libreactorng and libioma, so on the scored HTTP/1.1 profiles vanilla matches but does not beat the best C engines. The vanilla-epoll entry is slower at baseline-4096 (3,985,550) and at limited-conn-4096 (1,021,750). V compiles to C (gcc -O3 -flto), so this is a V-generated C server against hand-written C servers, not a different code generator. The vanilla entries are maintained by the vanilla author (meta.json maintainers: enghitalo). The vanilla README publishes no throughput numbers against C servers; docs/PERF_GAP_ANALYSIS.md treats libreactorng, zeemo and tokio as the faster reference servers. The Drogon entry builds only its handler against the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image and userver uses a prebuilt v3.2 image, so those ratios are weaker evidence than the nginx, h2o, libreactorng and libioma ratios.

name: zeemo
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG); same suite rows for libreactorng, libioma, mongoose, h2o (C) and Drogon, agensio, userver (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), 16x pipelined and limited-conn profiles on a bare-metal Zig HTTP/1.1 server: one io_uring reactor process per logical CPU via SO_REUSEPORT, hand-written incremental parser, registered provided-buffer rings.
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,422,489 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.35x, derived from page data), h2o 3,641,609 (1.21x), mongoose 3,707,598 (1.19x), libioma 4,255,834 (1.04x), libreactorng 4,377,377 (1.01x, within noise), Drogon 2,022,710 (2.19x). pipelined-4096: 49,860,224 vs libreactorng 43,424,448 (1.15x), nginx 4,037,345 (12.4x), Drogon 7,801,404 (6.4x). compiler_and_flags: zeemo: Zig 0.16.0 official tarball on ubuntu:24.04, zig build -Dtarget=x86_64-linux-musl --release=fast (ReleaseFast, stripped static musl binary on scratch); no -Dcpu is given, so Zig compiles for the baseline x86-64 CPU rather than the host, while the C rows use -march=native (frameworks/zeemo/Dockerfile, build.zig). C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom C handler module, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' (debian:trixie); libreactorng 7a65f8b configured CFLAGS='-O3 -march=native' and its server built gcc -O3 -march=native (no LTO); libioma and mongoose gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; h2o clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO; agensio CMake Release -DAGENSIO_NATIVE=ON; userver service CMake Release -march=native on the prebuilt userver v3.2 image; Drogon handler only, CMake Release on the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image (MDA2AV/HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).
hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, one NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json, site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). tradeoffs: Single-purpose HttpArena benchmark server (HTTP/1.1 only, a handful of endpoints), no TLS or HTTP/2 in this entry, Linux io_uring only; no license file found, so the code cannot be copied.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repository (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md and COPYING all 404; the repo page shows no license), so usability is reference. The margin over libreactorng at baseline-4096 is 1% (within run-to-run noise) and over libioma 4%; zeemo trails nginx (0.99x), libioma (0.96x), mongoose and libreactorng on limited-conn-4096, and the pipelined win (1.15x libreactorng) is on a reference-only profile. The README's '#1 on baseline-4096' is stale: zix (Zig) now leads at 4,442,329. The HttpArena entry is a minimal server built for the suite (forked worker processes pinned per CPU, routes /baseline11, /pipeline and /json) that sends no Date or Server header: bytes per response at baseline-4096 (derived from page data, bandwidth divided by req/s) are 62.9 against 108.7 for libreactorng (per-second cached Date header), 85.8 for libioma, 72.5 for mongoose, 98.2 for h2o and 135.4 for nginx, and at pipelined-4096 61.4 against libreactorng's 106.2, so part of each margin is header volume. The zeemo repo's later json-comp and TLS work (May 2026) is not part of the HttpArena entry, which runs only baseline, pipelined, limited-conn and the latency profiles. Each number is the best of 3 runs of 5 s with the server limited to 32 cores / 64 threads; results files are undated and rows come from different runs (zeemo.json last written 2026-08-30, libreactorng.json 2026-09-07, per git history). tradeoffs: Young Zig 0.16 network library and HTTP engine; the URING dispatch model is Linux-only and needs a recent kernel; the TLS static-file path is slower than nginx; project is pre-1.0.
caveats: The margin over the fastest C entries at baseline-4096 and limited-conn-4096 is 0-4% (libreactorng, libioma), within run-to-run noise; the clear wins are over nginx, h2o, mongoose, agensio and Drogon, which use epoll or Asio rather than io_uring, and on the pipelined, json-tls, h2c-json, h3 and static-h2 profiles. scripts/benchmark.sh keeps the best of 3 runs of 5 s per profile, but the results files record only the winning run, and each entry's file is saved at a different time (zix.json and nginx.json last changed 2026-08-30, libreactorng.json 2026-09-07 after a Connection: close fix), so rows are cross-run comparisons on the same machine; current.json (the CPU and kernel record) is undated. zix itself is fetched by branch name (0.5.x, 0.5.x-rc1), so the exact commit behind the numbers is not recorded. The H/2 and H/3 rows come from separate zix engines (zix.Http2, zix.Http3 with pure-Zig QUIC on std.crypto), not the Http1 engine. The C competitor entries (nginx with a custom C handler module, libreactorng, libioma, h2o, mongoose) are minimal handlers built by the suite maintainers or contributors; nginx is reasonably tuned (access_log off, reuseport, worker_processes auto). The Drogon entry compiles only its handler against the prebuilt drogon:latest image, so its 2x to 8x ratios are weaker evidence. Response sizes differ (bytes per response derived from bandwidth / req/s: baseline-4096 nginx 135.4, Drogon 134.4, libreactorng 108.7, libioma 85.8, mongoose 72.5, zix 62.9; baseline-h3 zix about 7.6, agensio about 17.4, nginx about 76), so zix writes the fewest bytes per request. In static-tls zix sends about 11.9 KB per response against about 3.1 KB for nginx and agensio (derived), consistent with nginx (gzip_static, brotli_static) and agensio serving precompressed variants that zix does not, so that profile is not like-for-like either way. The pipelined profile is reference-only in HttpArena's composite score. The zix README only links to HttpArena badges and gives no numbers.

At limited-conn-4096 it is behind Drogon and Cutelyst too (1,135,157 vs 1,694,883 and 1,736,401) and far behind nginx 2,626,297. json-tls: 1,157,219 vs nginx 1,313,755, h2o 1,229,462 and agensio 1,716,076 (ahead of Drogon 253,055 and mongoose 1,102,964). static-tls 55,882 and static-h2 51,989-64,019 vs nginx 720,869 and 796,607-802,090. Wins over Drogon also on json-comp (541,211 vs 127,466, where Drogon's jsoncpp allocation churn dominates), async-32000 (Drogon entry runs every delay timer on one loop, per wave 5) and fixed-rate CPU per request (latency-1m 24.9 vs 32.1 us). pipelined-4096 (16,338,425 vs Drogon 7,801,404 and nginx 4,037,345) is a reference-only profile excluded from HttpArena's composite score. actix.json still carries baseline-h2c/json-h2c rows although actix's meta.json no longer subscribes to them (stale). Rows come from separate runs on the same machine (actix last saved 2026-09-06, Drogon 2026-09-06, nginx 2026-08-30); the actix entry runs an unreleased actix-web git revision; Drogon is built from an unpinned image without -march=native while actix gets target-cpu=native and thin LTO; handlers are minimal (nginx is a custom C module). Third-party swerver-benchmarks (Docker Desktop on Apple Silicon, 2 CPUs) has actix 133,691 vs nginx 118,061 req/s, while statico's README has nginx ahead (832,082 vs 798,809 at four threads, 286,960 vs 213,756 at one).

name: cardigan
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, mongoose (C) and Drogon (C++) rows in the same table
workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections), plus pipelined, HTTP/2 and h2c baseline profiles, on one 64-core machine; cardigan is a Java io_uring HTTP engine using Panama FFI, virtual threads and the Vector API.
compiler_and_flags: cardigan 0.1.0-alpha.5: maven eclipse-temurin JDK 26 build, eclipse-temurin:26-jre runtime with --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -Xms512m -Xmx2g -XX:MaxInlineSize=150 -XX:FreqInlineSize=600 (frameworks/cardigan/Dockerfile); TLS through the system libssl.so.3/libcrypto.so.3 via Panama with opportunistic kTLS. nginx 1.31.4: -O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG with a custom C handler module, worker_processes auto, reuseport. Drogon: CMake Release with jemalloc preloaded. h2o: clang Release -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, single NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4, kernel 6.17.0-22, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json; site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). Server container and the gcannon/h2load load generator are pinned to separate halves of the same machine (load generator on CPUs 32-63,96-127) and talk over loopback with MTU 1500; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
tradeoffs: Experimental alpha Java server needing JDK 26 preview features, Panama FFI and the incubating Vector API; io_uring needs seccomp unconfined in containers; JVM heap 512m-2g and warm-up are not part of the throughput figure.
caveats: The win over nginx is architectural (io_uring thread-per-core vs nginx's epoll workers), not Java: the io_uring C engines on the same board beat cardigan at baseline-4096 (libreactorng 4,377,377, libioma 4,255,834 vs 3,947,346), and at limited-conn-4096 cardigan (2,613,832) is behind nginx 2,626,297, h2o 2,651,569, libreactorng 2,685,717, mongoose 2,701,933 and libioma 2,707,029. On h2/h2c nginx is the outlier: h2o leads baseline-h2-256 (16,106,978 vs 14,467,569) and agensio (C++) leads baseline-h2-256 (14,744,015) and h2c-256 (15,185,367 vs 15,144,652), so the 4.2x and 6.2x ratios measure nginx's HTTP/2 stack. TLS rows (baseline-h2, json-tls 1,703,461 vs nginx 1,313,755 and agensio 1,716,076) run OpenSSL 3 through Panama FFI with kTLS, so crypto is C or kernel code. pipelined-4096 (45,708,428 vs nginx 4,037,345; libreactorng 43,424,448) is a reference-only profile excluded from the composite score. Fixed-rate CPU per request is mixed (latency-1m 20.4 us, second only to libioma 19.3; latency-10k 31.7 us, behind most C/C++ entries; 8gbit 60.7 vs mongoose 57.4 and Drogon 58.3). Experimental alpha (0.1.0-alpha.5, 28 commits, 1 star), relies on unsupported JDK internals (APOLOGY.md), needs JDK 26 preview and incubator Vector API and Linux 6.1+. The entry was contributed by the cardigan author; rows come from separate runs on the same machine (cardigan last saved 2026-09-03, nginx 2026-08-30); the repo README states no benchmark numbers; handlers are minimal (nginx is a custom C module).

name: cpeak (Rust)
baseline: Drogon (C++) named in the README; userver, hical, Cutelyst (C++) and nginx, h2o, mongoose (C) rows in the same HttpArena tables
workload: HttpArena profiles on one 64-core machine: baseline (4096 connections), pipelined, json-comp (gzip JSON), json-tls and async-db; cpeak is an Express-style Rust framework on hyper with one single-threaded Tokio event loop per core and sonic-rs JSON.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ranked #1 of 95 frameworks on the HttpArena HTTP/1.1 leaderboard, surpassing Drogon (C++), Vert.x (Java), Bun (TS), Actix Web (Rust) and others'; 2.59 million plain requests per second and 1.28 million JSON responses per second over TLS. HttpArena JSON rows (ratios derived from page data): baseline-4096 2,586,588 vs Drogon 2,022,710 (1.28x), Cutelyst 2,153,860 (1.20x) but nginx 3,284,513 (0.79x); pipelined-4096 14,496,147 vs nginx 4,037,345 (3.59x), Drogon 7,801,404 (1.86x); json-comp-4096 493,187 vs userver 297,311 (1.66x), hical 261,955 (1.88x), Drogon 127,466 (3.87x); async-db-1024 320,543 vs userver 248,628 (1.29x); json-tls-4096 1,284,103 vs nginx 1,313,755 (0.98x), h2o 1,229,462 (1.04x), mongoose 1,102,964 (1.16x).

C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom C handler module built --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' (debian:trixie); h2o pinned commit ccea64b, clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO; mongoose 7.23 gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; libreactorng pinned 7a65f8b and its server gcc -O3 -march=native; agensio v0.1.0-alpha.23 CMake Release -DAGENSIO_NATIVE=ON; proxygen CMake Release on the pinned facebook/proxygen base image with mimalloc; Drogon CMake Release (handler only) on the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image; userver v3.2 image, CMake Release -march=native; hical gcc-14 CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native (MDA2AV/HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).
hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, one NUMA node, 8x DDR4-3200), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json; site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). The server container runs with seccomp=unconfined on the cpuset 0-31,64-95 for the H/1.1 profiles and the load generator on CPUs 32-63,96-127 of the same machine over loopback (scripts/lib/framework.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/lib/common.sh). current.json is undated and describes the machine now, not necessarily at the date of each results file.
tradeoffs: Rust framework with a Node.js sibling; started as an educational project; HttpArena lists the entry as 'emerging' and 'tuned' mode, so the #1 claim is on the tuned leaderboard filter.
caveats: The README's '#1 of 95' (rust/README.md; the root README says '#1') is the HttpArena framework board filtered to flagship and emerging types with tuned entries shown (badge link type=emerging,flagship&tuned=1). nginx, h2o and agensio are 'infrastructure' and mongoose, libreactorng, libioma and proxygen are 'engine' entries, ranked on separate boards, and hical is 'experimental' (hidden by default), so the '#1' beats only the C++ frameworks Drogon, Cutelyst and userver. In the raw rows cpeak is 0.79x nginx at baseline-4096 and 0.81x at limited-conn-4096 (2,118,981 vs 2,626,297), and behind h2o, mongoose, agensio, libreactorng, libioma and hical (3,228,043) at baseline-4096. cpeak's meta.json declares mode 'tuned' (non-default configuration in HttpArena's terms) while the C++ framework entries are 'standard', though the entry README says default configuration. Pipelined and async-db are reference-only in the framework composite; the pipelined ratio vs nginx is mostly nginx's pipelining cost. TLS is rustls on ring, whose AES-GCM is BoringSSL-derived assembly. The cpeak entry was added 2026-10-11 by the cpeak author (meta.json maintainers: agile8118), and the README numbers were added the same day (commit c8fb314); rows come from different runs on the same machine (cpeak.json 2026-10-11, nginx.json and h2o.json 2026-08-30, drogon.json 2026-09-06, userver.json 2026-09-11 per git history). Each number is the best of 3 runs of 5 s. Every entry is a minimal hand-written handler for the same endpoint contract (nginx runs a custom C handler module), baseline-4096 mixes GET and POST with query parsing, and Drogon is built against the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image. The http-arena.com board itself could not be opened here (DNS failure), so the rank is taken from the README.
