name: dusty
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C) and Drogon (C++) in the HttpArena suite; Hical (C++) and h2o (C) rows alongside
workload: HttpArena baseline profile (mixed GET/POST with query parsing, 4096 connections, 64-core machine) for the Dusty HTTP framework on the zio async runtime, 'standard configuration, no tuning'.
claimed_speedup: HttpArena, same harness but separate runs: baseline-4096 dusty 3,309,488 req/s vs nginx (C) 3,284,513 (+0.8%, derived from page data, a tie), Hical (C++) 3,228,043 (1.03x, derived), Drogon (C++) 2,022,710 (1.64x, derived); behind h2o (C) 3,641,609, mongoose (C) 3,707,598 and libreactorng (C) 4,377,377. json-tls-4096: 989,946 vs Drogon 253,055 (3.91x, derived) and Hical 549,765 (1.80x, derived), but behind nginx 1,313,755, h2o 1,229,462 and mongoose 1,102,964. json-comp-4096: 397,047 vs Drogon 127,466 (3.11x, derived) and Hical 261,955 (1.52x, derived). limited-conn-4096: 1,930,687, ahead of Drogon 1,694,883 but behind nginx 2,626,297, Hical 2,407,681 and h2o 2,651,569. pipelined-4096 (reference-only profile, excluded from the composite score): 4,379,900 vs nginx 4,037,345, but behind Drogon 7,801,404, Hical 4,851,267 and h2o 4,938,603.
compiler_and_flags: dusty: Zig 0.16.0, target x86_64-linux-musl, zig build --release=fast -Dcpu=x86_64_v3+aes+pclmul+adx (frameworks/dusty/Dockerfile). nginx 1.31.4 with the custom C handler module ngx_http_httparena_module.c, configured with --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG' on Debian trixie build-essential (frameworks/nginx/Dockerfile). Drogon: CMake Release build of main.cc on the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image, run with LD_PRELOAD=libjemalloc.so.2 (frameworks/drogon/Dockerfile). hardware: HttpArena dedicated machine: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (64 cores, 128 threads), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (site/data/current.json). name: grpc-dotnet (gRPC for .NET)
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc/grpc) servers cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc in the grpc_bench suite
workload: grpc_bench complex_proto unary SayHello over loopback: 50 client connections, 1000 concurrent requests, unlimited QPS, 120 s with 30 s warmup, ghz client. One run per server-CPU setting: 1 to 4 server CPUs in the 2026-04-22 run (commit c4c93b3, discussion #559) and 1 to 3 in the 2022-04-23 run (commit 14a8435, wiki).
claimed_speedup:
Newest maintainer run (discussion #559, 2026-04-22, commit c4c93b3, .NET 9 with Grpc.AspNetCore 2.66.0): dotnet_grpc is ahead of every C++ server at every CPU count. 1 CPU: 84,809 req/s vs cpp_grpc_mt 57,403, cpp_grpc_st 57,140 and cpp_asio_grpc 56,669 (1.48x, 1.48x, 1.50x). 2 CPUs: 123,609 vs cpp_asio_grpc 74,869 and cpp_grpc_mt 74,574 (1.65x, 1.66x). 3 CPUs: 136,452 vs cpp_grpc_mt 81,581 (1.67x). 4 CPUs: 135,948 vs 85,485 (1.59x).
2022-04-23 wiki run (commit 14a8435, .NET 6): 1 CPU 33,899 vs cpp_grpc_st 26,700, cpp_grpc_mt 26,376 and cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 (1.27x, 1.29x, 1.36x). 2 CPUs: 68,266 vs cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 (0.98x). 3 CPUs: 68,821 vs 71,806 (0.96x).
Third-party run (discussion #547, 2025-12-09, Ryzen 9 5900X, client CPUs equal to server CPUs, 10 s): near tie with cpp_grpc_mt, 0.92x at 1 CPU, 1.01x at 4 and 1.14x at 24.
All ratios derived from page data.
compiler_and_flags: dotnet_grpc in the 2026-04 run (c4c93b3): mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0, net9.0, Grpc.AspNetCore 2.66.0, dotnet build -c Release, Kestrel listener HTTP/2 only (dotnet_grpc_bench/Dockerfile, GreeterServer/GreeterServer.csproj, Program.cs). In the 2022 run (14a8435): sdk:6.0, net6.0, Grpc.AspNetCore 2.41.0 with DOTNET_ReadyToRun=0, DOTNET_TieredPGO=1 and DOTNET_TC_QuickJitForLoops=1. The HEAD Dockerfile now uses sdk:10.0. C++ baselines: cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_grpc_st are built with g++ --std=c++20 -O3 -flto over main.cpp and the generated stubs, linking jemalloc and Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++-dev from the base image (gcc:15.2.0 at c4c93b3, gcc:11 at 14a8435, gcc:16.1.0 at HEAD). The gRPC core's version and build flags are the distro package's and are not stated or pinned. cpp_asio_grpc uses asio-grpc v1.0.0, CMake Release with jemalloc, against the same distro libgrpc++.
hardware: Newest run (discussion #559, posted by maintainer LesnyRumcajs 2026-04-22, commit c4c93b3): Intel Xeon Gold 6548N (16) @ 2.80 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.3, kernel 6.8.0-71, DigitalOcean dedicated server. Server limited to 1, 2, 3 or 4 CPUs and 4096m RAM; client 11 CPUs. 2022-04-23 wiki run (commit 14a8435): Intel Xeon E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32 GB RAM. Server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs and 512m RAM; client 9 CPUs.
tradeoffs: .NET runtime and JIT required; it sits on Kestrel (ASP.NET Core).
caveats:
The result depends on the run.
- In the newest maintainer run (.NET 9) dotnet_grpc leads every C++ server by 1.48-1.67x at 1-4 CPUs. Its p99 at 1 CPU is worse (54.20 vs 21.81 ms for cpp_grpc_mt), and it uses about 4-6x the memory (127.87 vs 20.59 MiB at 1 CPU, 134.64 vs 31.71 MiB at 4).
- In the 2022 run (.NET 6) it led only at 1 CPU and trailed cpp_grpc_mt by 2-4% at 2 and 3 CPUs.
- In a client-bound third-party run (#547, by the wtx author) the two tie.
- The C++ servers link Debian's prebuilt libgrpc++, which is unpinned and of unstated version and flags, so the -O3 -flto applies only to the server code and stubs. They follow the helloworld async-example pattern: one completion queue and thread per server CPU, with one pre-posted request per queue (cpp_grpc_mt_bench/main.cpp). They scale poorly: cpp_grpc_mt does 57,403 req/s at 1 CPU and 85,485 at 4 CPUs while using 405% CPU. So the baseline is a stock but untuned gRPC C++ server.
- grpc-dotnet runs on ASP.NET Core Kestrel (dotnet/aspnetcore, a separate wave 14 record), so much of the HTTP/2 work is Kestrel's.
- The workload is a unary complex_proto SayHello only, over loopback on one host, with a single run per setting.
- The grpc-dotnet README makes no performance claim.

tradeoffs: Experimental HTTP/1.1 server for Linux built with Dart FFI and epoll; Linux/WSL only, minimal feature set.
caveats: The suite entry dart/jet_server/server.dart was written by the jet_server author (suite commits b869a75, ac9f6f2 and b3f17f2 by Wdestroier) and is specialised to the benchmark: it returns pre-built response byte arrays, routes by comparing raw bytes, sends no Content-Type header and uses no router, while the Drogon entry runs Drogon's routing (a sync advice for GET /, UserCtrl for the /user routes) and builds HttpResponse objects with Content-Type: text/plain; jet_server averages 62.3 bytes received per request vs 78.3 for Drogon (derived from total_bytes_received / total_requests), so handler work is not equal. The library is pure Dart: lib/src holds buffer_pool, constants, http_parser, jet_server_impl and syscall .dart files and the package depends only on ffi, so the event loop and parser are Dart code calling libc epoll/read/write through dart:ffi; the near-equal AOT and VM rows mean the JIT reaches AOT speed after warmup or both rows hit a common ceiling, not that a native C loop does the work. No Dart row in data.json (jet_server, shelf, relic, spry) carries the suite's server_cpu_saturation / server_cpu_cores validity probe, so whether jet_server was server-bound, or ran under the same 4-CPU allotment as Drogon, cannot be checked. The top rows at 256 connections cluster within 1.5% (morojs-engine 259,617, morojs 259,418, jet_server-vm 256,385, caprese 256,004, jet_server 255,549), consistent with a shared ceiling. The README prints no numbers and points to the-benchmarker; its own benchmarks/jet_vs_shelf compares only against Dart's shelf. The project calls itself experimental and targets Linux/WSL only; 8 commits, 1 star. Suite-level weaknesses: published snapshots move a lot between runs (Drogon 101,282-179,279 req/s across the 2026-09-15 to 2026-10-06 snapshots) and a snapshot gives no repeat spread; the suite README says a run is server-bound only above 75% CPU saturation and invalid below 50%, and in the 2026-10-06 snapshot the 60 fastest rows sit at 49-63% (Drogon 62-63%), so the ceiling for the fastest servers may be the load generator or the box rather than the server; the presence of the server_cpu_saturation / server_cpu_cores probe places this snapshot in the README's current zrk --closed keep-alive revision, although the README's contract paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; the workload is three trivial routes (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user) with near-empty bodies. The C/C++ rows are only Drogon 1.9.13 (cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release, threads_num 0 = auto, Server and Date headers disabled, no LTO), oatpp 1.3, agoo-c 0.7 and cwist 3.9 (C); cwist is the best C row at 64 connections (186,252) and agoo-c at 256 and 512; nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in this suite. Same table, losers to Drogon at 256 connections: Crystal toro 166,910, Go fasthttp 166,243, C# aspnet-minimal-api 147,805 vs Drogon 178,341. The CPU string 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' on an x86_64 Fedora kernel is not a recognisable CPU model, and no C++ compiler version is pinned in the suite files read (cpp/drogon/config.yaml language version '14/17'), which is why this is B and not A.

name: libxev (HttpArena baseline server)
baseline: libreactorng (C, io_uring) and h2o (C) in the HttpArena suite; also nginx 1.31.4 (C) and Drogon (C++)
workload: HttpArena baseline profile: mixed GET/POST /baseline11 requests with query parsing (sum of query integers plus the body), 4096 keep-alive connections, pipeline depth 1, 5 s runs. Server on 32 cores / 64 threads of a Threadripper PRO 3995WX, gcannon load over loopback. The HTTP/1.1 server is written in Zig on libxev's io_uring backend, with one forked worker per CPU, SO_REUSEPORT and TCP_NODELAY, and parses requests with picohttpparser (C).
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 4,381,919 req/s vs libreactorng 4,377,377 (+0.1%, derived from page data, a tie), h2o 3,641,609 (1.20x, derived), nginx 3,284,513 (1.33x, derived) and Drogon 2,022,710 (2.17x, derived). On limited-conn-4096 (connections close after 10 requests) libxev's 2,672,662 is behind libreactorng's 2,685,717 (-0.5%, derived) and level with h2o (2,651,569) and nginx (2,626,297). latency-1m/10k/500k-8cpu are fixed-rate profiles scored on CPU per request, not throughput.
compiler_and_flags: libxev entry: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native; picohttpparser.c is compiled by zig's C frontend at -O3 (frameworks/libxev/build.zig). libreactorng: Ubuntu 24.04 gcc, library configured with CFLAGS=-O3 -march=native and the server built with gcc -O3 -march=native. nginx 1.31.4: --with-cc-opt=-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG (Debian trixie gcc). h2o: clang with CMake Release and -march=native -mtune=native, no LTO. Drogon: CMake Release (CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG) in the drogonframework/drogon:latest image, without -march=native, with jemalloc LD_PRELOADed.
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, 8x DDR4-3200, one NUMA node), per HttpArena site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md. The server is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the gcannon load generator to the other half. Traffic goes over loopback with MTU set to 1500, the governor is set to performance, and the sysctls are raised by scripts/lib/system.sh.
tradeoffs: libxev is an event loop (timers, sockets, files) rather than a web server; the measured server is a minimal handler in the HttpArena repo, not part of libxev.
caveats: The libxev README says it will not post benchmark results and claims only that you 'shouldn't notice a slowdown' against other event loops, so the figure here is an HttpArena application, not a library claim. Request parsing is done by picohttpparser (C, compiled at -O3), so the Zig code is the event loop, the glue and the arithmetic. Against the best C entry (libreactorng, also io_uring and SO_REUSEPORT per CPU) the result is a tie on baseline (+0.1%), and libreactorng is 0.5% ahead on limited-conn. The margins over h2o, nginx and Drogon reflect io_uring against epoll engines and minimal handlers against full servers (nginx runs a custom C handler module), not Zig codegen. The libxev server does no routing (every path gets the sum response) while libreactorng dispatches on the path, a small saving for the Zig side. The results JSON files are undated and are rerun by the suite's maintainers; competitor rows come from sibling JSON files in the same directory. HttpArena is a smaller suite (about 128 GitHub stars) than TechEmpower.

name: PowPow
baseline: Drogon 1.9.13 (C++, trantor event loop; the-benchmarker cpp/drogon, cmake release build); also agoo-c 0.7 (C) in the same table
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks minimal HTTP contract (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user on port 3000), total_requests_per_s at 64, 256 and 512 connections, each framework in its own container.
claimed_speedup: powpow 0.2 in data.json updated 2026-10-06: 237,033 / 248,309 / 238,538 req/s at 64 / 256 / 512 connections vs Drogon 177,005 / 178,341 / 171,358 (1.34x / 1.39x / 1.39x, derived from page data); vs agoo-c (C) 1.65x at 64, 1.16x at 256, 1.19x at 512, and vs cwist 3.9 (C, best C row at 64, 186,252) 1.27x (derived from page data). Per busy server core: powpow 106.6k / 116.5k / 112.4k vs Drogon 69.9k / 71.8k / 69.3k req/s (derived from total_requests_per_s / server_cpu_cores). The win appears in this one snapshot only: the 2026-10-02 snapshot (commit 8657397), after the suite's 2026-09-30 commit 4cce691 'ensure powpow is running multithreaded', has powpow at 100,905 / 93,959 / 91,689 req/s with 13% CPU saturation (0.56x / 0.53x / 0.53x Drogon), and the 2026-09-24 snapshot (commit f673364) has it on one core at 0.63x / 0.55x / 0.55x (derived from page data). README 'Dummy Benchmarks' (first-party, no baseline, wrk 4 threads / 100 connections / 5 s run via GitHub Actions, hardware not stated): 202,743 req/s multi-threaded (4 workers, SO_REUSEPORT) keep-alive and 97,965 req/s single-threaded keep-alive.
compiler_and_flags: Nim 2.2 with -d:release --opt:speed (nim/config.yaml; Nim's default gcc speed options are -O3) plus -d:powpowPewPew (nim/powpow/config.yaml), no LTO; one event loop per reported CPU via SO_REUSEPORT (newHttpServer(countProcessors())). Drogon 1.9.13: cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release (CMake release flags), C++17, no LTO; no C++ compiler version pinned in the suite files read; config.json threads_num 0 (auto), log level WARN, Server and Date headers disabled.
hardware: data.json hardware field (published 2026-10-06): cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor', cpus 16, memory 7,733,008 kB, Linux 7.2.7-200.fc44.x86_64 (Fedora). Per-run server_cpu_cores / server_cpu_saturation imply about 4 CPUs allotted to each server container (derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Event-notification library (alternative to libuv and libevent) with a built-in HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 server, epoll/kqueue/IOCP and an io_uring option; no router, so the suite entry hand-matches paths.
caveats: The README says 'not production-ready and may contain bugs and security vulnerabilities' and claims 'Pow Pow is the #1 fastest HTTP server' from the same benchmark site, a first-party reading of this table. The suite entry nim/powpow was written by the powpow author (georgelemon commits, including 4cce691 on 2026-09-30); it has no router and dispatches on method and path by hand, while the Drogon entry runs Drogon's routing and HttpResponse path; powpow averages 99.3 bytes received per request vs 78.3 for Drogon (derived from total_bytes_received / total_requests). The win over Drogon is in one published snapshot only: on 2026-10-02 (after the multithreading fix) powpow ran at 13% CPU saturation and 0.53-0.56x Drogon, on 2026-09-24 at one core and 0.55-0.63x. The build flag -d:powpowPewPew does not appear in src/powpow.nim, src/powpow/{loop,net,types,proto}.nim or src/powpow/proto/{http,httpserver,multithread}.nim at HEAD, so its effect was not found (possibly a no-op). The README footer says 'All rights reserved' beside an MIT LICENSE file (2026 OpenPeeps); the LICENSE file governs. The README 'Dummy Benchmarks' (wrk -t4 -c100, 5 s) ran on a GitHub Actions runner with client and server on the same machine and no baseline. 20 stars. Suite-level weaknesses: published snapshots move a lot between runs (Drogon 101,282-179,279 req/s across the 2026-09-15 to 2026-10-06 snapshots) and a snapshot gives no repeat spread; the suite README says a run is server-bound only above 75% CPU saturation and invalid below 50%, and in the 2026-10-06 snapshot the 60 fastest rows sit at 49-63% (Drogon 62-63%), so the ceiling for the fastest servers may be the load generator or the box rather than the server; the presence of the server_cpu_saturation / server_cpu_cores probe places this snapshot in the README's current zrk --closed keep-alive revision, although the README's contract paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; the workload is three trivial routes (GET /, GET /user/:id, POST /user) with near-empty bodies. The C/C++ rows are only Drogon 1.9.13 (cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=release, threads_num 0 = auto, Server and Date headers disabled, no LTO), oatpp 1.3, agoo-c 0.7 and cwist 3.9 (C); cwist is the best C row at 64 connections (186,252) and agoo-c at 256 and 512; nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in this suite. Same table, losers to Drogon at 256 connections: Crystal toro 166,910, Go fasthttp 166,243, C# aspnet-minimal-api 147,805 vs Drogon 178,341. The CPU string 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' on an x86_64 Fedora kernel is not a recognisable CPU model, and no C++ compiler version is pinned in the suite files read (cpp/drogon/config.yaml language version '14/17'), which is why this is B and not A.

stars_or_usage: 163 stars; tako-rs crate 5,186 downloads (crates.io API, 2026-10-12; latest 2.4.1)
tradeoffs: Multi-transport Rust framework (HTTP/1.1, h2, h3, WebSocket, SSE, gRPC) on Tokio or Compio; the fast path is the thread-per-core 'per-thread' server with current-thread runtimes and SO_REUSEPORT listeners.
caveats: The suite win is architectural (thread-per-core runtime with SO_REUSEPORT listeners), not a Rust language effect, and margins are small (1.12-1.24x over Drogon; agoo-c (C) beats tako at 256 and 512 connections). The README's own benchmark compares only against Actix Web, ntex and Axum on a 24 vCPU EPYC 9655P container (not C or C++). the-benchmarker weaknesses: one published snapshot (data.json updated 2026-10-06, no repeat spread); the suite README says above 75% server CPU saturation the number is the framework's and below 50% it is not, and tako (56-57%) and Drogon (62-63%) both sit in the band between; the 57 of the 60 fastest rows at 256 connections that carry a saturation value range 49-69% (suite median 71%), so the fastest servers may be generator-bound; the README describes the current method as zrk --closed keep-alive (saturation fields exist only in that method, so this snapshot is probably that revision, inferred) but an older paragraph still describes oha with keep-alive disabled; three trivial routes with near-empty bodies. Flags differ: Rust side uses LTO and codegen-units 1, Drogon has no LTO; in HttpArena the Rust side is built with target-cpu=native and Drogon generically, and the HttpArena tako entry is maintained by the tako author (meta.json maintainers dancixx). HttpArena does not generalise the win to nginx: level on baseline-4096 (3,258,564 vs nginx 3,284,513, 0.99x) and far behind on HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (baseline-h2-256 741,740 vs 3,414,750; baseline-h3-64 534,205 vs 4,849,624) and static TLS (142,858 vs 720,869). nginx, h2o and lithium are not rows in the-benchmarker; same-table losers to Drogon at 256 connections include Crystal toro, Go fasthttp and C# aspnet-minimal-api.
found_via: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json (raw.githubusercontent.com HEAD) ranked by total_requests_per_s; followed by WebSearch 'TechEmpower Round 23 results Rust may-minihttp xitca-web faster than drogon' (TechEmpower pages are egress-blocked) and the repo README at github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks
why_faster: Thread-per-core design with one current-thread runtime per CPU and SO_REUSEPORT listeners (from the HttpArena entry description and the README).

hardware: 2026-04-23 run (discussion 559): Intel Xeon Gold 6548N @ 2.80 GHz (16 cores shown), 64 GB RAM; server limited to 1-4 CPUs and 4096m RAM, ghz client on 11 CPUs, 120 s with 30 s warmup, 50 connections, 1000 concurrency. 2022-04-23 run (wiki): Intel Xeon E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50 GHz, 32 GB RAM; server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs and 512m RAM, client 9 CPUs.
tradeoffs: Rust middleware web framework; the gRPC server is the separate thruster-grpc crate; the repository's last commit is October 2024.
caveats: The Thruster README gives no benchmark numbers, only 'Runs fast'. The measured server is thruster plus the separate thruster-rs/thruster-grpc crate on hyper's HTTP/2 stack and tokio, the same hyper/h2 base as tonic, so the result largely measures hyper/h2 rather than Thruster's own code. In the 2022 run the win was single-CPU only (cpp_grpc_mt led at 2 and 3 CPUs); the 2026 run shows rust_thruster_mt ahead of cpp_grpc_mt at 1-4 CPUs (1.54x to 1.81x), but java_vertx_grpc beats it at 2-4 CPUs and rust_tonic_st beats it at 1 CPU. The C++ baseline is Debian's distro libgrpc++ (1.51.1 per Debian's tracker, a December 2022 release; search snippet only), not an upstream gRPC built with the harness's -O3 -flto, so it is both older and built with distro flags. Server CPU limits use docker --cpus quotas, which penalise gRPC C++'s extra internal threads. Thruster's last commit is 2024-10-16 (stale).

name: tokio-uring (HttpArena minimal HTTP/1.1 server)
baseline: nginx 1.31.4 (C, custom handler module, -O3 -march=native) in the HttpArena suite; h2o, mongoose, libreactorng, libioma (C) and Drogon, Cutelyst, hical, agensio, userver (C++) rows alongside
workload: HttpArena H/1.1 profiles (baseline with 4096 connections, pipelined, limited-conn) on one 64-core machine; the entry is a hand-written HTTP/1.1 parser on tokio-uring (io_uring completion API, owned buffers), one runtime per core with SO_REUSEPORT, no HTTP framework.
claimed_speedup: baseline-4096: 3,565,878 req/s vs nginx 3,284,513 (1.09x, derived from page data), Drogon 2,022,710 (1.76x), hical 3,228,043 (1.10x), agensio 3,558,559 (1.00x); level with or behind h2o 3,641,609 (0.98x), mongoose 3,707,598 (0.96x). pipelined-4096: 48,876,057 vs nginx 4,037,345 (12.1x), Drogon 7,801,404 (6.27x) and libreactorng (C, io_uring) 43,424,448 (1.13x). limited-conn-4096: 2,636,459 vs nginx 2,626,297 (1.00x, a tie).
compiler_and_flags: tokio-uring entry: rust:1.95 image, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release with opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, thin LTO, panic=abort, tokio-uring 0.5 (frameworks/tokio-uring/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml). C/C++ rows: nginx 1.31.4 with a custom handler module, Debian trixie toolchain, --with-cc-opt='-O3 -march=native -DNDEBUG'; h2o clang CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native (no LTO); mongoose gcc-14 -O3 -march=native -flto; Drogon CMake Release in the unpinned drogonframework/drogon:latest image with jemalloc preloaded; hical gcc-14 CMake Release -march=native -mtune=native; libreactorng -O3 -march=native (HttpArena frameworks/<name>/Dockerfile).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, one NUMA node), 251 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.17.0-22-generic, Docker 29.3.0 (runc), performance governor (HttpArena site/data/current.json and site/content/docs/hardware/_index.md). The server container is pinned to cpuset 0-31,64-95 (32 cores / 64 threads) and the load generator (gcannon for H/1.1, h2load for HTTP/2) to 32-63,96-127 over loopback; 5 s runs, best of 3 (scripts/lib/common.sh, scripts/lib/profiles.sh, scripts/benchmark.sh).
stars_or_usage: 1.5k stars (tokio-uring); the server itself is an HttpArena entry
tradeoffs: tokio-uring needs Linux with io_uring and is still described by its README as very young (filesystem and network operations); the HttpArena server is a minimal hand-rolled parser, not a framework; the repo's last commit is from July 2025.
caveats: Not an io_uring win: the suite's plain tokio entry (epoll, same hand-rolled parser design, same Rust flags) is faster than tokio-uring on every shared profile (baseline-4096 4,187,085 vs 3,565,878; limited-conn-4096 2,721,455 vs 2,636,459; pipelined-4096 54,755,795 vs 48,876,057). The entry is a minimal hand-rolled server written for HttpArena (no maintainer listed, not the tokio-uring project's own code): it routes only /pipeline and answers every other path with the a+b sum, and sends about 63 bytes per response against about 135 for nginx (Date and Server headers; derived from page data, bandwidth over req/s), so the per-request work is not the same. At baseline-4096 it is behind libreactorng (4,377,377), libioma (4,255,834), mongoose (3,707,598) and h2o (3,641,609) and level with agensio; at limited-conn-4096 it ties nginx (1.00x) and is behind libioma, mongoose, libreactorng and h2o. The large pipelined ratio is on a reference-only profile (pipeline depth 16) and mostly reflects nginx's pipelining cost. 5 s runs, best of 3, server limited to 32 of 64 cores; results files are undated. The tokio-uring README states no benchmark numbers and calls the project 'still very young'; last commit 2025-07-07.

name: tonic (Rust gRPC)
baseline: gRPC C++ (grpc/grpc) servers cpp_grpc_st, cpp_grpc_mt and cpp_asio_grpc in the grpc_bench suite
workload: grpc_bench 'complex_proto' unary scenario: 50 client connections, 1000 concurrent requests, unlimited QPS, 120 s with 30 s warmup, server RAM 512m, commit 14a8435 (2022-04-22); server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs.
claimed_speedup: 1-CPU server (req/s, avg latency): rust_tonic_st 41,546 (23.77 ms) vs cpp_grpc_st 26,700 (37.33 ms), cpp_grpc_mt 26,376 and cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 (1.56x, 1.58x, 1.67x, derived from page data); rust_tonic_mt 35,443 (1.33x vs cpp_grpc_st). At 2 CPUs rust_tonic_st 42,072 vs cpp_grpc_st 26,229 (1.60x) but cpp_grpc_mt 69,882 and rust_tonic_mt 53,832 (0.77x); at 3 CPUs cpp_grpc_mt 71,806 vs rust_tonic_mt 64,091 (0.89x).
compiler_and_flags: 2022-04-23 run at grpc_bench commit 14a8435. rust_tonic_st: rust:1.59 image, cargo build --release --locked, [profile.release] opt-level 3, codegen-units 1, lto true; jemallocator 0.3.2, tonic 0.7, prost 0.10, tokio 1.17 current_thread. cpp_grpc_st: gcc:11 image, g++ -O3 -flto on main.cpp and the protoc-generated stubs, linked with -lgrpc++ -lprotobuf -lgrpc -ljemalloc from the distro packages (apt libgrpc++-dev). cpp_grpc_mt: the same plus --std=c++20 and -lpthread, one completion queue and thread per GRPC_SERVER_CPUS. cpp_asio_grpc: asio-grpc 1.0.0, CMake Release, the same distro libgrpc++. The gcc:11 image was presumably Debian bullseye, whose libgrpc++-dev is gRPC 1.30.2-3 (Debian package listing, search snippet only); that library was built with Debian's flags, not the benchmark's -O3 -flto.
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz, 32G RAM (grpc_bench wiki page 2022-04-23; server limited to 1, 2 or 3 CPUs, client 9 CPUs)
tradeoffs: Rust async gRPC on tokio and hyper; the winning variant is single-threaded, so it cannot use more than one core per process; calling it from C++ needs a separate process.
caveats: The win appears only with the server limited to 1 CPU. There, all three C++ servers (cpp_grpc_st 26,700, cpp_grpc_mt 26,376, cpp_asio_grpc 24,926 req/s) trail rust_tonic_st (41,546) and rust_tonic_mt (35,443). With 2 and 3 CPUs, cpp_grpc_mt (69,882 and 71,806) and cpp_asio_grpc (66,828 and 71,296) lead rust_tonic_mt (53,832 and 64,091). The wiki page states no compiler versions or flags; they come from the Dockerfiles at commit 14a8435, and the repo's current Dockerfiles (gcc 16.1, Rust 1.94) are newer than the run. The C++ servers link the distro libgrpc++ package (probably gRPC 1.30.2 from Debian bullseye, a 2020 release, against tonic 0.7 from 2022). That library is built with distribution flags, while the Rust stack is compiled whole with opt-level 3 and LTO. At 1 CPU, rust_grpcio, which compiles the gRPC C core from source, reached 31,035 req/s, also above every C++ server, so part of the gap may come from the distro build or the old gRPC version rather than from tonic. go_vtgrpc (44,074) topped the 1-CPU table. Both servers do the same echo work (copy the request string into the reply). It is a single run with no variance reported. The tonic README makes no performance claim; the evidence is the third-party grpc_bench suite, whose latest wiki results page is this 2022-04-23 run.
found_via: WebFetch github.com/LesnyRumcajs/grpc_bench (results live in the wiki), then the 2022-04-23 wiki page; Dockerfiles and Cargo.toml read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: bladebench Rust raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk 8 threads, 1000 connections, 10 s: Rust 49,388 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.21x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (1.50x, derived), ~0 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 blade_core.c, g++ -O2 blade_core.cpp, 'rustc blade_core.rs' with no -O or opt-level (an unoptimised debug build), and 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug by default). No compiler versions. The C/C++ side is not -O3, and the optimisation levels are not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. The Rust build has no optimisation flag while C and C++ use -O2. All four servers are the same single-threaded blocking loop (accept, one read, write a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK ... OK' response, close), so the time goes to kernel accept/close and the wrk client, not to language codegen. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715 req/s), which shows the run-to-run noise exceeds the claimed Rust margin. There is one 10 s run per server and no repetitions, and CPU, kernel and compiler versions are not stated. Minor asymmetries: the Rust server binds 127.0.0.1 while C and C++ bind INADDR_ANY (wrk connects to 127.0.0.1 in every case); Rust uses write_all and unwrap() (a reset would abort the server) where C and C++ do a single write; C reads 1023 bytes and C++ 1024. The listen backlog is 128 in C, C++ and Rust std alike. The Zig row (80,700 req/s) came with 701k write errors. The repo has 0 stars and a single commit (2025-07-12).

name: bladebench Zig raw TCP server
baseline: the same minimal blocking TCP/HTTP server in C (gcc -O2) and C++ (g++ -O2) from the same repo
workload: Single-threaded blocking accept loop that reads once, writes a fixed 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK' response and closes the connection, load-tested with wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s over loopback.
claimed_speedup: wrk -t8 -c1000 -d10s on loopback (first-party, single run): Zig 80,700 req/s vs C++ 40,715 (1.98x, derived from page data) and C 32,976 (2.45x, derived from page data); the same table marks the Zig row '701k write errors (buffer overrun)' and the C/C++ rows 0 errors. compiler_and_flags: Makefile: gcc -O2 and g++ -O2 for C and C++; 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' with no optimize flag (default Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per source banner). Not -O3 and not matched.
tradeoffs: Toy micro-benchmark, not a usable server library.
caveats: Not a valid language comparison. blade_core.zig accepts, writes the fixed response and closes without ever reading the request, whereas blade_core.c and blade_core.cpp read() once before writing; closing a socket with unread data makes the kernel reset the connection, which fits the 701k write errors the page reports for Zig (the page blames a 'buffer overrun'), so the Zig row measures less work and an abortive close rather than codegen. The Makefile builds Zig with a bare 'zig build-exe blade_core.zig' (Debug mode, Zig 0.12 per the source banner) and Rust with plain rustc (no -O), against gcc -O2 / g++ -O2 for C and C++; none is -O3. Each server is a single-threaded blocking accept loop that closes every connection, while wrk keeps HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and must reconnect after every response, so throughput is dominated by connection setup and teardown. Ports differ (8080, 8081, 8083) and only the Zig server sets SO_REUSEADDR. CPU, kernel, compiler and wrk versions are not stated; single run. The C and C++ servers are functionally identical yet differ by 23% (32,976 vs 40,715), which shows the noise. The README itself recommends 'Zig (if tuned)'. One commit, 0 stars.

name: kawipiko
baseline: NGINX (distribution package; configuration in the kawipiko examples/nginx folder), also darkhttpd
workload: Static 'Hello World!' file served from a CDB archive held in memory (kawipiko) or from tmpfs (NGINX), wrk over loopback with keep-alive, 512 to 16384 connections; plus a 250k-file OpenStreetMap tile set at 16384 connections.
claimed_speedup: Hello World over loopback, 2 server threads, 2 wrk threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 / 100,296.65 / 95,628.34 / 53,548.52 req/s at 512 / 2048 / 4096 / 16384 connections (section 'Last updated in August 2018') vs NGinx 79,816.08 / 78,211.46 / 75,970.82 / 43,909.67 (section 'Last updated in August 2019'), 1.34x / 1.28x / 1.26x / 1.22x (derived from page data, pairing the two separately dated sections). OpenStreetMap tile run (one section, August 2019, i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections, 2 minutes): kawipiko --archive-inmem 238,499.86 req/s, --archive-mmap 237,239.35, 8 processes mmap 248,266.83 vs NGinx 8 workers 188,255.32 (1.27x / 1.26x / 1.32x, derived); the author states ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency, ~40% lower p90 latency, ~25% less CPU per request, while NGinx used the least RAM and kawipiko about 1 GiB. The summary (December 2021) calls kawipiko 'at least on-par with NGinx'.
compiler_and_flags: Go build of kawipiko (version and flags not stated); NGINX from distribution packages (version and build flags not stated); server run with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable.
hardware: Laptop with Intel Core i7 3667U (2 physical cores, 4 threads), 8 GiB RAM for the Hello World runs; desktop Intel Core i7 4770 (4 cores, 8 threads), 32 GiB for the tile run; wrk and server pinned to separate physical cores, tmpfs.
tradeoffs: Serves only a prebuilt CDB archive, so content changes need a rebuild; HTTP/2 is about 6 times slower than its HTTP/1 path (Go net/http), where the author says NGINX is much better; kawipiko used about 1 GiB RAM in the tile run while NGINX used the least; AGPL licence.
caveats: First-party, measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U laptop, i7 4770 desktop) with an older kawipiko version (the author says the current one is at least 10% more efficient). The Hello World kawipiko rows (August 2018) and NGinx rows (August 2019) are in separately dated sections, so the 1.22-1.34x ratios compare runs a year apart; only the tile run is a same-session comparison. kawipiko was requested at '/' and NGinx at '/index.txt' (the author chose the path he says favours NGinx). NGinx is a distribution package with an author-tuned config (examples/nginx); kawipiko ran with --archive-inmem, --security-headers-disable and --timeout-disable (the author says timeouts cost 10-15%). wrk reports socket errors for kawipiko at every row from 512 connections (timeouts 86 / 4,449 / 2,288 at 2048 / 4096 / 16384, versus NGinx 11 / 187 / 1,121) and in both tile runs (kawipiko 7,032 timeouts, NGinx 16,833). The tile CDB was deduplicated to ~100k of ~250k files, and the wrk command shown targets a single URL, so how the tile list was driven is not shown. The author says kawipiko over HTTP/2 is about 6x slower than its own HTTPS over HTTP/1, where NGinx is not. The author says the real advantage is deployment simplicity. The win comes from the CDB in-memory design on fasthttp, not from Go versus C codegen.
found_via: WebSearch 'static file web server written in Rust OR Zig OR Go "faster than nginx" benchmark wrk requests/sec README comparison h2o lwan' (github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org filter)
why_faster: Content pre-indexed in a CDB archive held in memory with a compact lookup (no per-request file system calls), on Go fasthttp; the README says the advantage grows for many small files accessed in random patterns.

verification.tier_reason: First-party wrk numbers in documentation/readme/benchmarks.rst match the record (kawipiko 106,698.89 / 100,296.65 / 95,628.34 / 53,548.52 vs NGinx 79,816.08 / 78,211.46 / 75,970.82 / 43,909.67; tiles 238,499.86 vs 188,255.32); kawipiko's Go version and flags and NGinx's version and build are not stated, so C.
verification.notes: Numbers match benchmarks.rst; tier C stands (first-party, Go and NGinx builds unstated). Shortcomings: the Hello World ratio pairs kawipiko rows from August 2018 with NGinx rows from August 2019 (cross-run), only the 1.27x tile run is same-session; timeouts and security headers disabled for kawipiko; more wrk timeouts for kawipiko than NGinx at 4096 connections; 2013-era CPUs, old version; the author calls it 'at least on-par'.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: 512 connections, 2 server threads: kawipiko 106,698.89 req/s vs NGINX 79,816.08 (1.34x, derived from page data); 2048 connections: 100,296.65 vs 78,211.46; 4096: 95,628.34 vs 75,970.82; 16384: 53,548.52 vs 43,909.67. Tile benchmark (i7 4770, 8 threads, 16384 connections): kawipiko 238,499.86 req/s vs NGINX 188,255.32 (1.27x, derived), with ~25% more requests/s, ~29% lower average latency and ~25% less CPU per request stated by the author.
corrected_fields.caveats: First-party; the per-connection rows are marked 'Last updated in August 2018' and the summary 'December 2021', measured on 2013-era CPUs (i7 3667U, i7 4770), the author says the current version is at least 10% more efficient. NGINX is a distro package with an author-tuned config; timeouts and security headers are disabled in the kawipiko run (author says timeouts cost 10-15%). Socket errors and timeouts appear in the 2048 and 16384 connection rows for both servers. The author states the real advantage over NGINX is deployment simplicity, not raw speed, and calls the result 'at least on-par'.

name: monolake
baseline: nginx 1.24.0 (C); build flags not stated
workload: HTTP and HTTPS proxy/serving throughput of the Monolake reference proxy (Rust on the io_uring-based monoio runtime) against nginx, measured as requests per second versus response body size (512 B to 64 KiB) and versus worker threads (1 to 16); load generator, nginx configuration and backend setup are not stated.
claimed_speedup: No numbers in the text; four chart images only. Approximate values read from the charts (not stated by the project). HTTPS vs worker threads: 16 threads about 526k req/s vs nginx about 450k (about 1.17x), 12 threads about 436k vs about 370k (about 1.18x), 8 threads about 359k vs about 334k (about 1.07x), 4 threads about 148k vs about 126k. HTTPS vs body size: 512 B about 152k vs about 128k (about 1.19x), 4096 B about 124k vs about 108k (about 1.15x), roughly equal at 8192 B, then nginx ahead at 16384 B (about 55k vs about 59k), 32768 B (about 34k vs about 41k) and 65536 B (about 20k vs about 23k). Plain HTTP: nginx ahead or equal everywhere, 16 threads about 707k vs about 688k (monolake about 0.97x), 4 threads about 194k vs about 168k (about 0.87x), 512 B about 186k vs about 168k (monolake about 0.91x), equal at 32768 and 65536 B. Older tabulated first-party proxy run (benchmark/README.md at commit d02397f, Nov 2024, wrk2, 4-core proxy, nginx backend): HTTPS tiny 141,883.70 req/s vs nginx as proxy 127,167.08 (1.12x, derived from page data), small 116,831.85 vs 114,350.27 (1.02x), medium 63,390.91 vs 62,450.58 (1.02x); HTTP tiny 161,101.29 vs 187,973.44 (0.86x); against Envoy 1.31.0 (C++): HTTP tiny 4.36x, HTTPS tiny 4.15x (derived from page data, Envoy configuration not tuned or stated).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README charts. Repository pins Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml); the older benchmark/README.md built Monolake with cargo build --release (a release-lto profile exists in Cargo.toml, use not stated) and installed nginx from the Amazon Linux package (yum), so nginx build flags are the distro's and unstated.
hardware: AWS c6a.8xlarge, AMD EPYC 7R13, 16 cores / 32 threads, 64 GB RAM, Linux 6.1.94-99.176.amzn2023.x86_64 (Amazon Linux 2023.5.20240805), nginx 1.24.0 (README Performance section)
stars_or_usage: 66 stars, 12 forks; README says it was deployed in production at ByteDance
tradeoffs: Archived by the owner on 2025-08-29 and marked no longer recommended for use; needs Rust nightly and Linux io_uring (falls back to epoll elsewhere); HTTP/Thrift proxy framework rather than a general web server.
caveats: First-party charts with no tabulated numbers, so values here are eyeballed from PNGs. The win is confined to HTTPS with small bodies (and more worker threads); plain HTTP and large HTTPS bodies favour nginx or tie. The nginx build and configuration (workers, logging, TLS library), whether the charts measure proxying or direct serving, the body size used in the thread charts and the load generator are not stated for the current charts. Monolake's default tls feature uses monoio-native-tls (OpenSSL on Linux), with rustls also available; which stack the charts used is not stated. An older benchmark/ directory (present at commit d02397f, Nov 2024; gone from HEAD) had wrk2 scripts, a three-machine proxy topology with an nginx backend, and a tabulated 4-core run showing only a 1.02-1.12x HTTPS edge and nginx 14% ahead on HTTP tiny; its Envoy and Traefik rows ran stock configurations, so the 4x lead over Envoy is weak evidence. Repository archived on 2025-08-29 with a notice that the project is no longer recommended. Tier C: first-party, partial methodology.
found_via: WebSearch 'monolake Rust proxy benchmark vs Nginx throughput cloudwego' surfaced the project; github.com/cloudwego/monolake README Performance section and its four chart PNGs (raw.githubusercontent.com .github/images) opened
why_faster: Thread-per-core io_uring runtime (monoio) with no work stealing, versus nginx's epoll workers; the README gives no explicit explanation for the HTTPS win.

Found an older tabulated first-party run in the removed benchmark/ directory (commit d02397f) with a smaller HTTPS edge (1.02-1.12x) and an Envoy (C++) comparison; still tier C. Shortcomings to record: eyeballed charts only, win limited to small-body HTTPS, no plain-HTTP win, no flags or nginx config, repository archived.

name: Orion Proxy
baseline: Envoy Proxy (C++)
workload: HTTP reverse proxy to an nginx upstream, wrk at 2048 and 16384 connections, 1 to 48 cores assigned to the proxy.
claimed_speedup: README: '2x-4x better throughput and latency than Envoy Proxy'. HTTP chart (docs/pics/performance/baseline/wrk-reqsec.png), requests/s orion-mr-st vs envoy: 2048 connections, 1 core 46,593 vs 12,819 (3.63x, derived from page data), 48 cores 1,881,522 vs 310,231 (6.06x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 38,573 vs 17,059 (2.26x, derived), 48 cores 1,410,611 vs 514,254 (2.74x, derived). HTTPS chart (tls/wrk-reqsec.png): 2048 connections, 1 core 30,398 vs 11,268 (2.7x, derived), 48 cores 1,478,634 vs 324,135 (4.56x, derived); 16384 connections, 1 core 26,354 vs 14,096 (1.87x, derived), 48 cores 738,429 vs 483,069 (1.53x, derived). The latency chart (baseline/wrk-latency.png, microseconds, percentile not stated, lower is better) does not support a 2x-4x latency win across the board: with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2, 8, 16, 24, 32 and 48 cores (e.g. 48 cores 251,325 vs 201,636; 16 cores 193,495 vs 85,659) and lower only at 1 core (280,347 vs 323,953), about equal at 4; with 16384 connections Orion is worse at 1, 2 and 4 cores (1,879,395 vs 1,789,400; 1,944,476 vs 1,769,852; 971,338 vs 633,244) and better at 8-48 cores (e.g. 270,335 vs 1,815,855 at 16 cores).
hardware: Two-host testbed: DUT proxy host and tester host with wrk on NUMA 0 and nginx upstream on NUMA 1, 25 Gbps Mellanox and Intel NICs, IRQ affinity tuned (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Envoy xDS-compatible Rust proxy aiming at a drop-in replacement for common use cases only; not the full Envoy filter set.
caveats: First-party; the numbers exist only as chart images, and the repo carries no benchmark scripts, wrk invocation, Envoy or Orion configuration (docs/performance holds only performance.md; tools/ has no bench files). The methodology lists 'Envoy, Ng-proxy, and Nginx' as compared proxies and scaling at 1-32 cores, but the charts show only Orion (series 'orion-mr-st', a runtime mode the page does not explain) and Envoy, at 1-48 cores. Envoy version, build and config, Orion build flags and the CPU model are not stated, so tier C. The README's 2x-4x is lower than the 6x seen in the 2048-connection HTTP chart at 48 cores and does not hold for latency: the latency chart is mixed (with 2048 connections Orion's latency is higher than Envoy's at 2 and 8-48 cores; with 16384 connections it is worse at 1-4 cores and better at 8-48 cores). The TCP (L4) chart shows Envoy at 53 and 47 req/s on 1-2 cores with 2048 connections and 0 req/s on 1-4 cores with 16384 connections, which points to a broken or saturated Envoy setup in this testbed and casts doubt on how Envoy was configured for the other charts.
found_via: WebSearch 'Monolake Rust proxy benchmark vs Nginx Envoy throughput latency' returned the kmesh-net community issue about Orion
why_faster: README credits Rust's zero-cost abstractions and memory safety guarantees (no profiling or mechanism analysis is given).

verification.tier_reason: First-party chart images (docs/pics/performance/{baseline,tls,tcp}/wrk-*.png) compare Orion with Envoy; the repo holds no benchmark scripts, wrk commands, Envoy or Orion configs, and no CPU model, Envoy version or build flags are given, so it falls short of A.
verification.notes: Chart labels match the record's HTTP numbers exactly; added TLS rows and the latency and L4 observations. Shortcomings to record: no published harness or configs, no CPU model or Envoy build, latency half of the 2x-4x claim contradicted at 2048 connections (Orion latency higher at most core counts), Envoy L4 rows near zero suggest a misconfigured baseline. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 39 stars, 22 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-03-02 (active).

Chart labels in docs/pics/performance/baseline/wrk-reqsec.png, requests/s Orion vs Envoy: 2048 connections, 1 core 46,593 vs 12,819, 48 cores 1,881,522 vs 310,231 (6.1x, derived from page data); 16384 connections, 1 core 38,573 vs 17,059, 48 cores 1,410,611 vs 514,254 (2.7x, derived).

name: routez
baseline: nginx 1.30.5 (C) and HAProxy 3.2.23 (C)
workload: nginx-style edge server in Zig 0.17 measured with wrk, keep-alive, 256 connections, 3 workers each, median of 3 x 10 s runs, on Docker Desktop on an Apple M-series Mac (10 cores).
claimed_speedup: requests/s routez vs nginx: fixed response 627k vs 529k (1.19x, derived from page data), reverse proxy to keep-alive upstream 262k vs 208k (1.26x), TLS fixed response 582k vs 324k (1.8x), TLS 10 KB static file 208k vs 152k (1.4x), TLS new connection per request 17k vs 13k; p99 at a held 208k req/s fixed response 3.6 ms vs nginx 21.2 ms.
compiler_and_flags: routez: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dcpu=native (native+aes+sha2 on arm64) with Zig 0.17.0 inside an ubuntu:26.04 container (bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile); nginx 1.30.5 is the nginx.org stable Ubuntu package and HAProxy 3.2 comes from the vbernat PPA, both on OpenSSL 3.5, with compile flags not stated. nginx config (bench/conf/nginx.conf) is tuned: reuseport, keepalive_requests 100000, open_file_cache, sendfile, TLS 1.3 pinned to AES-128-GCM and X25519.
hardware: Apple M-series Mac, 10 cores, Docker Desktop VM (the author writes 'a VM is not a benchmark machine'), 20 Sep 2026
tradeoffs: Pure Zig edge server with HTTP/1.1, HTTP/3, TLS 1.3, ACME, reverse proxy and load balancing; no license file found, so reference only.
caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 10 KB static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; gzip on the fly through the proxy 5.5k/s vs HAProxy 15k/s; a new connection per request 187k/s vs nginx 231k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms; at the held 208k req/s fixed-response row HAProxy's p99 (3.2 ms) beats routez's 3.6 ms; a reload every 2 s under load fails 74 requests vs HAProxy 0. Rows come from different passes: the 10 KB static row reads 308k (tie) in the main table but '343k/s, 10% ahead' in the 'rows that have come off this list' table. The README itself says two runs of one build on a busy Mac differed by 90% and that a VM is not a benchmark machine; numbers are a median of 3 x 10 s runs on Docker Desktop on an unnamed Apple M-series Mac. routez is built with -Dcpu=native while nginx and HAProxy are generic distribution packages. The build needs a sibling checkout of endel/quic-zig (public, MIT). No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE returns 404, GitHub shows no license), so usability is reference. Harness strengths: a correctness gate checks byte-identical responses and identical TLS parameters before each row, servers are measured one at a time with rotated order and pinned cores, and nginx gets its best settings.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: Worker threads with SO_REUSEPORT on libxev, an open-file cache and sendfile for plain-HTTP static files (README feature list); no profile attribution for the wins.

verification.tier_reason: Benchmark code is public (bench/run.sh, bench/bench.sh, bench/lib.sh, bench/Dockerfile, bench/conf/nginx.conf, bench/workloads.txt) and the routez build flags are stated, but the hardware is 'Apple M-series Mac (10 cores)' under a Docker Desktop VM (no CPU model) and nginx is a distribution package with unstated compile flags, so not A; first-party, so C.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers match README.md (fixed 627k vs 529k, proxy 262k vs 208k, TLS fixed 582k vs 324k, TLS 10 KB 208k vs 152k, TLS new connection 17k vs 13k, p99 3.6 vs 21.2 ms). Shortcomings to record: VM on a vague Apple M-series host, single first-party run set with a stated 90% run-to-run drift, native-tuned routez vs generic nginx package, many rows where routez loses, no license. Metadata checked: 6 stars, 0 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-03 (active).

corrected_fields.caveats: The author's own table is mixed: 10 KB static file 308k vs nginx 312k (a tie); full RSA-2048 TLS handshakes 1.0k/s vs nginx 3.6k/s; HTTP/3 static file 94k/s vs 247k/s; p99 at a held rate proxied 4.30 ms vs HAProxy 1.79 ms. Benchmark code is in the repo (bench/run.sh) but the run is on a macOS VM with a vague CPU, a single run set, and nginx's build is not given, so tier C.

name: rproxy
baseline: nginx as a reverse proxy (version and config not stated); HAProxy 2.8.5 (vendored build) as a second row
workload: HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy in front of an nginx backend answering '200 OK' with a 2-byte body, wrk -t4 -c100 -d10s keep-alive, two proxy workers each for rproxy and nginx on two pinned cores, loopback.
claimed_speedup: June run (bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md, 2026-06-27, median of 3 after warmup, proxies pinned to cores 2-3 with 2 workers each): rproxy 189,810.00 req/s (557 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 153,484.52 (662 us) = 1.24x; rproxy before its hot-path optimisation 135,700.79 (0.88x); backend ceiling 362,163.20. August run (README, measured 2026-08-16 with bench/haproxy_baseline.sh, labelled median of 3 but the script keeps the best of 3): rproxy 323,035 (352 us) vs nginx reverse proxy 282,032 (400 us) = 1.15x and HAProxy 2.8.5 266,603 (395 us) = 1.21x; ceiling 632,175. rproxy with TLS 134,168 req/s (no TLS comparison against nginx).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo release profile: lto = 'fat', codegen-units = 1, panic = 'abort', opt-level = 3, debug = true; monoio 0.2.4 with io_uring. nginx version and build flags not stated (installed from the system, per the script's 'command -v nginx'); HAProxy 2.8.5 vendored build, flags not stated.
hardware: 12th Gen Intel Core i5-12450H, 12 logical cores; June run: wrk on cores 4-7, backend nginx on cores 0-1, proxy on cores 2-3. The August script does no pinning: backend nginx and the nginx proxy each run worker_processes 4, HAProxy and rproxy use their defaults, all on the same box.
tradeoffs: Not a general reverse proxy: the author positions it as a filtering layer (JWT, rate limiting, ACL and canonicalization checks) behind nginx; Linux with io_uring (kernel 5.6+); rate limit and cache state are per worker; TLS rate 134,168 req/s vs ceiling 629,459.
caveats: First-party; both runs (2026-06-27 and 2026-08-16) predate the repo's first public commit (2026-08-18), so the measured revisions are not in public history. The August three-proxy run's script (bench/haproxy_baseline.sh) labels its result 'median-of-3' but keeps the best of 3 runs, pins no cores, gives the nginx proxy worker_processes 4 and reads rproxy's worker count from bench_config.yml, which is not in the repo, so the equal-core claim holds only for the June run; that also explains the ceiling jump from 362k (2 pinned backend cores) to 632k (4 unpinned workers). The June nginx proxy config is not published and its upstream keep-alive is not stated (bench/nginx_proxy.conf in the repo listens on 8081 and proxies to 8081, so it is not the config used). The README is internally inconsistent about HAProxy: it shows a measured HAProxy row and then says 'HAProxy was not measured on the current rig' and no HAProxy comparison is claimed. Tiny 2-byte keep-alive body, same box, no TLS comparison; larger bodies, no keep-alive or TLS may differ. No LICENSE file, so reference. 0 stars, 2 commits. The README positions rproxy as a filter behind nginx, not a replacement. The win is architectural (prefork thread-per-core monoio workers on io_uring, coalesced head+body writes), not a Rust language effect.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust OR Go reverse proxy benchmark vs nginx HAProxy Envoy requests per second github README results wrk' (github.com filter)
why_faster: Prefork thread-per-core monoio workers on io_uring with a zero-allocation hot path (README architecture section).

verification.tier_reason: First-party numbers in the README and bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md match the record (June 189,810 vs nginx 153,484; August 323,035 vs 282,032 and HAProxy 266,603); the August script bench/haproxy_baseline.sh is public but needs a missing bench_config.yml and a vendored HAProxy not in the repo, and nginx's version and build flags are not stated, so C.
verification.notes: Numbers match README and bench/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md; tier C stands. Shortcomings: haproxy_baseline.sh reports best-of-3 labelled median and pins nothing, needs a bench_config.yml absent from the repo; June nginx config unpublished (repo copy is a self-loop); measured code predates public history; contradictory HAProxy statements; 2-byte keep-alive body only; no licence; 0 stars.

name: Spire
baseline: HAProxy 2.7.3 (C) and Envoy 1.22.8 (C++) reverse proxies; nginx 1.23.3 in the same table is faster than Spire
workload: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET through each reverse proxy to one echo-server backend under docker-compose, with the proxy and backend each limited to 4 CPUs and 8 GB. The hey container's limit differs between runs in the checked-in compose files: 12 CPUs for Spire and nginx, 4 CPUs for HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy. The Traefik run used the jmalloc/echo-server backend; the others used ghcr.io/lsk569937453/echo-server:0.0.5. Each proxy had one run of about 1 s. Harness adapted from NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks; configs are in benchmarks/{spires,haproxy,envoy,nginx,traefik,caddy}/.

All proxies ran as prebuilt Docker images: lsk569937453/spire:0.0.24 (jemalloc via JEMALLOC_SYS_WITH_MALLOC_CONF), haproxytech/haproxy-ubuntu:2.7.3, envoyproxy/envoy:v1.22.8, nginx:1.23.3, traefik:v2.9.8 and caddy:2.6.4. caveats: Crippled baseline harness. The compose files committed with the 2025 numbers give the hey load generator 12 CPUs for the Spire and nginx runs but 4 CPUs for the HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik and Caddy runs, while benchmarks.md says every service was limited to 4 cores. Only the two 12-CPU rows jumped between runs (Spire 66,370 to 114,512 req/s, nginx 42,388 to 148,677); HAProxy stayed at 81,674 to 85,406. Configs differ: nginx is tuned (4 workers, upstream keepalive 100), HAProxy has a minimal config with no timeouts, and Envoy's concurrency is not set. Envoy also adds headers that the echo backend returns, so its response is 294 bytes vs Spire's 155. Even so, Spire is slower than nginx in its own table (114,512 vs 148,677 req/s; p99 11.8 ms vs 4.9 ms). Each proxy had one hey run of about 1 s on the same PC as the load generator, with old HAProxy and Envoy releases and unstated build flags. The checked-in Spire compose sets CONFIG_FILE_PATH to /temp/app_config.yaml but mounts the file at /tmp/app_config.yaml, and app_config.yaml uses an older schema than the README, so the published harness may not run as checked in. name: statico
baseline: nginx (static in-memory 'return' response)
workload: Synthetic static in-memory HTTP response served to 1024 connections at 1, 2 and 4 server threads, comparing statico runtimes with nginx, HAProxy, Go net/http, fasthttp, Axum and actix-web.
claimed_speedup: requests/s, 1 / 4 threads: statico (tokio) 399,025 / 1,071,433 vs nginx (return) 286,960 / 832,082 (1.39x / 1.29x, derived from page data); statico (monoio) 656,517 / 1,436,420 (2.29x / 1.73x, derived); README text says standard statico is about 40% faster single-threaded.
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release with per-runtime feature flags; Cargo.toml [profile.release] is opt-level 3, lto fat, codegen-units 1, panic abort, mimalloc as default allocator (profile added in the 2026-09-12 commit 'Optimize release build for performance', after the table was last updated on 2026-04-25 'Benchmarks updated.'). nginx build and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Designed strictly for benchmarking: returns a fixed response from memory, no routing, no logging; Linux-only io_uring runtimes.
caveats: First-party; no CPU model, load generator (or whether it pipelines requests), nginx configuration or nginx build is published, so tier C. The table was last updated 2026-04-25, before the current release profile (2026-09-12) and the removal of the tokio-local runtime (2026-08-20). The README's key observations disagree with its own table: they list tokio-uring leading at 1.39M, monoio 1.36M and compio 1.27M at four threads, while the table gives monoio 1,436,420, compio 1,395,047 and tokio-uring 1,393,573, so the prose and table come from different runs. The io_uring runtimes write a response pre-encoded once per connection (src/response.rs build_response; any Date header frozen at connection start), while nginx builds its headers per request, so the io_uring rows do less work per response. statico is a benchmarking stub that returns one configured response, not a general web server. Actix-web (798,809) is slower than nginx (832,082) at four threads in the same table, and the README does not say whether nginx used tuned worker settings. src/monoio.rs builds a Vec with Vec::from_raw_parts pointing into the middle of another Vec's allocation (forgotten after the read), an unsound pattern.
found_via: WebSearch 'paper performance evaluation HTTP server written in Rust outperforms nginx C requests per second arXiv' returned docs.rs statico pages; repo from crates.io API (repository field)
why_faster: Pre-built responses held in memory, HTTP pipelining, thread-per-core io_uring runtimes (tokio-uring, monoio, glommio, compio) with CPU pinning for glommio and compio (README).

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table and pic/benchmark.png compare statico with nginx's 'return'; no benchmark script, load generator, nginx configuration or CPU model is published, so C.

Set same_algorithm false because the io_uring rows send a once-per-connection pre-encoded response while nginx builds headers per request; standard tokio statico uses Hyper per request. Shortcomings to record: no hardware, load generator or nginx config; prose vs table mismatch; numbers predate current release profile. Metadata checked: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 1 star, 0 forks, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-16 (active), crates.io 872 downloads, version 0.18.0.

name: swerver
baseline: nginx (openresty/openresty:alpine Docker image, unpinned tag; tuned nginx.conf with worker_processes auto, reuseport, 'return 200' for /health and content_by_lua for /echo)
workload: swerver-benchmarks: k6 scenarios against minimal endpoints (/health, /echo, /blob) in Docker with 2 CPUs and 512 MB per container, swerver vs nginx, actix, http-zig and APISIX.
claimed_speedup: GET /health, 100 VUs, 30 s: swerver 147,435 req/s vs nginx 118,061 (1.25x, derived from page data), actix 133,691; no keep-alive connections/s 90,657 vs nginx 19,206 (4.7x); rapid-fire 143,437 vs nginx 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs nginx 80,053; TLS /health h2 161,781 vs nginx 107,741.
compiler_and_flags: swerver (April 2026 results, harness commit f5eb7c1): Zig 0.16.0-dev.3133+5ec8e45f3 aarch64-linux, zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (servers/swerver/Dockerfile); HEAD now builds a bench app with .ReleaseFast hard-coded in servers/swerver/app/build.zig on Zig 0.16.0. nginx: openresty/openresty:alpine image, whose OpenResty configure adds -O2 by default (util/configure) and whose Dockerfile passes only -D/-I cc-opts, so nginx is built at -O2, not -O3.
hardware: Docker Desktop VM on macOS Apple Silicon (chip not stated), 2 CPUs and 512 MB per server container via docker-compose limits, k6 load generator in an unconstrained container on the same VM, April 2026
tradeoffs: Alpha release; library API will change; HTTP/3 first version runs at 16.5K req/s.
caveats: First-party benchmark by the swerver author, single run reported (no medians or repeat counts). Hot endpoints (/health, /plaintext, /json) are served from a per-second-refreshed pre-encoded response cache that skips the router, middleware and encoder, and the HEAD bench config sets disable_middleware: true; nginx answers /health with 'return 200' and /echo through content_by_lua. swerver container runs with seccomp unconfined so io_uring is used; nginx uses epoll. nginx is built at -O2 (OpenResty default), not -O3. Worker counts are not pinned equal (nginx worker_processes auto; swerver --workers defaults to 1 per its README, April image ran it without a config). Hardware is an unnamed Apple Silicon chip under Docker Desktop's VM. Results are mixed: mixed workload 36,929 vs nginx 36,969 (tie), /echo latency scenario nginx 8,659 vs swerver 8,517, actix-web ahead of swerver on TLS throughput (171,726 vs 161,781), h2 throughput (129,428 vs 111,698) and error handling (141,755 vs 114,455). The native wrk table (274,617 req/s on /health) has no nginx row. swerver's own README concedes feature-stripped reference servers edge it by 1-2% on raw HTTP/1.1 HttpArena tests. The harness has changed since the April results (Jul 2026 commit 'serve the benchmark endpoints + unbreak the baseline build'), so HEAD does not reproduce the measured build exactly.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than nginx" Rust OR Zig OR Go reverse proxy web server benchmark wrk results README' (github.com filter)
why_faster: io_uring backend plus a pre-encoded response cache for hot endpoints that skips the router, middleware and response encoder (swerver-benchmarks README).

verification.tier_reason: First-party k6 suite by the swerver author (harness public in swerver-benchmarks: docker-compose.yml, servers/*/Dockerfile, servers/nginx/config/nginx.conf, k6/scenarios/*.js) with swerver built ReleaseFast and nginx from the OpenResty alpine image at OpenResty's default -O2, but the hardware is only 'Docker Desktop on macOS Apple Silicon' with no chip model, so it falls short of A; no independent nginx comparison found.
verification.notes: All claimed numbers match the swerver-benchmarks README tables (throughput 147,435 vs 118,061; connections 90,657 vs 19,206, page states 4.7x; rapid-fire 143,437 vs 125,346; error handling 114,455 vs 80,053; TLS h2 /health 161,781 vs 107,741). For wave 14 the win is not a language-level one: different server architectures (io_uring plus response cache vs epoll nginx), nginx at -O2 rather than -O3, so same_algorithm and same_opt_level are false; the baseline is tuned, not crippled, so tier C stands. name: wut-server
baseline: nginx (C; own build with all optimization options, LTO, static OpenSSL, ngx_headers_more; 1 worker, 1024 worker connections, HTTP/2, TLS 1.3 only)
workload: wrk, 10 s, 6 threads, 1000 connections (from the wrk output header), against https://ip.erix.dev (nginx, port 443) and https://ip.erix.dev:11313 (wut-server) on the same host. Both servers terminate TLS and return the caller's IP address as the body; wrk speaks HTTP/1.1.
claimed_speedup: 38,110.60 requests/s (382,057 requests in 10 s) vs nginx 25,650.31 (257,322), about 49% more per the page (1.49x, derived from page data); transfer 3.27 MB/s vs 2.79 MB/s; max latency 279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms; nginx had connect 95 and read 17 socket errors.
compiler_and_flags: wut-server: Cargo.toml [profile.release] lto = true, codegen-units = 1, strip = true (default opt-level 3); hyper 0.14 with hyper-rustls 0.24, rustls 0.21 and tokio 1.34; rustc version not stated. nginx: 'all optimization options enabled', LTO, static OpenSSL and ngx_headers_more; version, compiler and exact flags not stated.
hardware: Server: single-core AMD EPYC 7302P, 1 GB ECC RAM, 1 Gbit/s uplink; client: AMD Ryzen 5600, 32 GB ECC RAM, 250 Mbit/s uplink; OS not stated; network benchmark, not loopback.
tradeoffs: Single-purpose server that returns the caller's public IP over HTTP and HTTP/2; not a general web server.
caveats: First-party single run per server, with no variance, no wrk command line, no versions, and the two runs were not interleaved. The author calls it a 'non-scientific comparison'. Both servers use TLS 1.3 over HTTPS (the wut-server wrk URL is https://...:11313, and the binary requires --cert-path and --key-path), but the TLS stacks differ: rustls 0.21 with ring on the Rust side, statically linked OpenSSL in nginx. Average latency is higher for wut-server (45.00 ms vs 28.07 ms), while max latency is lower (279.57 ms vs 520.46 ms). nginx logged 95 connect and 17 read socket errors, so it served fewer than the 1000 connections. wut-server formats the client IP once per connection, while nginx evaluates $remote_addr per request. The benchmark harness is not in the repo. The repo has 2 commits and 0 stars.
